items.author: Our Correspondent
items.content:
The Asia-Pacific Telecommunity (APT) Symposium on Digital Transformation and the Universal Service Fund (USF) concluded in Islamabad with member states aligning on a collective roadmap to move universal service funds from traditional voice and basic coverage models towards agile, outcome-oriented frameworks supporting high-speed fibre, gigabit broadband and resilient digital ecosystems, according to a statement issued by the Ministry of Information Technology and Telecommunication (MoITT) on Thursday.
The three-day forum was co-hosted by the ministry and USF Pakistan, bringing together policymakers, regulators and telecom industry leaders from across the region. APT Secretary-General Masanori Kondo announced the conclusion, describing the symposium as a platform for practical exchanges, partnerships and advancing the Tokyo Statement 2025 commitments.
Speakers and experts engaged across 10 sessions on future-proofing universal service funds, shifting from simple infrastructure access to quality, capability and AI readiness. Discussions covered low-cost fibre backhaul, mobile broadband, satellite connectivity and green telecom infrastructure to scale deployment in underserved and rugged terrains.
The forum examined regulatory incentives, device subsidy programmes and financial mechanisms to improve affordability and sustainable financing, making connectivity accessible to low-income households, small enterprises and marginalised communities. Sessions covered targeted policy interventions, digital literacy programmes for women and girls and digital entrepreneurship support to close the gender digital divide.
Stakeholders also stressed empowering local content and ecosystems through culturally appropriate, language-specific digital services and e-government platforms to stimulate local economies and drive digital adoption.
Delegates also deliberated on harnessing emerging technologies, bridging persistent digital divides and driving equitable digital transformation across member states, reviewing regional digital progress under the Tokyo Statement 2025 and aligning regional strategies.

items.author: Arsalan Khattak
items.content:
Nora is preparing to introduce two electric vehicles, the NEO and Metro, in Pakistan, offering urban commuters modern features and a claimed driving range of up to 300 kilometers.
Both models fall into the L7 quadricycle category and share several key specifications, including battery capacity, motor power, maximum speed, and charging time.
The Nora NEO and Metro feature a 23.1 kWh lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery paired with a 4 kW motor. Both vehicles have a claimed range of 250 to 300 kilometers on a single charge and a top speed of 70 km/h.
The electric vehicles feature rear-wheel drive, a 72-volt electrical system, and a charging time of approximately six to eight hours. Each model can accommodate four passengers.
Nora NEO Features
The Nora NEO features a modern exterior design and a range of convenience and safety features. Its equipment includes a 9-inch HD touchscreen, keyless entry, push-button start, and a multifunction steering wheel.
The vehicle also comes with an electronic parking brake and disc brakes on all four wheels. The NEO has a wheelbase of 2,300 mm and ground clearance of 180 mm. It rides on 175/70 R13 tires.
Nora Metro Features
The Nora Metro offers a different design and equipment package, including touchscreen infotainment, keyless entry, push-button start, power windows, and a reversing camera.
It shares the NEO’s battery capacity, motor power, claimed driving range, and maximum speed. However, the Metro has a longer wheelbase of 2,360 mm and greater ground clearance of 210 mm. It also features larger 195/70 R14 tires.
Prices
The Nora NEO and Metro are reportedly priced below Rs. 3 million in Pakistan, although the company has yet to officially confirm their prices.

items.author: Press Release
items.content:
Copyright protected content copied from PhoneWorld website.
The Pakistan Telecommunication Authority (PTA) has advised mobile users on the importance of using appropriate network settings on their mobile phones and effectively utilising advanced technologies, including Voice over LTE (VoLTE), Wi-Fi Calling, and VoWiFi, to improve their calling and mobile internet experience.
According to PTA, in case of unclear voice quality during calls or delays in connecting 4G/LTE calls, consumers should check the network settings on their mobile phones and enable the 4G/LTE option if it is not already activated. Consumers should also ensure that both their mobile phone and SIM support 4G services.
Voice over LTE (VoLTE) is an important feature for improved calling, enabling voice calls over a 4G network. It can help improve voice quality and facilitate faster call connection. To benefit from this facility, the mobile phone, SIM, and relevant mobile operator must support VoLTE.
Similarly, Wi-Fi Calling and VoWiFi can be particularly useful in locations where mobile network signals are weak, such as inside homes or in basements. These facilities enable consumers to make calls over a Wi-Fi connection, provided that their mobile phone and mobile operator support VoWiFi. Consumers therefore need to enable the Wi-Fi Calling option in their mobile phone settings and connect their phone to a Wi-Fi network.
Consumers are advised to enable the Voice over LTE (VoLTE), Wi-Fi Calling, and VoWiFi options in their mobile phone settings. VoLTE requires the phone to support a 4G network, while VoWiFi provides the facility to make calls over Wi-Fi in areas with weak mobile network signals. The availability and use of these facilities are subject to compatibility between the mobile phone and the relevant mobile operator.
For further information and guidance regarding the availability, activation, and use of these facilities, consumers may contact their respective mobile phone operator.

items.summary:
Bahrain has introduced new employment rules allowing foreign workers to temporarily work for other employers for up to 90 days, giving expatriates more flexibility in taking up short-term jobs.
Previously, foreign workers were not allowed to work for companies other than their sponsoring employers. Under the new rules, they can work for another employer as long as they have a valid work permit throughout the temporary employment period.

items.title: Total Reserves Near $27 Billion

The country’s total liquid foreign reserves stood at $26.863 billion as of October 9, up by $65.9 million.
This includes $21.470 billion held by the SBP and $5.394 billion maintained by commercial banks.
Reserves with commercial banks are up by $50.1 million compared to a week earlier.
The current dollar reserves can cover imports for 3.04 months.

items.title: Pakistan condemns Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, calls for immediate halt at UN
items.summary:
Pakistan on Thursday strongly condemned continued Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, including its civilian and economic infrastructure, and called for an immediate halt to the strikes while reaffirming its unwavering support for the kingdom’s security, sovereignty and territorial integrity.
Speaking at a United Nations Security Council (UNSC) debate on the Middle East, Pakistan’s Acting Permanent Representative to the UN, Ambassador Usman Jadoon, expressed deep concern over the rapidly deteriorating situation in Yemen.
He said Pakistan backed the UN special envoy’s efforts to revive dialogue aimed at securing a comprehensive and lasting peace in Yemen.
Statement by Ambassador Usman Jadoon,
Acting Permanent Representative of Pakistan to the UN,
At the UN Security Council Open Debate on the Situation in the Middle East
(15 October 2026)

I thank Acting Special Coordinator – Mr. Ramiz Alakbarov for… pic.twitter.com/UJyj2sVlYY

items.author: Web Desk
items.content:
Pakistan on Thursday strongly condemned continued Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, including its civilian and economic infrastructure, and called for an immediate halt to the strikes while reaffirming its unwavering support for the kingdom’s security, sovereignty and territorial integrity.
Speaking at a United Nations Security Council (UNSC) debate on the Middle East, Pakistan’s Acting Permanent Representative to the UN, Ambassador Usman Jadoon, expressed deep concern over the rapidly deteriorating situation in Yemen.
He said Pakistan backed the UN special envoy’s efforts to revive dialogue aimed at securing a comprehensive and lasting peace in Yemen.
Statement by Ambassador Usman Jadoon,
Acting Permanent Representative of Pakistan to the UN,
At the UN Security Council Open Debate on the Situation in the Middle East
(15 October 2026)
***********
Madam President,
I thank Acting Special Coordinator – Mr. Ramiz Alakbarov for… pic.twitter.com/UJyj2sVlYY
— Permanent Mission of Pakistan to the UN (@PakistanUN_NY) October 15, 2026
The ambassador strongly condemned continued Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, including its civilian and economic infrastructure, and called for an immediate halt to the strikes.
“We reiterate our unwavering support for the security, sovereignty and territorial integrity of the brotherly Kingdom, and reaffirm its right to self-defence under international law against any external attacks,” he said.
The condemnation comes amid an escalation in Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia. The Saudi-led coalition said the Houthis had launched 20 attacks on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh this month, killing 17 people and injuring 333 others. Abha airport in southwestern Saudi Arabia was also targeted amid renewed hostilities.
Yemen’s civil war reignited in July after a UN-brokered truce collapsed, months into a wider Middle East war. Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government have since claimed hundreds of strikes on Houthi-held territory. The Houthis say the attacks have killed civilians, including women and children. Reuters could not independently verify those claims.
The Saudis entered the Yemen war in 2015 at the head of an Arab coalition to try to force the Houthis out of ‌the Yemeni capital ⁠Sanaa. The war became a bloody stalemate, with hundreds of thousands of Yemenis killed by fighting and famine.
A 2022 ceasefire reached by the Saudis and the Houthis unravelled this summer, culminating in a lightning Houthi advance that took the Red Sea chokepoint of Bab el-Mandeb from Saudi-backed government forces.
Jadoon said that Pakistan remains committed to advancing dialogue and diplomacy in the region to help de-escalate tensions, resolve differences and promote lasting peace and stability in the region.
Turning to the Palestinian issue, the ambassador said the two-state solution remained the internationally agreed framework and an indispensable foundation for a just and lasting peace.
“This international commitment to the two-State solution must be accompanied by concrete measures to preserve the territorial integrity and viability of the State of Palestine,” he said, while expressing support for the full and good-faith implementation of relevant UN resolutions and the New York Declaration.
Read: Saudi Arabia accuses Iran of encouraging Houthis as attacks intensify
Expressing concern over Israeli actions in Gaza and the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem, he said settlement expansion, particularly the E1 project, threatened to sever Palestinian territorial contiguity.
“Settler violence, demolitions, land seizures and forced displacement are entrenching annexation and dismantling the foundations of peace,” he said.
He called for an end to all settlement activities in accordance with relevant UN resolutions, a halt to settler violence and accountability for those responsible.
E1, which stands for “East 1”, is an area east of Jerusalem between East Jerusalem and the large Israeli settlement of Ma’ale Adumim. Experts have warned that the project could divide land the Palestinians hope will form part of an independent state, threatening the possibility of a two-state solution.
Jadoon also strongly condemned what he described as provocative and illegal incursions into Al-Aqsa Mosque/Al-Haram Al-Sharif and called for respect for the historical and legal status quo of the holy sites.
He said continued ceasefire violations, the killing of Palestinians and restrictions on humanitarian access in Gaza remained a matter of grave concern.
The approaching winter threatened to worsen the suffering of families living amid widespread destruction without adequate shelter or essential services, he added.
Also Read: UK, France and Canada sanction Israeli West Bank settlements, in support for two-state solution
“The ceasefire must be fully upheld, humanitarian assistance delivered unhindered and at scale, and recovery and reconstruction advanced without delay,” he said, stressing that the indispensable work of the United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees (UNRWA) must be supported.
Pakistan rejected forced displacement and any attempt to fragment Gaza and the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, which, he said, constituted a single territorial unit.
The ambassador also called for the release of withheld Palestinian revenues to enable the Palestinian Authority to fulfil its responsibilities.
He said collective efforts must focus on a credible, time-bound and irreversible political process to end the Israeli occupation and establish an independent, sovereign, contiguous and viable State of Palestine on pre-1967 borders, with Al-Quds Al-Sharif as its capital.
“This remains the only credible foundation for a just and lasting resolution of the Palestinian question,” he said.
“So long as the occupation continues and the Palestinian people’s legitimate yearning for self-determination goes unfulfilled, lasting peace in the Middle East will remain out of reach,” he said, reaffirming Pakistan’s unwavering support for the Palestinian people.
On Lebanon, Jadoon said full implementation of UN Security Council Resolution, respect for the cessation of hostilities and Israel’s withdrawal from occupied territory remained essential.
He said the Lebanese government’s call for the continuation of the United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon (UNIFIL) and a sustained UN presence in the country merited serious and favourable consideration by the Security Council.
On Syria, Pakistan welcomed the government’s efforts to foster internal stability and put the country on a positive trajectory.
“We reaffirm support for Syria’s sovereignty, unity and territorial integrity,” he said, adding that the 1974 Disengagement Agreement and Security Council resolutions 338 and 497 must be fully respected.

items.title: Iran’s precision strikes picked apart Gulf infrastructure, blunting US war plans
items.summary:
Iran and its proxies have carried out dozens of pinpoint strikes on infrastructure in the Gulf since the start of the war, systematically disabling critical equipment and causing cascading failures and economic damage region-wide in a deft campaign that helps explain how the Islamic Republic has held its own against the more powerful US military.
Iran and the allies it arms went after vital oil-routing systems at Fujairah in the United Arab Emirates, the main port outside the Strait of Hormuz, disabling operations for weeks. They hit Qatar’s Ras Laffan liquefied natural gas facility, striking two of the “cold boxes” that house cooling equipment that liquefies gas. They targeted airports across at least four countries, this month striking one in Saudi Arabia four days in a single week. And they incinerated a pumping station and damaged two others along a key Saudi pipeline, cutting off another main bypass around Iran’s blockade of Hormuz.

items.author: Reuters
items.content:
Iran and its proxies have carried out dozens of pinpoint strikes on infrastructure in the Gulf since the start of the war, systematically disabling critical equipment and causing cascading failures and economic damage region-wide in a deft campaign that helps explain how the Islamic Republic has held its own against the more powerful US military.
Iran and the allies it arms went after vital oil-routing systems at Fujairah in the United Arab Emirates, the main port outside the Strait of Hormuz, disabling operations for weeks. They hit Qatar’s Ras Laffan liquefied natural gas facility, striking two of the “cold boxes” that house cooling equipment that liquefies gas. They targeted airports across at least four countries, this month striking one in Saudi Arabia four days in a single week. And they incinerated a pumping station and damaged two others along a key Saudi pipeline, cutting off another main bypass around Iran’s blockade of Hormuz.
Attacks like these on Gulf infrastructure have been announced without detail during the war by governments in the region and other players. But a Reuters investigation reveals how precise these strikes have been, the resulting failure of critical equipment at key facilities, and the extent of the damage – both physical and economic.
Read: Iran widens retaliation after fresh US strikes
Iran has targeted infrastructure across the Gulf Arab countries – in Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Iraq, Qatar, Kuwait, Oman and Bahrain. In all, the Islamic Republic has launched at least 135 drone and missile attacks on at least 84 infrastructure sites in the Gulf since the US and Israel launched a bombing campaign against Iran on February 28, Reuters found.
The attacks have spread fear across the Gulf, sent oil prices soaring and helped Iran blunt months of American military pressure. Coupled with the Islamic Republic’s blockade on the Strait of Hormuz, the ability to launch precision attacks creates an enduring threat to its Gulf Arab neighbours and gives Iran huge sway over the global economy and leverage in its peace negotiations with the US.
Some targets are hidden beneath rooftops and sunshades, invisible from space. Others span just a few meters. Many have purposes not immediately obvious to anyone without expertise in fields like oil refining, nuclear technology or smelting.
Some targets are hidden beneath rooftops and sun shades, invisible from space. Others span just a few meters. Many have purposes not immediately obvious to anyone without expertise in fields like oil refining, nuclear technology or smelting 5/6 pic.twitter.com/evyOzp8iRz
— Reuters Investigates (@specialreports) October 15, 2026
Without visiting the sites, Reuters could not always determine how successful Gulf air defences were or the full extent of the damage. But time and again, Reuters found, the Iranian strikes were precise, and the equipment struck was vital.
Without visiting the sites, Reuters could not always determine how successful Gulf air defenses were or the extent of the damage. But time and again, Reuters found, the Iranian strikes were precise and the equipment struck was vital 6/6 https://t.co/YOOg9fmWTS
— Reuters Investigates (@specialreports) October 15, 2026
Ryan Stevens, a former US Marine Corps special operations airstrike coordinator who reviewed Reuters’ findings, said Iran’s strikes showed “precision, targeting expertise, and patience.”
Read More: Iran defiant as strikes hit Gulf transport, energy hubs
The US, which has imposed a blockade on Iranian oil, repeatedly downplays Iran’s capacity for destruction. Arab Gulf countries often fail to acknowledge major damage and frequently blame harm to their facilities on falling debris from successful interceptions of Iranian munitions.
“US Central Command has been crystal clear in communicating the threats posed by Iran regionally and globally,” said US Navy Captain Tim Hawkins, a CENTCOM spokesman. He said the US has repeatedly condemned Iran “for indiscriminately targeting more than a dozen neighbouring countries and hundreds of commercial ships as well as risking millions of innocent lives over the past seven months.”
Iran’s mission to the United Nations in Geneva, which is responsible for international media queries, did not respond to a detailed request for comment.
The success of Iran’s systematic infrastructure assault is another example of how the Islamic Republic has withstood years of international economic sanctions and now months of war with the US and Israel. In previous reports, Reuters has shown how Iran exploits crypto exchanges and illegal gambling networks to tap illicit revenues and circumvent sanctions, how the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps consolidated control of Hormuz, and how the war has ushered in a new era of repression.
Some places suffered periods of near-daily bombardment and face billions of dollars in repairs and lost revenue. Others, like one of the world’s largest aluminium smelters in Abu Dhabi, were devastated in a single day. Some of the attacks were carried out by the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen and the Iraqi Shiite militias controlled from Tehran.
Among those hit the most was the Fujairah port, whose location just south of Hormuz allowed the UAE to bypass Iran’s blockade. The port served as a life raft for global trade by easing the most severe disruption to oil supplies in decades.
In all, Reuters found that Iranian drones and missiles have struck Fujairah at least 19 times since the war began on February 28, crippling critical pieces of its operations.
“We were watching it come in and watching the helicopters blast the drones out of the sky,” said a foreign businessman who watched a wave of attacks on Fujairah in mid-March from a nearby road. His description of the scene was supported by a Reuters review of photos of the attack. “They were sending swarms of drones and one or two got through.”
Reuters interviewed 36 people familiar with the infrastructure attacks, compiled images and videos of the strikes, and analysed official statements and data from radar, optical and weather satellites for evidence of the damage and timing of attacks. Reporters presented the resulting findings before publication to facility operators and national governments hit by the attacks.
In at least 34 official statements following strikes, governments emphasised that any damage was caused by falling debris from successful interceptions. Gulf military air defences are located near some of the most sensitive sites, including what Janes, the defence intelligence company, confirmed as American-made Patriot missile defences visible by satellite that were positioned about 3 kilometres north of Fujairah.
“History has shown that instability in the Middle East often extends beyond the region’s borders, with far-reaching repercussions,” the UAE government said in response to detailed questions about the Reuters findings. “In this regard, renewed efforts to de-escalate tensions are essential to prevent the potential escalation into a broader conflict.”
Gulf states are suppressing information about the toll. It is illegal in the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, Qatar, Kuwait and Saudi Arabia to take or distribute certain photos or video of the aftermath of strikes. The countries also routinely cite laws against the spread of rumours and misinformation when restricting reporting about strikes. Reuters and other international media have published verified visual evidence of strikes during the war.
Also Read: Houthis hit Aramco HQ, vow more attacks
“Gulf states now treat damage assessments as if they were state secrets,” said Matthew Reed, president of the oil consultancy firm Foreign Reports. The US and Israel have also kept damage to US bases and Israeli sites under wraps, but many details have emerged through reports by governments and media, including Reuters.
Bahrain’s government, the only Gulf state to respond to questions about the restrictions, said they were in place “to protect public safety, safeguard the integrity of investigations, and prevent such material being used to assess or plan further attacks.”
Iran’s attacks on the Gulf’s economic infrastructure have come in tandem with strikes on American military assets in the region. The US Defence Department’s inspector general told Congress Iran hit hundreds of structures on US bases, in addition to dozens of aircraft.
To gauge the extent of the infrastructure damage and what specifically was hit, Reuters shared its findings and imagery with 11 insiders from the industries of the sites struck, ex-Marine Stevens, another former American service member who now works in security in the region, and a former US security official with expertise in counter-terrorism and satellite analysis.
All 14 said it was highly improbable that damage to essential equipment at dozens of major infrastructure sites was caused primarily by debris falling haphazardly from the sky. Many of them cited visual evidence of explosive detonations, rather than just the impact of a chunk of metal, and pointed to the operational importance of the targets themselves.
Gulf officials have publicly called for a peace deal that addresses Iran’s drone and missile programs, fearing they will threaten the region far into the future. Saudi Arabia’s crown prince directly asked US President Donald Trump for military assistance after a series of attacks in early September by Yemen’s Houthis and was rebuffed, Reuters has reported.
A September 10 attack on the Saudi East-West Pipeline – another main bypass around Hormuz – suspended the flow of crude there, threatening up to 4% of the global oil supply. Saudi Arabia said that the attack came from militias in Iraq, which are armed and backed by Iran. Even more disruptive were Iran’s strikes on Qatar’s Ras Laffan LNG plants, which threatened nearly 20% of the world’s liquefied natural gas flows.
In an interview with Reuters in March, QatarEnergy chief Saad al-Kaabi estimated full repairs to the critical LNG cold boxes destroyed in two Iranian strikes would take three to five years.
The Ras Laffan LNG plant was one of at least four infrastructure sites across the Gulf that will take about a year or more for full restoration. Also among them are Qatar's Pearl gas-to-liquids refinery, the UAE’s Habshan Gas Complex, and the Emirates Global Aluminium Al Taweelah smelter, according to company statements and an assessment by IIR Energy, an intelligence and analytics firm.
“Every single target was civilian: Airports, terminals, refineries, gas processing plants, residential areas, shopping malls, and most recently, the Barakah nuclear power plant,” Sultan Al Jaber, the chief executive officer of the Abu Dhabi National Oil Company, known as ADNOC, said in a May interview with the Atlantic Council.
“They are targeting our infrastructure,” said Al Jaber, who is also the UAE minister of industry and advanced technology. “But what they're really targeting is our way of life.”
The governments of Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait and Iraq did not respond to requests for comment, nor did ADNOC.
Originally envisioned as an economic development project, Fujairah port started full operations in 1983.
That same year, a secret US Central Intelligence Agency assessment found Iran was likely to respond to perceived threats with attacks on energy infrastructure in Kuwait, Bahrain, Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the UAE. That assessment, released in 2019, found that “even a few attacks against well-chosen targets could do considerable damage to Gulf oil facilities.”
Iran struck the UAE more than any of its other Gulf neighbours during the first two months of the war, and Fujairah was the most targeted site in the country, the Reuters examination found. For the first three months of the war, the port was either under attack or making repairs.
The first Fujairah attack was announced on March 3. Two days later, the flaming tanks could still be seen from space. Two oil storage firms suspended operations.
The next attack, announced on March 9, did more than destroy fuel. Satellite imagery showed this strike took out the first matrix manifold, a transfer system of 62 pipelines that feeds crude oil and finished petroleum products from oil terminals to shipping berths.
Emirati officials blamed the damage from the first two attacks on falling debris.
Ramanan Krishnamoorti, a petroleum engineering professor at the University of Houston who reviewed the Reuters findings, said it stretched credibility that debris could simply have tumbled onto the matrix manifold. “This is a wound to the brain and heart.”
More strikes came on March 14, 16 and 17, beginning hours after the US attacked military targets at Iran's Kharg Island oil export terminal. One of these strikes damaged Fujairah’s other matrix manifold, according to a Reuters analysis of satellite imagery, four experts who reviewed the imagery, and a person familiar with the damage.
The damage to the second manifold has not been reported previously. It explains why oil loading at Fujairah fell to 440,000 barrels per day in the week beginning March 16, less than half of the daily average in 2025, according to export data from analytics firm Kpler.
The war pushed Brent oil futures prices near or above $120 a barrel in March, April and May, up from around $70 per barrel in February. Brent closed yesterday at $106.
Thomas Warrick, former deputy assistant secretary for counter-terrorism policy at the US Department of Homeland Security, said Iran has plenty of people “who understand the oil industry and people who know how to build and aim missiles.”
Before the war, Iran had the largest stockpile of ballistic missiles in the Middle East, including cluster munitions that are difficult for air defences to block, according to the US government. In addition, Iran has a thriving drone industry; pre-war it was capable of producing around 10,000 a month, with the Shahed as the flagship explosive aircraft.
In at least six government statements since the conflict began on February 28, Emirati authorities blamed the damage on debris from intercepted Iranian drones or missiles. No statement indicated major damage.
“American forces have and continue to stand with regional partners in defending against Iranian threats, intercepting thousands of attack drones and missiles with an integrated shield that has saved countless lives,” said Hawkins, the CENTCOM spokesman.
Repairs proceeded after the mid-March strikes, with satellite imagery showing cranes at damaged sites. At the end of March, Fujairah's exports hit a weekly record of 3.2 million barrels per day, according to Kpler, which began tracking data at the port in 2013.
But Iran kept attacking. An April 6 strike hit a structure housing critical oil-routing equipment for ADNOC, according to a Reuters analysis of satellite imagery, which was confirmed by Warrick and a person familiar with Fujairah’s layout.
Then, on May 4, the Iranians hit Fujairah again with a drone, smashing a collection of pipes leading to the first matrix manifold that was damaged in March. The primary bypass route for UAE crude around the Strait of Hormuz was again in flames. But, more critically, Fujairah’s exports of refined petroleum essentially stopped for a month. Only a single ship went out from the day of the attack until June 1, according to Kpler data.
Refined petroleum exports would not recover until September.
The Emirates acknowledged the May 4 Iranian drone strike. The Iranians hit at least one other target in the UAE, the Barakah Nuclear Power Plant, on May 17.
Then, in June, the UAE agreed to unlock at least $10 billion in Iranian funds that had been frozen in the Emirati banking system, four sources with knowledge of the arrangement told Reuters at the time. They said $3 billion was released. In return, according to two of those sources, Iran agreed to stop attacking ⁠the UAE.
The UAE foreign ministry denied any agreement. In a statement, it said that “ no frozen Iranian funds have been released, transferred or facilitated through the UAE.”
A senior Iranian official in August confirmed the transfer of funds but told Reuters the transaction had nothing to do with attacks on the UAE. It was due, he said, “to the correction of the UAE’s behaviour.”
There have been no reports of strikes on UAE infrastructure since May 17.
In September, as Iran bombed ADNOC tankers at sea, Fujairah hit a monthly record of 2.62 million barrels per day for all its exports. Refined fuel and crude were flowing like never before.
Iran’s Intelligence
US officials believe Iran may have received intelligence from Russia and China. In addition, Iran relies upon networks of informants with access to sensitive sites to pass along photos and location information, according to three officials familiar with the issue – one from Iran and two in the Gulf.
Asked about intelligence sharing, China’s Foreign Ministry said it “consistently and strictly fulfilled its international obligations.” Russia did not respond to a request for comment.
The three officials said Iran had information including the Barakah Nuclear Energy Plant’s floor plan and the location of an electrical substation that was struck at the plant.
The UAE said the drone that struck the nuclear plant on May 17 was one of three sent “by armed factions in Iraq.” The strike on the substation forced one of its four reactors onto emergency diesel generators, according to the International Atomic Energy Agency.
In imagery captured June 16, the earliest clear view Reuters could obtain, there was damage in two places on the roof of a building housing the controls for the plant’s electricity lines – about 130 meters from one of the reactors.
The attack, IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi said, demonstrated a detailed level of knowledge about the plant.
"This means whoever was or is behind this knew exactly what they were doing,” Grossi said during a June 2 visit to the UAE.
Emirates Nuclear Energy Corporation, which operates the plant, did not dispute the analysis of the damage. The IAEA did not respond to a request for comment.
“The plant's safety systems and established procedures responded as designed, nuclear safety was maintained, there were no injuries or radioactive releases, radiation levels remained within normal ranges, and there was no risk to the public or the environment,” ENEC said in a statement to Reuters.
For Kuwait, as with the UAE, having a US military presence and advanced American weaponry weren’t enough to stop the attacks.
Iran systematically hit Kuwait’s energy export infrastructure and its airport almost as soon as the war began. Iranian strikes homed in on a sprawling industrial area in Ahmadi Governorate, about 50 kilometres south of Kuwait City. The zone encompasses the Mina Al-Ahmadi and Mina Abdulla refineries, Shuaiba Port and the Shuaiba power and desalination plant.
The Kuwait Port Authority suspended operations for 24 hours on the first day of the war after debris fell near Shuaiba Port. Within three weeks, the neighbouring Mina Al-Ahmadi and Mina Abdulla refineries were also struck.
In April, Kuwait didn’t export a single barrel of crude oil, a first since 1991, according to tanker-monitoring firm TankerTrackers.
By the end of July, Iranian projectiles had damaged at least 13 structures across the vast Shuaiba industrial area, satellite imagery shows.
The attacks went well beyond refineries, oil fields and other energy facilities.
Iranian munitions hit airports in Bahrain, Kuwait and especially the UAE and Saudi Arabia. The deadliest attack, blamed on Houthis, killed 12 people at Saudi Arabia’s King Khalid International Airport on Saturday.
Kuwait’s airport was struck eight times. One hit came two days after Kuwait had reopened a major terminal upon completing repairs from a prior attack.
Iran struck advanced digital infrastructure such as Amazon data centres in the UAE and in Bahrain, where service remained down six months later because the damaged equipment couldn’t be fixed. Amazon declined to comment directly about the Reuters findings but pointed to a public statement from September 15 saying the company continued “to work on recovering regional resources.”
And Iran cut off operations for all 1,262 smelting cells at the Emirates Global Aluminium Al Taweelah smelter. It took two months until the first cell could be restarted. By late August, only a quarter of them had been brought online, the company said. Production is not expected to return to normal until 2027, according to the company.
The Iranian attack on the smelter hit the facility’s power plant and one of its three smelting cell lines, arrays of hundreds of pots that produce molten aluminium, said Frank Davis, who worked in the aluminium industry for 42 years at nine smelters around the world and has visited the EGA plant. Davis reviewed satellite images obtained by Reuters. A strike on one cell line would not affect the two others, he said. But the strike on the power plant froze operations entirely, he said.
“What a shame, too,” Davis said. “It is an extraordinary facility."
Emirates Global Aluminium did not respond to a request for comment.
The global price of aluminium climbed 5% to a four-year high after the attacks on the UAE smelter and a less-destructive hit the same weekend on a smelter in Bahrain.
“The deliberate targeting by Iran of facilities that communities rely on for power, water, travel and their livelihoods is a clear violation of international law,” Bahrain’s government statement said. “The safety of everyone who lives in and visits Bahrain remains our priority. Where incidents have occurred, the authorities have acted swiftly to protect lives and contain damage.”
Most dramatically, Iran went after the power and water supply in Kuwait.
It was Trump who first publicly threatened the water supply of Iran in March. But it was the Iranians who turned that threat into a reality for its neighbours, said Michael Christopher Low, director of the Middle East Centre at the University of Utah.
The threat was especially acute for Kuwait, a desert country that draws 90% of its drinking water from desalination plants. These facilities are often connected to coastal power plants because filtering the water takes massive amounts of heat and electricity.
Reuters found Iran hit at least four of Kuwait’s eight dual power-and-desalination plants from March 2 through July 20. Some were struck repeatedly. During one four-day period in July, Iran attacked what the government described as “several” desalination plants, including one at least twice in that brief period.
Low said Kuwait does not have the natural water resources to survive without its desalination plants. “If you were to attack enough of their capacity, we’re talking about running out of water in days or weeks,” he said.
Kuwait’s government conducted a campaign asking citizens to conserve electricity and water in “the spirit of shared responsibility.”
Red Sea Front
Oil and gas exports function as a system – from wells that extract, to pipelines that transport across hundreds of kilometres, to refineries that process, to ports where ships can load cargo bound for global markets.
In Saudi Arabia, the Gulf’s largest petrostate, this web offers an almost inexhaustible number of targets – a weakness that has been flagged repeatedly over decades, including in the 1983 CIA report. The kingdom produces around 10% of the world’s crude oil, as well as natural gas and petrochemicals.
Nearly all of Saudi Arabia’s oil exports flow through two main ports. The largest share typically flows through its Ras Tanura port on the Gulf. But the kingdom can also export oil from the large King Fahd Industrial Port in Yanbu, the largest on the Red Sea coast.
When the war started, Yanbu and the East-West Pipeline leading to it became a critical outlet for Saudi oil to avoid Hormuz. Most ships that sail from the Red Sea port must instead pass Houthi-controlled territory in Yemen and the narrow Bab al-Mandeb Strait.
In March and April, more than 1,000 kilometres from the Iranian border, drones hit Yanbu at least twice, according to two industry sources familiar with the operations.
The Iranians hit Saudi Aramco Mobil Refinery Limited's Yanbu Refinery with a drone on March 19, limiting production to about 70% of capacity until April 9, said Hillary Stevenson, vice president of energy intelligence at IIR Energy. Scorch marks appeared in a satellite image of Yanbu from around that date, but Reuters could not determine what precisely was hit at the refinery.
Attacks on the Red Sea then went quiet as an initial ceasefire between the US and Iran took hold in early April.
But on July 13, after the ceasefire agreement fell apart, commanders from Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps flew to Yemen bearing missile and drone equipment for the Houthis, Reuters reported.
The next day, Trump promised strikes against Iranian infrastructure. A Reuters visual analysis shows that from July 16 to 18, US forces hit at least three bridges and a tunnel along the main roads leading to the southern Iranian port of Bandar Abbas, headquarters of Iran’s navy along the Strait of Hormuz.
The Houthis attacked Saudi Arabia in retaliation. The Saudis’ Red Sea petroleum operations were heavily targeted. Iran has said it is not responsible for the actions of the Houthis, who claimed responsibility for the strikes. The Houthi spokesman did not respond to a request for comment about the attacks.
The Jazan refinery, less than 100 kilometres from Yemen’s border, was hit at least four times from July 25 through September 7, Reuters found. The first of those attacks damaged the refinery’s tank farm and the adjacent Integrated Gasification Combined Cycle complex, which transforms oil into the gas that powers the refinery, said Stevenson of IIR Energy.
Jazan’s refining volumes dropped to zero after the attacks, according to Stevenson and two people familiar with Aramco operations. Kpler said only one ship has been loaded at the refinery since July 24.
Since the start of the war, Iranian-linked strikes have damaged five of Saudi’s nine biggest refineries and three of its major oil processing hubs, including what Aramco describes as the world’s largest, Reuters found.
Saudi daily oil production dropped below 7 million barrels for most of the first six months of the war, down from over 10 million barrels pre-war. That translates into a loss of over $50 billion at current prices.
Major Western energy firms, including ExxonMobil and Shell, operate sites as joint ventures and have reported tens of millions of dollars in losses all told because of the strikes. Aramco, ExxonMobil and Shell did not respond to requests for comment.
On September 7, Iran’s parliament speaker made the intent of the attacks explicit.
“It’s simple: the oil and gas production chain here is sprawling, accessible, and exposed,” the speaker, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, wrote in a post on X. “American oil and gas companies across these waters and facilities share that exposure.”
Three days later, an aerial attack hit three pumping stations in the Saudi desert, turning one of them into a blackened husk and halting the flow of crude along the East-West Pipeline to Yanbu. Oil again popped above $100 a barrel.
Another alternative to the Strait of Hormuz was closed.

items.content: Banks that have announced quarterly earnings so far showed double digit net profit growth in the July-September quarter, riding on core income even as treasury earnings remained subdued due to mark to market losses given the hardening of bond yields.The state-owned Indian Bank reported a 14.7% year-on-year rise in second quarter at Rs 3462 crore against Rs Rs 3018 crore in the year ago period. Its operating profitstood 46.68% higher at 7090 crore against Rs 4837 crore in the same period last year. It has increased its provisions to Rs 2222 crore from Rs 739 crore, despite asset quality improvement, as it looks to build a buffer ahead of the transition to the credit loss framework, which will be implemented from April 1, 2027. It set aside Rs 1500 crore this quarter, taking the total buffer to Rs 2500 crore while the expected impact would be Rs 3500 crore, managing director Binod Kumar said. The bank's gross non-performing assets ratio improved to 1.16% at the end of September from 2.6% a year prior. Indian Bank booked Rs 123 crore mark to market losses but its treasury income stood higher on account of the one-off gain from the divestment in NSE.134979783UCO Bank reported a 27% year-on-year increase in net profit at Rs 786 crore in the quarter ended September 2026 against Rs 620 crore a year ago led by strong loan growth and an improvement in net interest margin. Total advances increased 25% to Rs 2.87 lakh crore led by a 27% growth in advances to the retail, agriculture and MSME sectors. Retail was the fastest growing segment with a growth of 30%. Net interest margins improved 10 basis points year on year to 3% during the quarter. Net interest income increased 14% year on year at Rs 2886 crore supporting profits. Its gross NPA declined 60 basis points year on year to 1.96%. The bank garnered $635 million through FCNR (B) deposits, CEO Rajendra Kumar Saboo said. The bank's treasury earnings for the second quarter came 72% lower at Rs 29 crore.Private sector South Indian Bank posted a 21% rise in second quarter net profit at Rs 426 crore as compared with Rs 351 crore in the year ago period. Its operating profit stood 37% higher at Rs 732 crore against Rs 536 crore. The bank's treasury and forex earnings fell 38% at Rs 80 crore in the quarter against Rs 129 crore in the year ago period, capping the overall earnings growth. It gross advances grew 19% year-on-year to Rs 1.10 lakh crore at the end of September with gold loan portfolio expanding 41% to to Rs 26,603 crore. The bank's asset quality improved with gross non-performing assets ratio declining to 1.24% at the end of September from Rs 2.93% a year prior.Karur Vysya Bank reported a 37% year-on-year growth in net profit at Rs 788 crore in the quarter ended September 2026 from Rs 574 crore a year ago due to strong loan growth while asset quality remained stable. Total advances increased 20% to Rs 1. 11 lakh crore. Net interest income increased by 18% to Rs 1,497 crore from Rs 1,261 crore. Net interest margin at 4.34% was higher than the 4.24% reported for the corresponding quarter of the previous year. The cost of deposits has decreased by 11 basis points to 5.49%. Gross non-performing assets (GNPA) decreased by 7 bps to 0.69% of gross advances as on September 30, 2026 from 0.76% as on September 30, 2025.

items.author: Web Desk
items.content:
The Federal Board of Revenue (FBR) on Thursday extended the deadline for filing income tax returns for Tax Year 2026 by another 16 days to Oct 31.
“In exercise of the powers conferred under Section 214A of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001, the Federal Board of Revenue is pleased to further extend the date of filing of Income Tax Returns for Tax Year 2026 up to 31st October, 2026,” the FBR said in a post on X.
The extension applies to people who were required to file their returns by Sept 30 and whose deadline had earlier been extended to Oct 15 through a circular issued on Sept 30.
Read: FBR extends income tax returns filing deadline to Oct 15
The FBR said the latest extension had been granted in view of requests received from various trade bodies and tax bar associations.
This is the second extension announced by the revenue authority in a month. On Oct 1, the FBR had extended the deadline for filing income tax returns for Tax Year 2026 from Sept 30 to Oct 15.
The FBR has been under pressure to broaden Pakistan's narrow tax base and meet ambitious revenue targets set under an agreement with the International Monetary Fund, making digitisation and taxpayer facilitation central to its stated reform agenda in recent years.
For the current fiscal year, the government and the International Monetary Fund (IMF) have agreed on the annual tax target of Rs15.263 trillion. This requires a 17.4% increase over last year's receipts. Unlike in the past, the IMF has made it binding to meet tax targets and the approval of its sixth loan tranche hinges on achieving the H1 target.
Provinces have promised to give a little over Rs1 trillion in grants to the federal government for defence and water projects, subject to the condition that the FBR collects Rs15.263 trillion in revenues. The government has also taken revenue and enforcement measures of over Rs1 trillion in the budget to enable the FBR to reach the target.
According to provisional statistics, the tax authority got over Rs685 billion in income tax, falling short of the two-month target by a wide margin of Rs74 billion. The income tax collection was also Rs29 billion less than the last fiscal year, marking negative growth of 4%.
Also Read: Aurangzeb says Pakistan’s fiscal deficit falls to 22-year low
For the second consecutive month, the sales tax collection remained higher than the target. The FBR received Rs719 billion worth of sales tax, exceeding the target by Rs85 billion. The sales tax collection was also 14%, or Rs86 billion, higher than last year.
Of the total, Rs496 billion, or 69%, of sales tax was generated at the import stage. In the budget, the government has changed the law in order to collect sales tax at market prices of goods, instead of factory-gate prices, for numerous items. This has reduced chances of tax evasion but has broken the value-added chain.
The collection of federal excise duty stood at Rs118 billion, which was almost equal to the target and Rs3 billion higher than the last year. Customs duty collection hit Rs198 billion, which was slightly lower than the target and equal to the previous year's receipts.

items.summary:

B2B manufacturing company Zetwerk’s IPO received muted response on day one as it was subscribed just 23%. The issue received bids for 4.17 Cr shares against 18.51 Cr shares on offer.
The offer saw the highest subscription from qualified institutional buyers (QIBs) who placed 2.96 Cr shares against their quota of 9.89 Cr shares, or 30% subscription.
Retail individual investors bid for 74.32 Lakh shares out of the 3.42 Cr shares reserved for them, translating to a 22% subscription of their quota.
Non-institutional investors (NIIs) placed bids for 44.08 Lakh shares, or just 9% of their quota of 5.13 Cr shares.

B2B manufacturing company Zetwerk’s ₹5,012.3 Cr IPO got off to a rather slow start today, receiving a mere 8% subscription as of 14:00 IST. Investors have placed bids for 1.50 Cr shares against 18.51 Cr shares on offer, as per BSE data.
Qualified institutional buyers (QIBs) have been the most bullish on the public float till now, placing the highest number of bids for 75.67 Lakh shares. However, this translated to a mere 8% subscription of their quota of 9.89 Cr shares.
Retail individual investors followed closely as they bid for 51.79 Lakh against 3.42 Cr shares reserved for them, translating to a 15% subscription of their quota.
Non-institutional investors (NIIs) subscribed to just 4% of their earmarked portion, bidding for 21.55 Lakh out of 5.13 Cr shares allocated to them.
Meanwhile, employees of the manufacturing company placed bids for 1.34 Lakh shares against the 7 Lakh shares reserved for them, subscribing to their quota by 19%.
Zetwerk’s IPO closes on October 19. The company set a price band of ₹143-₹151 per share for its IPO, indicating a valuation of around ₹25,583 Cr at the upper end.
The issue comprises a fresh issue of ₹2,830 Cr and an offer for share component of up to 14.45 Cr shares, worth ₹2,182.3 Cr at the upper end, as per its RHP.
Ahead of opening the issue, Zetwerk raised ₹2,251.2 Cr from anchor investors yesterday. Domestic mutual funds including SBI Mutual Fund and ICICI Prudential Mutual Fund accounted for around 46% of the anchor book, while global institutional investors like Goldman Sachs, BlackRock, and ADIA also picked up stake.
Founded in 2018 by Amrit Acharya, Srinath Ramakkrushnan, Vishal Chaudhary, Zetwerk operates a full-stack manufacturing platform serving businesses across industrial and consumer goods categories.
It combines capacity from third-party suppliers and its own facilities to manage manufacturing orders across sectors including renewable energy, consumer electronics, aerospace, defence, oil and gas, and industrial automation.
The company has raised over $900 Mn in funding to date from investors like Peak XV Partners, Lightspeed Venture Partners, Accel India, Greenoaks Capital Partners, and D1 Capital Partners.
On the financial front, Zetwerk posted a consolidated net loss of ₹733 Cr in Q1 FY27 against operating revenue of ₹4,117.9 Cr.

items.author: Reuters
items.content:
A failure ​by the United States and Iran to agree within weeks on a UN-backed plan for moving fertiliser through the Strait of Hormuz could cause a ‌food security crisis in parts of Asia and Africa, an official overseeing the proposed scheme said on Wednesday.
The United Nations set up a task force in March to facilitate passage of fertilisers through the strait. It has yet to implement the mechanism it drew up, but United Nations Under-Secretary-General Jorge Moreira da Silva said this could be activated within seven to 10 days of an agreement between Washington and Tehran.
Read: Hunger lurks as Hormuz standoff blocks fertiliser
"It's absolutely crucial to ​get the deal in the next few weeks. Otherwise, we will miss the planting season," he said in an interview in Bangkok, on the sidelines of ​the International Monetary Fund and World Bank annual meetings.
The chokepoint at the Strait of Hormuz is driving a global energy, fertilizers and food security crisis that could have dire consequences for millions of people around the world.
“It’s absolutely crucial to get the deal in the next few weeks. Otherwise, we will miss the planting…
— Jorge Moreira da Silva (@UNOPS_Chief) October 14, 2026
In response to questions from Reuters, a US State Department spokesman said the US military ⁠has assisted thousands of commercial vessels with transiting the strait.
"The United States will continue to take decisive action against Iran's attempts to disrupt freedom of navigation through the Strait ​of Hormuz and hold the global economy hostage," he said.
The White House and Iran's Embassy in Bangkok did not immediately reply to a request for comment.
Iran has sought to tighten ​its grip on the Strait of Hormuz since US and Israeli strikes on February 28, using the chokepoint to pressure Washington, which has been pressing its own naval blockade of Iranian ports.
A failure by the United States and Iran to agree within weeks on a UN-backed plan for moving fertilizer through the Strait of Hormuz could cause a food security crisis in parts of Asia and Africa, an official overseeing the proposed scheme says. pic.twitter.com/WdAsQcmYuU
— Al Arabiya English (@AlArabiya_Eng) October 15, 2026
Before the war, the waterway handled roughly a third of globally traded urea — the world's most widely used fertiliser — and nearly half of seaborne sulphur, a key input. It is also a major conduit for global oil supplies.
Fertiliser ​shipments out of the Gulf region remained largely halted more than six months after the start of the conflict, the Washington-based International Food Policy Research Institute said in a note ​last month. Fertiliser products accounted for a "very negligible" share of the resumption of some shipping during a ceasefire between mid-June and mid-July, it said.
Five vessels a day
If the Hormuz disruption continues, commodity prices could ‌rise by ⁠up to 81% for cereals, 66% for oil crops and 30% for animal products, according to an August report by the International Chamber of Commerce.
"If we miss that planting season, the productivity of agriculture would significantly drop, and the impact on prices will significantly increase," said Silva, who is also the executive director of the United Nations Office for Project Services.
Read More: Hormuz closure raises urea import cost
The proposed operation would use a coordination centre in Oman to register vessels and coordinate safe passage, with UN monitors working alongside local authorities at Gulf ports to verify ​cargo loading.
The passage of only five vessels ​per day through Hormuz could keep fertiliser supplies flowing to countries in critical need, Silva said.
Ships would be tracked during transit, and additional inspections could be carried out if countries raised concerns about a vessel or its cargo, he added.
Multiple shipping chokepoints
Iran and the United States have exchanged proposals through ​intermediaries since a June interim ceasefire collapsed, but efforts to reopen the Strait of Hormuz have stalled over Tehran's conditions and ​Washington's insistence on addressing ⁠Iran's nuclear programme from the outset.
The proposed UN mechanism could operate alongside negotiations on a comprehensive deal aimed at securing lasting peace and freedom of navigation, Silva said.
"What we are telling them is, while you continue your discussions towards a comprehensive deal, let us work, let us do our job," he said, declining to specify the exact bottlenecks to a deal as ⁠discussions continue ​with both sides.
Beyond the Hormuz crisis, a deteriorating situation in the Black Sea region, where cargo vessels have come ​under attack, and an offensive by Iran-backed Houthi militants along a key Red Sea shipping route are compounding the threat to global food security.
"What we are witnessing now is a concentration of factors," Silva said. "Climate ​crisis, simultaneous disruption of maritime chokepoints on the Black Sea, on the Red Sea and on Hormuz."

items.author: Akshit Pushkarna
items.content:
Jio Financial Services’ consolidated net profit declined 51% to ₹340.4 Cr in the second quarter of the financial year ended March 2027 (FY27) from ₹695 Cr in the year-ago quarter.
Operating revenue rose 73% to ₹1,699.3 Cr from ₹981.4 Cr in Q2 FY26. The company also registered an other income of ₹13 Lakh during the quarter as against ₹21.1 Cr other income registered in the year-ago quarter.
Sequentially, net profit fell 59% from ₹830.3 Cr, while operating revenue declined 15.2% from ₹2,004.5 Cr.
The profit decline came amid higher expenses and the absence of dividend income during the quarter. Jio Financial Services had recorded dividend income of ₹269 Cr in Q2 FY26 and ₹508.6 Cr in Q1 FY27.
Total expenses for the quarter rose 167% YoY and 15% QoQ to ₹1,166.1 Cr. The uptick in costs was primarily driven by higher finance costs (up 325% YoY to ₹577.7 Cr) as the group expanded its borrowings to fund asset expansion, alongside elevated operational and staff costs as JFS continued to scale its digital financial ecosystem and super app ambitions.
The company’s top line during the quarter was largely driven by sustained momentum and scale-up in core operational verticals — particularly disciplined loan book expansion at Jio Credit, robust growth in fee income from insurance broking, and expansion in asset management AUM under joint ventures.
“FY27 marked yet another quarter of strong operational growth across our financial services platform. Our strategic playbook is now visibly taking shape with key global partnerships established across our core pillars — lending with Bank of America, investments with BlackRock, and insurance with Allianz Group. These marquee JVs bring world-class capabilities, institutional track records, and global best practices to India, while we drive growth on our digital platform and customer engagement ecosystem,” said JFS CEO and MD Hitesh Sethia.
Here’s a breakdown of the performance of the company’s key verticals during the quarter.
Jio Credit
Continuing its strong growth momentum, JFS’ NBFC arm saw its gross disbursements expand nearly double YoY to ₹13,135 Cr in Q2 FY27. Assets under management (AUM) jumped 154% YoY to ₹37,320 Cr. During the quarter, Bank of America entered into a landmark joint venture agreement with JFS to acquire up to 49.9% in Jio Credit for an investment of up to ₹18,268 Cr, subject to regulatory approvals.
Jio Payments Bank
Jio Payments Bank continued to expand its footprint, with total income surging 213% YoY to ₹94 Cr in Q2 FY27. Customer deposits grew 53% YoY to ₹643 Cr, while CASA customer accounts expanded to around 40 Lakh accounts, with an average balance per customer of ₹1,573.
Jio Payment Solutions
The digital payments vertical recorded total payment value (TPV) of ₹14,682 Cr, representing an 8% YoY increase. Gross fee and commission income grew 70% YoY to ₹130 Cr, while net fee and commission income rose 74% YoY to ₹21 Cr. Operating leverage and merchant mix optimisation helped expand the net processing margin to 14 bps.
Emerging Businesses
Jio BlackRock Asset Management saw its closing AUM expand 57% YoY to ₹22,746 Cr. Its Liquid Fund sustained quarterly average AUM above ₹10,000 Cr, ranking number one since inception, while the recently launched Prism Specialised Investment Fund (SIF) scaled to ₹478 Cr in AUM.
Regulatory approval was also received from IFSCA for the JioBlackRock Advantage World Equity Fund (IFSC) in GIFT City.
In insurance, Jio Insurance Broking facilitated insurance premiums worth ₹346 Cr in Q2 FY27, generating fee and commission income of ₹54 Cr (up 46% YoY).
On the digital front, the JioFinance App reached 3.2 Cr unique users and logged an average of about 36,000 product purchases per day. New ecosystem features introduced during the quarter included JioFinance+, JioFinance360 and JioSilver.

items.author: Debarghya Sil
items.content:
Commerce technology company Shopify is preparing to bring its accelerated checkout product, Shop Pay, to India by the first quarter of 2027, sources told Inc42.
The company is in talks with payment orchestration platforms to integrate payment service providers, the sources added.
Shopify provides software that helps businesses build and run online stores, manage inventory and orders, and integrate payments and other services. A plethora of Indian D2C brands use its platform to run their online businesses.
These existing merchant relationships would give Shop Pay a route into India’s D2C checkout market, where startups such as GoKwik, Shopflo, Razorpay, and Shiprocket help brands improve purchase conversion and manage checkout.
Shopify has not publicly confirmed the proposed launch timeline. Questions sent to the company remained unanswered till the time of publication.
What Shop Pay Adds To Shopify Checkout
Shop Pay allows customers to save their payment, shipping, and contact information to complete purchases faster across participating stores. Shopify claims the product can deliver up to 50% higher conversion than guest checkout.
Shopify already offers its native Shopify Checkout. Shop Pay adds an optional accelerated checkout experience using saved customer information. The product sits within Shopify’s broader commerce ecosystem, which includes storefront technology, merchant tools, and its consumer-facing Shop platform.
Whether Shop Pay replaces any of those services will depend on its India-specific features, payment support, and overall cost.
Competition Goes Beyond Faster Checkout
India’s checkout market includes Shiprocket’s Fastrr Checkout, Razorpay’s Magic Checkout, Cashfree Payments, GoKwik, and Shopflo, among others.
Shop Pay’s entry would bring these providers into closer competition with the platform on which some of their merchant customers already operate.
“GoKwik and Shopflo would need to find how to compete against a giant like Shopify. For others, checkout services contribute a small portion of revenue,” a person familiar with the payment gateway industry told Inc42 on condition of anonymity.
However, competing providers also have businesses and capabilities beyond accelerated checkout. GoKwik offers products spanning customer engagement, shopper identification, advertising, and returns management. Shopflo, meanwhile, is part of Pine Labs, which announced its acquisition in April 2026 to expand its payments and commerce offering.
Umair Mohammad, founder of Nitro Commerce, said Shopify’s brand recognition could give Shop Pay an advantage, but its entry would also widen merchants’ choices.
“Shopify will definitely have an advantage given that it is such a big brand. But more importantly, merchants will have more options to choose the best possible checkout solutions. Shop Pay’s entry does not automatically mean that other checkout services will struggle,” Mohammad said.
He added that checkout providers offer capabilities beyond saving addresses, including return-to-origin (RTO) intelligence and payment orchestration.
“So there are multiple factors at play, and a lot will also depend on pricing and how they position Shop Pay,” he said.
Pricing And Integration In Focus
Shop Pay’s India pricing has not been confirmed. A comparison with existing providers would need to account for any checkout charges, payment-processing fees, and applicable Shopify transaction fees.
While Native integration could make Shop Pay attractive to existing Shopify merchants, the incentive to switch would depend on whether it can meet their payment and operational requirements at a competitive cost.
For competing providers, the challenge would be to demonstrate the value of their broader services alongside faster checkout.

Thursday’s one-day summit, hosted by Azerbaijan as the current CICA chair, brought together representatives of member states, observer countries, and partner international organisations.
Discussions were set to focus on regional cooperation, connectivity, digitalisation, and sustainable development under Azerbaijan's chairmanship of the group.

Turkish foreign minister urges CICA members to support Palestinian rights

Addressing the 7th CICA Summit in Baku, Fidan said: “We cannot uphold this commitment while Israel, a CICA member, violates the fundamental rights of the Palestinian people through a systematic policy of oppression.”

“Turkiye is committed to strengthening CICA as Asia’s most inclusive security forum,” he said.

The federal government on Thursday decreased the price of petrol by Rs3.63 per litre, while increasing the price of high-speed diesel (HSD) by 31 paisas per litre for October 16.
According to a notification issued by the Petroleum Division, the price of petrol was fixed at Rs390.23 per litre, while HSD would cost Rs396.96 per litre for Friday.
The latest revision comes a day after the government increased the price of petrol by Rs1.2 per litre, while decreasing the price of HSD by 17 paisas per litre for October 15.
The government has revised the prices of petroleum products for Friday@Official_PetDiv #RadioPakistan #News https://t.co/oDJYfsoO8j pic.twitter.com/5MAI7dEq4W
— Radio Pakistan (@RadioPakistan) October 15, 2026
Read: Govt hikes petrol by Rs1.2, cuts diesel by 17 paisas for Oct 15
On July 17, the government announced a new pricing mechanism under which petroleum product prices would be reviewed and notified daily, replacing the weekly pricing mechanism, as renewed tensions between the United States and Iran continued to drive volatility in global oil markets and raise concerns over fuel supplies.
On September 13, PM Shehbaz announced a special relief scheme offering Rs100 per litre off petrol for motorcycles, three-wheeler rickshaws and cars with engines up to 800cc, in an attempt to shield lower-income consumers from the impact of rising petroleum prices.
Under the proposal, an estimated 11.8 million beneficiaries would be covered. Around 10 million two-wheeler users and 800,000 three-wheeler users would be entitled to relief on 20 litres of fuel per month, translating into a maximum monthly benefit of Rs2,000 per beneficiary.
Another one million users of cars up to 800cc would receive relief on 30 litres per month, providing them with a maximum benefit of Rs3,000 each.
On Sept 17, the government reintroduced austerity and fuel conservation measures amid rising fuel prices, tightening business operating hours and restricting public events.
Under the measures, notified with immediate effect, shops, markets, shopping malls, bazaars, departmental stores, grocery stores, general stores and kiryana shops would close by 9pm throughout the week, according to a notification issued by the Cabinet Division.
Marriage halls, marquees and other commercial venues hosting festive events would close by 10pm, while restaurants, cafes, eateries, food outlets and standalone fruit and vegetable shops would be allowed to operate until 11pm. Takeaway and home delivery services would remain exempt from the timing restrictions.
Global geopolitical developments continue to pose significant risks. International oil prices are influenced by decisions taken by OPEC+, conflicts in the Middle East, sanctions on oil-producing nations, and disruptions in critical shipping routes such as the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea. Any interruption in these supply chains can immediately increase crude oil prices and freight costs. Since Pakistan imports the majority of its petroleum requirements, these developments quickly translate into higher domestic fuel prices.
Brent crude ​was little changed on Thursday as investors weighed possible US steps to ease restrictions on the ‌world’s "shadow fleet" of tankers, while conflict in the Middle East kept a geopolitical risk premium in the market.
The international benchmark was up 2 cents, or 0.02%, at $106.08 at 12:14 pm EDT (1614GMT).
 
US West Texas Intermediate crude futures were up $2.96, or 3.11%, to $98.05 a barrel, after a ​large US crude stock draw helped support prices.
"The ongoing conflict between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis ​is keeping a geopolitical premium ​in oil markets, but ⁠energy infrastructure has not been attacked in the last several days," MUFG analysts said in a note.

items.content:
Copyright protected content copied from PhoneWorld website.
Pakistan and Alibaba have discussed ways to strengthen cooperation in the digital economy, e-commerce, financial technology, and artificial intelligence to support local businesses and expand the country’s digital trade.
Federal Minister for Finance and Revenue Senator Muhammad Aurangzeb met with the leadership of Alibaba International Digital Commerce (AIDC) in Bangkok, Thailand, on the sidelines of the World Bank Group and International Monetary Fund (IMF) Annual Meetings. The meeting focused on Pakistan’s digital economy and potential areas of collaboration.
During the meeting, both sides discussed digital payments, the promotion of a cashless economy, social protection funding and the transparent delivery of targeted subsidies. Aurangzeb appreciated Alibaba’s role in supporting small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), local brands and Pakistani exports through Daraz and Alibaba.com.
Pakistan and Alibaba Explore New Opportunities in E-Commerce and Technology
The two sides also exchanged views on improving the e-commerce tax system. They discussed ways to make taxation more effective and fair while expanding the tax base and encouraging business activities.
The discussions highlighted the importance of developing a regulatory and tax framework that supports digital businesses while improving tax compliance.
Focus on Digital Payments, AI and Cloud Infrastructure
Pakistan and Alibaba also explored opportunities to improve the e-commerce platform of Pakistan Single Window (PSW). The discussions covered cross-border payments, better monitoring of export proceeds and the use of technology to improve tax administration.
Both sides considered expanding cooperation in cloud infrastructure and artificial intelligence (AI). They also stressed the need for integrated data systems, stronger cybersecurity and improved institutional capacity to support digital transformation.
These initiatives could help improve the efficiency of government systems and create better opportunities for businesses operating in Pakistan’s growing digital economy.
Pakistan Post Modernisation and Agricultural Exports
The meeting also covered the modernisation of Pakistan Post’s sorting system. The participants discussed how improved logistics and Alibaba’s retail network could help increase exports of Pakistani agricultural products to China.
Better logistics and access to international retail channels could help local producers reach more customers and expand their presence in overseas markets.
The discussions reflect Pakistan’s efforts to strengthen digital trade, improve access to international markets, and encourage technology-driven economic growth.
By exploring cooperation with Alibaba, Pakistan aims to support local businesses, improve digital payment systems, and create new opportunities for exporters through e-commerce and technology.

items.title: India expected to overtake Japan as world's 4th largest economy in 2027: IMF
items.summary:
India is expected to become the world's fourth-largest economy by 2027, overtaking Japan, according to International Monetary Fund (IMF) projections that on Thursday laid out the Asian nations' contrasting trajectories.
The IMF said Japan would remain the fourth-largest country by nominal gross domestic product this year, but in 2027 India is set to take its place, with a GDP reaching $4.52 trillion.
Japan is slated to slip to sixth place that year, falling behind both India and the United Kingdom, the projection showed.
India has shown strong growth in recent years despite global economic headwinds, with the IMF this week raising its forecasts for 2026 growth to hit 7%.

Japan, by contrast, is plagued by an ageing population and other structural problems that have seen the Asian giant's growth stagnate.
The United States is the world's largest economy, followed by China and Germany.
Releasing the IMF's regional economic outlook for Asia-Pacific on Thursday, Asia Director Krishna Srinivasan said India entered the current energy price shock caused by the US-Israel war on Iran from a strong position.
"India entered this with very strong fundamentals," he said. "Growth was strong, fiscal prudence was pretty much enshrined, they had lots of reserves and so on. And so in that context, they have responded well to the shock."
Growth in Japan, by contrast, is projected to slow to 0.7% in 2026, with the country hard hit by an increase in energy prices -- and wider inflation -- that has seen the Bank of Japan raise interest rates to their highest level in three decades.

The country, long haunted by deflation, has seen a sustained increase in consumer prices since the spring of 2022, and spiking energy prices from the Iran war have further fueled those rises.
The fall of the yen, which hit its lowest level in 40 years against the dollar over the summer, is further driving up the cost of imports.
Japan's ageing population is also weighing on economic activity.
The IMF's Srinivasan said Japan's economy was benefiting from the boom in artificial intelligence investments, but not as much as its regional neighbours.
The benchmark Nikkei index in Tokyo fell by nearly 5% on Thursday, dragged down by a plunge in technology stocks amid doubts over the profitability of the AI sector.

items.title: ECP snubs Punjab govt's plea to delay LG polls, seeks immediate poll schedules
items.summary:
The Election Commission of Pakistan (ECP) on Thursday decided to proceed with local government elections in Punjab and cantonment areas, directing its offices to immediately submit draft election programmes for approval amid delays in preparations.
The decision was taken at a meeting chaired by Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Sikandar Sultan Raja and attended by ECP members Nisar Ahmed Durrani, Babar Hassan Bharwana and Justice (retd) Ikramullah Khan, along with the ECP secretary and other senior officials.
At the onset of the meeting, it was informed that the Punjab government had responded on October 14 to the ECP’s October 2 letter and draft election programme, proposing that local government elections be held in three phases in April 2027.
The provincial government cited dense fog and severe winter conditions in December, followed by the beginning of Ramazan in February, as reasons for seeking a revised election schedule.
#ECP pic.twitter.com/uxJItBgmaF
— Election Com
items.author: Afzal Talib
items.content:
The Election Commission of Pakistan (ECP) on Thursday decided to proceed with local government elections in Punjab and cantonment areas, directing its offices to immediately submit draft election programmes for approval amid delays in preparations.
The decision was taken at a meeting chaired by Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Sikandar Sultan Raja and attended by ECP members Nisar Ahmed Durrani, Babar Hassan Bharwana and Justice (retd) Ikramullah Khan, along with the ECP secretary and other senior officials.
At the onset of the meeting, it was informed that the Punjab government had responded on October 14 to the ECP’s October 2 letter and draft election programme, proposing that local government elections be held in three phases in April 2027.
The provincial government cited dense fog and severe winter conditions in December, followed by the beginning of Ramazan in February, as reasons for seeking a revised election schedule.
#ECP pic.twitter.com/uxJItBgmaF
— Election Commission of Pakistan (OFFICIAL)🇵🇰 (@ECP_Pakistan) October 15, 2026
However, the ECP termed the response unsatisfactory, noting that consultations with the provincial government under Section 219(3) of the Elections Act had been completed on August 20. During those consultations, the provincial government had agreed to hold local government elections in Punjab between December 15, 2026, and January 15, 2027.
The commission expressed concern over the provincial government’s attempt to revise the previously agreed dates, stating that it had decided to proceed with the elections in fulfilment of its constitutional and legal responsibilities.
Subsequently, the ECP directed its office to immediately submit the draft election programme for Punjab for the commission’s approval.
CEC Raja also expressed disappointment over the provincial government’s failure to provide lists of officers for appointment as district returning officers, returning officers and assistant returning officers.
The provincial government was ordered to submit the required lists within a week.
Read: ECP agrees to hold Punjab local polls between Dec 15 and Jan 15
The meeting was also briefed on progress regarding local government elections in cantonment areas.
The ECP was informed that a consultative meeting had been held on April 15, with the additional secretary of the Ministry of Defence and the director general of the Military Lands and Cantonments Department. During the meeting, the commission had asked the Ministry of Defence secretary to forward a summary to the federal government so that it could formally request the commission to conduct cantonment elections under Section 19(D) of the Cantonments Act, 1924.
According to the briefing, the commission had sent several letters to remind the Ministry of Defence to no avail.
CEC Raja said he also wrote to the prime minister on the matter and was waiting for a response.
Taking note of the delay, the commission decided to proceed with cantonment elections in line with its constitutional and legal obligations and directed its office to immediately submit the draft election programme for cantonment areas too.
