With winter almost here, it’s almost time to reopen those trunks and suitcases holding the family’s woolen and warm clothes. The sweaters, shawls and jackets go through trials before being rolled out for the season.
This is a familiar routine for anyone who lives in a city or town with a winter to speak of, and every season brings the same challenges of keeping up with the trends and the changing needs of everyone in the family.
For everyday wear, keeping an old favourite sweater or cardigan makes sense, but going on a holiday or dressing up for an occasion in winter changes things. Plus, if you live in Mumbai or Chennai or any other temperate city with no real cold months, buying winter wear for that occasional trip to the mountains or cold cities means spending on things you will barely touch once you’re back home.
Take a casual look at the online aisles of winter wear on Myntra or AJIO or any fashion platform. The total expense adds up rather quickly and grows quite large when the whole family needs new winter clothes.
For instance, Decathlon lists a snow jacket somewhere at ₹5,999 and a winter parka at ₹6,999. And those are some of the less pricey options out there when it comes to gear that keeps you warm in true cold.
Beyond the price, there’s the responsibility of cleaning, storing and maintaining it until the next use. For many, this is simply not worth the hassle. So can rental change the game?
Mumbai-based winter apparel and thermo-layer brand Kosha is offering winter wear rentals with a good number of options starting at ₹990 for seven days. Bengaluru’s SharePal is renting a wide assortment of products at rates as low as ₹50 per day, while Mumbai-based Roamwear has packaged winter wear into its travel wardrobe rental for women.
Rentals are not a new idea in India. We touched upon the circular fashion economy earlier and Gen Z’s interest in thrifting and value-conscious shopping is being seen in winter wardrobes too. Just like in wedding wear and designer fashion earlier.
Unsurprisingly, the market for winter rentals is quite large in markets where winter travel is a major tourist attraction. But players such as Finland-based Winterent, Sweden’s SkiStar, Austria’s SkiGala and Japan’s Soranoshita offer outdoor winter clothing near ski retreats. These largely target tourists and not individuals in the region.
That’s the key difference between these players and the Indian startups we spoke to. In India, winter wear rental is undoubtedly an experiment. The question is: is the market big enough for the startups to scale?
Where’s The Ceiling?
Rishav Jain, managing director, Alvarez & Marsal India, says the idea of creating a shared economy matters more than which category is being targeted. Anything with a high average selling price and low usage can move into the rental or shared economy game, especially in a market like India.
Kosha founder Yuktie Jhangiani Verma believes that traction is inevitable even though the category is small today.
“This is a brand new space. It is still too early to define its absolute ceiling, the growth momentum is undeniable. Exciting shifts are happening across consumer behaviour every single month,” she added.
One of the key differences between renting and direct sales is that the former targets premium products that are not widely available or are out of reach of individuals due to their price.
This is why rental for winter wear as a business is positioned and linked with travel. Startups are targeting customers that are booking ski trips, treks or their next European winter holiday. This makes rental a small add-on cost to the overall travel budget.
“Fashion renting works when the item costs above roughly ₹6,000-8,000 and you expect two or fewer trips. Rental typically prices at 10-20% of retail per rental period, so a ₹10,000 jacket at ₹1,490 a week is a clear saving, compared to another jacket that sells for ₹3,299, where that rental price will be 45% of directly buying one. In the latter case, most customers would prefer to buy the jacket than rent it,” TDV Partners’ founder and managing partner Ujwal Sutaria said.
For instance, a published comparison by Indiahikes’ Crosstrek says renting a full set of trekking gear comes up to ₹2,435 for six days, compared to ₹18,250 for buying that same gear. This includes trekking shoes, a padded jacket, rain jacket, backpack and accessories. These are indicative prices rather than what a typical customer might end up spending if they take their time researching the options in the market but not everyone has the time for that.
Sutaria said that as more and more Indians make international trips, the market for rentals is growing. India reported 32.71 Mn overseas departures in 2025, and Japan alone went from 233K to 315K+ Indian visitors between 2024 and 2025. The market for Indian tourists to Northern European destinations like Sweden, Iceland and Norway has grown tremendously in the past two years.
“Viable categories are heavy parkas, ski and snow suits, snow boots and trek gear. Frequency is the ceiling, because by the third trip the customer buys,” he added.
But purely depending on customers planning travel can end up becoming a paradox for rental platforms. More travel plans means more rental opportunities, but it means customers are also more likely to purchase rather than rent every time.
Which is why rental platforms cannot just market the affordability; it’s also about keeping up with the latest styles, materials and trends. Even a short weekend trip can be a window for rental platforms. Some are targeting customers that change their wardrobe with the destination rather than using their existing winter wardrobe.
“When you rent, you have the flexibility of a changing wardrobe with every itinerary. You get a sleek trench for a city break, a technical parka for sub-zero trips, and a vibrant ski jacket for the slopes, all at a fraction of the retail cost,” Kosha’s Verma told Inc42.
Small factors like holiday photographs and social media posts influence choices too. Customers who want a different look on each trip may keep renting even when they can afford to buy. The stigma around rented clothing is disappearing fast among metro users.
So what can brands do in this space to scale? According to Sutaria, customer experience and discovery are the critical levers here. Distribution also matters because the category is sensitive to other parts of the economy i.e. travel.
Founders in this space added that resale of retired rental stock is a second revenue line but that requires a captive audience base as well.
The next demand signal is therefore whether customers return for another itinerary, and whether those orders extend beyond the same short travel season. And that dictates the whole economic model for rental platforms.
Going Beyond The Rental Season
Once the holiday is over and the heavy winter coat comes back to the platform, the startup has to prepare it for another paying customer.
So maintenance and upkeep is a central challenge and can skew unit economics. Any company in this space has to provide for reverse pickup without which the rental proposition does not work.
The dry cleaning and storage is managed by platforms to limit the exposure to costs and to maintain high quality of products. At Kosha, Verma said, clothes go through a 10-point checklist before being rented out again.
So the key metric here would be rentals-per-SKU. The margins are baked into the rental fee, so the actual growth should be seen in the number of rentals for every jacket, coat or sweater in the inventory.
This is just like the RentoMojo or Furlenco business model, and it’s a parallel for which we have numbers too.
As per recently listed RentoMojo’s disclosures, the company had 8.51 Lakh items as of March 2026, of which 83.34% were out on rent. Items purchased nearly ten years ago had already earned 5.12X their original cost by this point in time.
More than 56% of the assets added in 2017 and 60.92% of those added in 2018 were still generating revenue in FY26. These are metrics that even rental platforms have to track, and the shelf life of a wool sweater may be much shorter than that of a hardwood table or other items that Rentomojo offers on rent.
In other words, the business for fashion rental platforms — which includes winter wear — depends on how much of the stock is out on rent, how long each item lasts and how much it costs to put it back into circulation.
For winter wear, the peak demand sits in a short travel season, so the share of stock out on rent across the full year is also another number to watch when assessing startups and their operations.
As of now, none of the companies we have spoken to have hit the kind of scale to speak meaningfully about these metrics and their revenue in detail. That itself gives us a clue as to how winter wear startups are still figuring their way around the economic models of this business. Perhaps the end of this winter season may give us an idea of where this is headed.
SPOTLIGHT | HOW UPLIANCE.AI IS MAKING HOME COOKING SMARTER
Bengaluru-based Upliance.ai builds AI-powered kitchen appliances designed to simplify everyday cooking. Its flagship device automates chopping, stirring, grinding and heating through a smart jar, built-in weighing scale and touchscreen-guided recipes.
The appliance offers more than 750 guided recipes across 34 cuisines, covering everything from Indian curries and biryanis to pasta, soups and desserts. Users follow step-by-step instructions on the screen, while the device manages cooking temperature, timing and stirring.
Upliance.ai is expanding beyond its cooking assistant into smart air fryers powered by its UpAI technology. The fryers let users turn food photos, recipe reels and YouTube recipes into cooking settings. The startup reports more than 6.6 Lakh meal sessions since November 2022 and sales crossing 7,500.
THE DEEP DIVE
ECOMMERCE BUZZ
Nat Habit Raises ₹142 Cr: The personal care brand’s Series C round was led by Trident Growth Partners, with existing investors participating. Nat Habit plans to expand its retail network tenfold to two lakh stores, enter modern trade, strengthen quick commerce and launch sunscreens and serums.
Bewakoof’s FY26 Net Loss Jumps 19%: The D2C fashion brand’s operating revenue grew 40.6% YoY to ₹243.1 Cr in FY26, while net loss widened from ₹73.2 Cr. Total expenses rose 35.4% to ₹335.6 Cr, even as its EBITDA loss narrowed marginally.
KISAH Bags ₹35.9 Cr To Scale Men’s Fashion: The ethnicwear brand raised its first institutional round, led by Fireside Ventures at a ₹211 Cr post-money valuation. KISAH plans to expand beyond its 12 stores, targeting 100 outlets and ₹500 Cr in revenue while remaining profitable.
DailyObjects Secures ₹332 Cr For Offline Expansion: The lifestyle accessories startup’s Series C round was co-led by Xponentia Capital Partners, Anicut Capital and Axiom Asia Private Capital, valuing it at ₹1,050 Cr. DailyObjects plans to expand to 150 exclusive brand outlets, strengthen product development and explore international markets.
Swish Pilots Restaurant Food Delivery: The quick food delivery startup is testing Swish Go in select Bengaluru pincodes, sourcing orders from third-party restaurants and cloud kitchens. The service advertises zero packaging and platform fees, marking a shift from Swish’s own-kitchen model to compete with Swiggy’s Toing and Rapido’s Ownly.
Lumio Secures Series A: The consumer electronics brand raised $12 Mn in a Series A round led by Blume Ventures, with participation from Stellaris Venture Partners and 3one4 Capital. Lumio plans to expand its product portfolio, strengthen software and after-sales support, and build an offline retail presence.
Beyond Appliances Raises ₹110 Cr: The smart kitchen startup raised ₹110 Cr in a Series B round led by Fireside Ventures. Beyond Appliances plans to establish a new manufacturing facility in South or West India and launch ovens within 9–12 months, expanding beyond smart chimneys and hobs.

items.author: Shrishti Bisht
items.content:
MakeO, the parent of clear aligner brand Toothsi, has raised ₹90 Cr (about $9.4 Mn) in a funding round led by Singularity AMC, with participation from DSP family office, Genesis, and Unispace Ventures.
The Mumbai-based startup will use the fresh capital to expand its offline presence across India and Southeast Asia and strengthen its manufacturing operations. It will also invest in consumer experience, clinical centres, and backend technology.
MakeO is also evaluating acquisitions of dental and aligner businesses across India and Southeast Asia as part of its offline expansion
The fundraise follows its acquisition of Singapore-headquartered Zenyum, which expanded its presence across Southeast Asia. MakeO had announced an agreement to acquire Zenyum in February.
In 2025, it also acquired Apple Dental for ₹10.9 Cr in a cash-and-stock deal. The chain operates 20 clinics across Andhra Pradesh and Telangana, extending MakeO’s offline presence beyond major Indian cities.
Following the Zenyum acquisition, the combined group has a network of around 1,100 partner dentists across 10 countries. It also operates more than 60 offline clinical centres and has served over 4 Lakh consumers, according to the startup.
Founded in 2018 by Arpi Mehta, Pravin Shetty, Manjul Jain and Anirudh Kal, makeO initially offered teeth aligners under the brand toothsi. In 2022, it merged its brands toothsi and skinnsi under makeO to offer dental, skin and hair treatments on one platform.
MakeO had raised over $100 Mn before the latest round from investors including Eight Roads Ventures, 360 ONE Asset, and Paramark Ventures. Its earlier fundraises include ₹100 Cr in June last year and a $16 Mn round led by 360 ONE Asset and the investment office of Ashish Kacholia in January 2024.
MakeO said its combined business has crossed ₹500 Cr in revenue and turned EBITDA profitable earlier this year. It aims to double revenue over the next two to three years.
The startup’s expansion plans come amid projected growth in India’s clear aligner market. According to Market Research Future, the market is projected to grow from $466.99 Mn in 2025 to $2.83 Bn by 2035, at a CAGR of 19.74%.

items.content:
African technologists and entrepreneurs are applying blockchain in innovative ways, creating a new financial infrastructure for the continent with wide-ranging benefits, including for the humanitarian sector.
Through its Blockchain Ventures investment programme – supported by Ethereum Foundation and GSR Foundation – UNICEF Office of Innovation provides funding and technical assistance to emerging market startups building innovative blockchain-based solutions.
Unreliable and expensive internet access locks millions out of the digital economy, but as XMesh founder Benjamin Yan explains, blockchain could help equip ordinary people to act as a hyper-local connectivity provider and earn an income from their unused bandwidth.
What problem were you trying to solve when you came up with XOneFi?
I love adventure travelling and I use Starlink in remote areas. I was paying a fair amount of money for that service and I’d find that people around me also wanted to get online, but there was no way to share the connection and there was no way to charge people who want to use my internet, so that’s when I began thinking about a usage-based solution for sharing the internet.
How does XOneFi work?
Anyone with an internet connection can become a provider. They purchase their upstream connection, and then install an XOneFi-enabled router, set their rate and they are good to go.
Nearby customers can use their phones or computers to discover the network, purchase internet access by time or data usage, and the XOneFi firmware meters the session and automatically sends the payment from the customer to the provider.
Where does blockchain come in, and why is it essential?
The blockchain is valuable because we are facing an open network with many independent providers and customers who don’t know the infrastructure owners.
Blockchain is fully transparent, offers tamper-resistant usage accounting – so that providers and customers cannot cheat– and automated micro payments. If a customer is paying $4 a month, maybe every hour you are only paying several cents, which is a very small amount of money, and without blockchain we really cannot transact that.
How are prices set so they work for providers and customers?
We provide a default rate, but providers can adjust it based on their own payment for the internet. When the customer connects they see how much they need to pay and, if they agree, they click, and the transaction starts.
How does the connectivity gap you are bridging affect children and schools?
School administrators tell us connectivity issues are really a big problem: their internet is not reliable, the data rate is very low. Sometimes they cannot sustain a Zoom call or YouTube video, and you can’t even talk about coding or using AI. It is really a missed opportunity for the kids to get a better education, to get the opportunities that they want.
Why did you choose Nigeria to test XOneFi?
Nigeria is a growing economy with big cities and a large population of young people looking for opportunities. They want to utilise the digital economy to improve their living standards.
What is happening on the ground now?
We are running a pilot project at two Nigerian schools and planning to expand to community centres and business centres. Our chief financial officer and our director – both are women – are really moving things forward and identifying and solving challenges on the ground.
Looking ahead, what is your vision for connectivity and local digital economies?
The ultimate vision is that a child or any other user does not need to know where the connection comes from – whether it’s fibre, cellular, satellite or any other technology – but will be able to find an affordable network that they can use. For providers, they can operate their own access points, earn income and reinvest in the hardware to get a better connection. So, everyone has the opportunity to become a mini, hyper-local provider of connectivity, and everyone can get affordable and reliable internet.

items.content:
Copyright protected content copied from PhoneWorld website.
Pick up a slim phone and you already know the catch. Thin has always meant less: less room, less battery, less of the day before the charger comes out. TECNO is about to bring a phone to Pakistan that claims the catch is gone.
The upcoming POVA Curve 2 5G is positioned as the slimmest phone in its segment, and it carries the POVA name, a name built on staying power. Those two things are not supposed to fit in the same body. TECNO has not said how it made them fit, which leaves one question hanging over this launch: how much power can a phone this slim actually hold?
The rule every slim phone has obeyed
The pattern is familiar. Day one is a delight: light in the pocket, easy in the hand. Then the afternoon arrives, the percentage starts falling, and the hunt for a charger or a power bank begins. Thinness and battery life have long been treated as opposites, because every millimetre shaved off a phone is space the battery used to have.
Pakistan punishes that trade-off harder than most places. Long commutes, load-shedding, hours of social media, video calls and mobile gaming drain a phone quickly. A phone that turns heads at breakfast and dies by mid-afternoon is not much of a phone.
The phone that refuses to choose
The POVA Curve 2 5G walks straight into that problem. The “Curve” in its name points to the design: softer lines and a shape made to sit comfortably in the hand. The “slimmest in segment” claim is the bolder part, and putting it on a POVA suggests TECNO believes the old trade-off has been beaten.
TECNO is framing the phone as Beauty and Beast. The Beauty is in plain sight: the slim, curved body. The Beast is the part nobody has seen yet, the power packed inside it, and TECNO is holding that back for the reveal. If the early signals are right, the answer may be far bigger than a phone this thin has any right to give.
Three questions before launch day
Until TECNO lifts the curtain, these are the questions worth asking:
How does it feel in the hand? Slim phones live or die on comfort and grip, and a curved body should count in its favour.
How long does it last? This is the test every slim phone eventually fails, and the one TECNO seems most eager to take. The number behind that confidence could be the headline of the launch.
How does the segment respond? If a slim phone can match or beat its thicker rivals on stamina, every other phone in the segment has some explaining to do.
The POVA Curve 2 5G arrives in Pakistan on October 15. Until then the question stays open, and TECNO seems to be enjoying the suspense: how much power can the segment’s slimmest phone hold?

items.author: Rizwana Omer
items.content:
Copyright protected content copied from PhoneWorld website.
The Higher Education Commission (HEC) and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MoFA) have signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) to set up digital degree verification between their attestation systems. The aim is to let HEC-attested academic credentials be checked directly through a secure link between the two bodies.
The MoU is an agreement of intent. It does not say when the connection will go live.
What the MoU says
According to HEC, the MoU provides for secure, API-based integration between the attestation systems of the two institutions. An API (application programming interface) lets one software system ask another a question and get an answer without a person in between. In this case, the question is whether a degree carries a valid HEC attestation.
Executive Director HEC Prof Dr Zia Ul Haq and Foreign Secretary Asim Iftikhar Ahmad signed the document. Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Mohammad Ishaq Dar and HEC Chairman Prof Dr Niaz Ahmad Akhtar witnessed the signing, along with senior representatives of both organisations.
Where the two offices sit in the process
HEC has recently moved its own side online. It now runs a fully online, paperless degree attestation system that removes the need to visit HEC offices or submit original documents. Under that process, the applicant’s details are checked against NADRA records, the university verifies the credentials against its own records, and HEC issues an e-Attestation Certificate after a final review.
MoFA’s role comes after that step. One applicant, writing publicly, says MoFA requires university degrees to be HEC-attested before they go through its authentication and apostille process. That is a user’s account, not an official statement, but it matches how the two offices are generally understood to work together.
Stage
Body
Current form
Institutional verification
University or HEI
Checks records, reports to HEC
Attestation
HEC
Online, issues e-Attestation Certificate
Authentication for external use
MoFA
Requires HEC attestation first
Link between HEC and MoFA
Both
MoU signed; API integration planned
Why the link matters
A credential passes through several offices before an employer or university abroad accepts it. If each office checks the previous one by looking at a stamped document, every stage depends on paper or PDFs that can be altered or lost. A direct system-to-system query lets MoFA check the status against HEC’s own record instead of trusting the copy in front of it.
For Pakistani graduates applying for jobs, study places or residency overseas, the practical gain would be fewer chances for a document to be rejected or delayed over a doubt about its origin. That outcome depends on how the integration is built, which the announcement does not describe.
This is also not HEC’s only recent data link. In July, HEC signed an MoU with the Pakistan Software Export Board to connect its degree verification system to a planned national digital workforce platform and a verified digital talent repository of students and IT professionals. Taken together, HEC’s attestation record is being wired into more systems, each with its own audience: employers in one case, the foreign service in the other.
What the announcement leaves open
HEC’s statement does not say several things. It gives no launch date. It does not say whether foreign embassies, employers or universities will be able to query the system, or only MoFA. It does not cover fees or how personal data will be protected when two government systems exchange it.
There is also a question about older records. The applicant quoted above asks why a degree already attested under the old system should have to go through verification again after the move to digital. That is one person’s complaint, and HEC has not responded to it in the material reviewed. It does point to a gap the MoU’s authors may need to address: how legacy attestations are carried into the new setup.
What to watch
Attestation works as a chain of custody, and each stamp is only as strong as the link before it. Replacing paper hand-offs with an API strengthens that link but adds new points of failure. System downtime, mismatched records and unclear rules on who can query what would all become policy problems, not just technical ones.
The test of this MoU is simple. If an applicant needs fewer steps and fewer repeat payments after the integration, it has worked. If the same documents are still requested at each counter, the API will exist, and the process will not have changed. The agreement is a necessary first step, and the details that follow will decide whether it delivers.

items.author: Arooj Fatima
items.content:
Jhang is set to host its first-ever Desert Rally 2026 alongside a three-day cultural festival from October 16 to 18 in the Thal Desert at Rehmat Abad, Tehsil 18-Hazari.
Deputy Commissioner (DC) Jhang Babar Sahib Din announced the event during a press conference in Lahore, saying it is being organized under the vision of Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz Sharif to promote tourism, highlight regional culture and introduce Jhang’s attractions to national and international audiences.
The rally will feature a 95-kilometer off-road racing track, with around 100 drivers and riders from across Pakistan expected to participate, including female jeep racers. Renowned racer Nadir Magsi is also among the leading competitors expected to take part.
Sahibzada Sultan Muhammad Ali, founder and leader of the off-road racing team Team Sultan, confirmed his participation and invited motorsport enthusiasts to attend the event.
He said the rally would provide an opportunity to showcase racing talent and establish a new sporting tradition in Jhang. He expressed confidence that participation from leading national and international racers would help make the first edition successful and one of the district’s most memorable sporting events.
The event’s main sponsor, Mukarram Waheed Sheikh, also encouraged tourists and sports enthusiasts to visit Jhang and experience its landscape, hospitality and cultural heritage.
Alongside the desert racing competition, the three-day festival will feature traditional sports, adventure activities and family entertainment. Planned attractions include tent pegging, horseback archery, kabaddi, volleyball and paragliding.
Sheikh particularly highlighted tent pegging and horseback archery as major attractions expected to generate public interest.
MPA Col. (R) Ghazanfar Abbas Qureshi, former MPA Faisal Hayat Jaboana, Ameer Abbas Sial and other participants at the press conference also expressed support for efforts to promote tourism, preserve local culture and encourage recreational activities.
Organizers expect between 50,000 and 100,000 visitors during the three-day event, although actual attendance will depend on public response and event arrangements.
By bringing together desert racing, traditional equestrian sports and cultural activities, organizers aim to establish Jhang as an emerging adventure tourism destination while showcasing the heritage and hospitality of southern Punjab.
The post Jhang to Host Its First-Ever Desert Rally This Week appeared first on ProPakistani.

items.author: Rizwana Omer
items.content:
Copyright protected content copied from PhoneWorld website.
Pakistani advertisers are moving money toward social media creators, and they are changing how they pay them. A Retail News Asia analysis describes a market where flat sponsorship fees are giving way to commissions tied to sales.
Influencer marketing in Pakistan now rests on a large audience. The more useful question for brands is what a post actually sells.
A large audience, with a caveat attached
DataReportal counted 79.9 million social media user identities in Pakistan in October 2025, equal to 31.2 percent of the population. A user identity is an account, not a unique person, so one individual can account for several.
TikTok’s advertising reach is close to 80 million adults, YouTube at about 54 million and Instagram at about 22 million. Other trackers give different numbers. A TikTok agency guide citing DataReportal puts TikTok at 66.9 million adult users in early 2026. NapoleonCat counted 25.6 million Instagram users in Pakistan in September 2026.
The gaps come from dates and methods, but they also point to a real distinction. Ad reach estimates the audience an ad tool may be able to reach, which is different from active users. It is a planning figure, not a count of people who watch or buy.
The report also lists creators with audiences large enough to rival broadcasters:
Creator
Platform
Followers (as reported)
Jannat Mirza
TikTok
Over 25 million
Hania Aamir
Instagram
Over 20 million
Ducky Bhai
YouTube
Over 10 million subscribers
Rajab Butt
Not specified
Around 9 million
Flat fees give way to commissions
According to the report, deals are moving from flat fees to direct affiliate commissions. Smaller creators often accept free merchandise or modest cash retainers. Top celebrities still charge premium rates.
Retailers are handing out trackable discount codes and custom referral links. A merchant that gives unique codes to 100 creators can see within days which accounts produce orders.
For consumer startups and domestic cosmetic lines, this offers distribution without the upfront cost of a television run. The creator is paid when the sale happens, so the brand carries less risk before it knows what works.
Relevance over follower count
The analysis argues that fit now matters more than size. Its example is a specialist account with 50,000 motorcycle enthusiasts, which it says regularly converts better for vehicle parts suppliers than an entertainment channel with five million subscribers.
The report compares this to live-stream selling in Southeast Asia and China, where a product demonstration leads straight to payment and delivery. It says Pakistan has similar conditions: growing smartphone use, digital payment systems and a young urban population used to buying on mobile.
Authenticity and measurement problems
Growth has brought disputes over audience quality. The report names synthetic engagement, bought followers and unclear commercial disclosures as risks. It says they are most serious in regulated sectors such as consumer health and financial services.
Marketing teams are responding by judging creator deals on customer acquisition cost, basket size and repeat orders. The report says this demand is supporting talent agencies, affiliate platforms and analytics firms in Karachi and Lahore.
Promo codes have their own weakness, and the report does not address it. A code proves a sale happened. It does not prove which post caused it. Codes also spread to coupon sites and group chats, so a buyer may use a code from a creator they never watched. Brands comparing 100 creators on code redemptions will be comparing noisy numbers.
What to watch next
Billboards, print and television still draw institutional budgets, the report says, but broadcasters no longer control consumer reach. Its closing expectation is that budgets will follow verified checkouts and that brands will watch whether creator live streams deliver steady sales through the coming festive shopping cycles.
That season is the practical test. A creator-led campaign that tracks well but sells poorly will look different against year-end sales pressure than it does in a pilot.
The commission model also moves risk around. Under flat fees, the brand pays whether or not the post works. Under commissions, the creator carries the conversion risk, and the brand carries the tracking risk. The side with better data will have the stronger position in the next negotiation, and for now that is more often the brand. Creators and agencies that can show buyer-level results, not just reach, are likely to command the better terms.

items.author: Prasetyo Herfianto
items.content:
Ketika flagship rilisan OPPO membawa inovasi merata namun lebih fokus pada sektor kamera, lain halnya dengan OnePlus yang lebih fokus pada sektor performa. Melalui sebuah acara peluncuran khusus di China kemarin malam (12/10), OnePlus 16 akhirnya debut sebagai flagship dengan performa andalan. Hadir dalam desain khas, sekaligus membawa peningkatan pada sektor kamera.
Smartphone OnePlus umumnya dijadikan opsi bagi konsumen yang menginginkan sebuah perangkat dengan performa andal, namun tetap tampil dalam desain stylish, sekaligus sistem operasi yang juga andal—mengingat kini sudah mengusung ColorOS rancangan OPPO. Dan melalui OnePlus 16, aspek performa benar-benar dibuat lebih serius, lewat tambahan fitur hardware maupun software.
Lewat acara peluncuran yang berlangsung luring, OnePlus 16 juga dirilis bersamaan dengan sejumlah aksesori pelengkap yang tidak kalah menarik. Mulai dari power bank 10.000 mAh yang mendukung pengisian daya 67W, hingga pendingin berbasis hardware dengan mekanisme magnetik. Memberikan kemampuan smartphone agar bisa terus berperforma kencang dalam waktu lebih lama.
Baca juga: OPPO Reno X Dirumorkan Usung Layar 16:9, Lebar Bodi Capai 85 mm
Aspek Performa OnePlus 16 Dibuat Maksimal
Bisa dibilang desain OnePlus 16 masih terlihat identik dibandingkan generasi sebelumnya, dengan semua sudut dibuat flat, lengkap dengan bentuk modul kameranya. Hanya saja kini tersedia dalam opsi warna berbeda, yakni Starlight, Dark Forest, serta Martian Masterpiece—di mana salah satu opsi warnanya memberikan corak LED khusus pada sisi bodi belakangnya.
Namun sisi depan smartphone tidak kalah spesial, di mana layar OnePlus 16 mengusung panel BOE X4 versi kustom berukuran 6,78 inci, dan diklaim menjadi smartphone pertama dengan “global refresh rate” hingga 165Hz. Tak sampai di situ, layar smartphone bisa naik ke 185Hz untuk memberikan pengalaman gaming 185fps pada sejumlah judul game tertentu.
Tepi bezelnya sangat tipis, hanya 1,15mm saja. Sementara pada sektor hardware, selain cip Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6, OnePlus 16 juga membawa P4 display chip tambahan, G3 eSports chip, hingga T3 touch chip—semuanya hadir untuk memberikan pengalaman gaming yang lebih optimal. OnePlus janjikan akan ada setidaknya 23 judul game populer yang bisa berjalan hingga 185fps, dengan pengalaman lebih imersif lewat giroskop yang lebih presisi.
Baterai OnePlus 16 juga tergolong andalan, karena kini berkapasitas 9000 mAh, dengan dukungan fast charging hingga 100W. Menariknya, smartphone ini juga bisa mengisi daya perangkat lain, hingga 27W. Tentunya opsi seperti bypass charging juga ikut hadir.
Kamera Lebih Andal, Harga Mulai Rp16 Jutaan
Umumnya smartphone rilisan OnePlus membawa setup kamera yang lebih inferior dibandingkan flagship lainnya. Kabar baiknya, setup kamera OnePlus 16 sudah ditingkatkan. Sensor utamanya kini beresolusi 200MP, mengusung sensor Samsung HPE berukuran 1/1,4 inci. Dan sensor tersebut dipasangkan bersama telefoto 50MP 1/1,95 inci 3x optical zoom, dan 50MP ultra-wide yang juga mendukung autofokus.
Pada sisi depan, juga disematkan sensor kamera 50MP yang mendukung autofokus. Harga OnePlus 16 dibanderol mulai CNY5999 atau sekitar Rp16 jutaan untuk kapasitas 12+256GB. Namun untuk varian tertinggi dengan kapasitas 16GB+1TB, mencapai CNY8499 atau sekitar Rp22,7 jutaan. Sayangnya, smartphone OnePlus sudah lama absen secara resmi di Indonesia.

items.content:
Dominating The AI Shelf Space
Thirty years after the internet’s first ad banner went live, digital marketing is undergoing its biggest transformation yet. As users swap search engines for AI chatbots, the rules of brand discovery and consumer engagement are being rewritten.
Ads In AI Era: Rather than typing keywords into Google and navigating links, consumers are now using AI tools for product recommendations. This behavioural pivot has given rise to answer engine optimisation and generative engine optimisation. But unlike legacy SEO systems, AI platforms offer no common ranking system or standard playbook.
Attribution Problem: For marketers, the biggest challenge is determining whether AI visibility actually drives traffic, customers and sales. This is because multi-step queries and zero-click answers make traditional click attribution nearly impossible. Inconsistent citations and reliance on third-party content further weaken brand control.
As such, experts believe that brands should build a consistent information flow across their digital ecosystem to avoid appearing next to misinformation or unsuitable content.
Ads Enter The Chat: As marketers struggle with the AI RoI question, OpenAI is also creating a new commercial layer around its AI assistants. It has begun rolling out ads for ChatGPT’s free and Go users in India, with more than 50 brands expected in the initial rollout. By tapping ad agencies and opening a self-serve ads manager, OpenAI is looking to monetise its huge user base in the country.
The New Toolkit: Meanwhile, a new wave of startups is building tools to bring measurement and commerce to AI search. While the likes of RankinLLM are tracking brand mentions and sentiment, TruCommerce is connecting product catalogues directly to AI platforms to enable in-chat purchasing. Then, there is also Gushwork that helps small businesses create content optimised for AI tools.
As chatbots compress the path from discovery to decision, can brands solve the challenges around visibility, attribution, measurement and control? Let’s find out…
From The Editor’s Desk
Zetwerk Gears Up For IPO
The B2B manufacturing startup’s public issue will open for subscription on October 15 and close on October 19. It has also set a price band of ₹143-₹151 per share for its IPO, which will value the company at ₹25,583 Cr at the upper end of the spectrum.
The ₹5,012 Cr public issue will comprise a fresh issue of shares worth ₹2,830 Cr and an OFS of up to 14.45 Cr shares, worth ₹2,182.3 Cr at the upper end. This comes a couple of months after Zetwerk filed its updated DRHP with SEBI in August.
Separately, defence tech company Tonbo Imaging has also set a price band of ₹665-₹700 per share for its upcoming IPO, which will also open on October 15. The ₹852.1 Cr public issue will consist solely of an OFS component of up to 1.22 Cr equity shares.
Tessolve Bags $75 Mn
The semiconductor startup has raised ₹718 Cr in a round led by Vector Line Capital to fuel acquisitions, broaden its service offerings and strengthen its international business. It is also already in talks to close multiple acquisitions over the next couple of quarters.
Founded in 2004, Tessolve designs AI chips and provides end-to-end engineering services across chip architecture, validation and testing. Hero Electronix acquired a controlling stake in the company in 2016. It has raised $265 Mn to date.
The fundraise comes amid growing investor interest in the Indian deeptech sector, which is being driven by regulatory push, subsidies, a pivot to IP-driven products and a growing talent pool. The sector raised $290 Mn in Q3 2026, up 176% YoY.
PharmEasy’s FY26 Show
The online pharmacy’s parent API Holdings managed to slash its net losses by 67% YoY to ₹520 Cr in FY26. This came as operating revenue rose 12.7% YoY to ₹6,618.5 Cr, driven by higher margins, capacity utilisation and fewer discounts.
Giving a breakdown, the company said that its B2B businesses generated ₹4,082.4 Cr in revenue in FY26 with an EBITDA loss of ₹3.6 Cr. On the other hand, the B2C arm generated ₹1,334.5 Cr in revenue and reported an EBITDA loss of ₹44.1 Cr in FY26.
Meanwhile, expenses also continued to bite. API Holdings’ consolidated expenditure stood at ₹7,146.7 Cr in FY26, albeit down 0.9% YoY. Purchases of stock-in-trade remained its biggest cost centre at ₹5,244.8 Cr, up 10.9% YoY.
Top-Level Rejig At Nazara
Founder Nitish Mittersain is stepping down as the MD of the gaming giant after a 27 year-long stint. CFO Rakesh Shah has also resigned to pursue external opportunities. Shah will be replaced by ex-Ness Digital Engineering executive Arun Agrawal.
CaratLane founder Mithun Sacheti has also been elevated to the role of executive whole-time director role for a period of five years. Meanwhile, Rohit Sharma has stepped down from the post of whole-time director.
The reshuffle comes as much is happening at Nazara. Last month, Raymond Stauffer took over as the new CEO of the gaming giant. Nazara also de-subsidiarised its esports arm NODWIN Gaming earlier this year even as losses continue to pile up.
The RDI Boost For Deeptechs
The government has announced the first cohort of 19 second-level fund managers to deploy ₹7,131 Cr from the RDI fund. Fourteen AIFs and five focused research organisations have been selected to channel the capital to the eligible startups.
The fund managers are also expected to mobilise capital equivalent to the RDI Fund’s contribution, expanding the pool of financing available for research-led startups. The Centre also plans to onboard additional fund managers going forward.
Launched in November 2025, the RDI Scheme has an outlay of ₹1 Lakh Cr and aims to address the funding gap faced by startups developing high-impact technologies. Earlier this year, the fund had also allocated ₹2,000 Cr allocated to deeptech companies.
Inc42 Markets
Inc42 Startup Spotlight
Can Nextup Make Muscle Recovery Less Pricey?
For people dealing with post-workout soreness, recovery tools can be difficult to choose. While many cheaper gadgets lack useful features, premium devices can stretch the budget. Nextup is plugging this gap with Pulse, which combines practical features with an accessible price point.
Going Mass-Premium: Founded in 2024, Nextup is positioning itself between budget recovery gadgets and higher-priced products. Its flagship massage gun Pulse, features a 30W copper motor, a top speed of up to 4,200 RPM, four interchangeable massage heads and a 3,000mAh battery. Nextup claims that Pulse is quiet and operates at under 45 dB.
The In-House Edge: The bootstrapped startup leverages a D2C-led model, selling through its own website and marketplaces such as Amazon. It also runs an in-house assembly facility, which gives it more control over quality and lets the team make product changes based on consumer feedback. It competes with the likes of Cult, Dr Physio and Agaro.
Road Ahead: Going forward, the D2C brand plans to scale Pulse across online channels and build its creator community to spur repeat demand. It has also set its eyes on launching additional products as it expands from recovery into personal wellness and broader consumer electronics. So, can Nextup build a mass-premium wellness brand for Indians?

Sixteen Indian entrepreneurs earned a combined ₹43.4 Cr in fixed remuneration in FY26. Even founders of loss-making Meesho, Swiggy and Ather took home crores in paycheques. Here is all about it…

items.content:
Several security operatives and civilians have been killed in multiple attacks on communities in Bukkuyum, Maru and Gusau local government areas of Zamfara State in the past one week.
The incidents happened as the state battled repeated attacks by armed groups operating from forests, displacing residents, destroying livelihoods and imposing levies on communities.
The military, operating under Operation Fansan Yamma, has launched offensives against the armed groups, killing some of their members and rescuing dozens of kidnapped victims.
Recently, the Nigerian Army activated three new infantry battalions in Zamfara as part of efforts to strengthen security operations and improve rapid response to threats across the state.
Despite these measures, armed groups have continued to attack communities and travellers across the state.
The latest incident happened on Sunday in Bukkuyum LGA where at least 20 security personnel and civilians were reportedly killed when bandits ambushed traders travelling from Gwashi district to Gurusu market.
A resident said eight security personnel and 12 civilians were killed, while several others sustained injuries in the attack.
He said the security personnel killed comprised five soldiers, two mobile policemen and an officer of the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC).
However, casualty figures provided by residents differed, with another source putting the number of security personnel killed at nine.
The attack reportedly disrupted activities at the Sunday market in Gurusu, leaving traders and residents in fear.
A resident commended the courage of security personnel operating in the area but called on the government to provide them with better equipment to confront the attackers.
“As a matter of urgency, provide bulletproof vehicles to the military at the Anka-Bukkuyum axis. Our soldiers are brave, but they are exposed. How can they fight enemies with superior arms in open Hilux vans?” he asked.
Troops destroy 3 IEDs
 
Traders ambushed on Dansadau road
Earlier on Saturday, traders travelling towards Dansadau in Maru LGA were reportedly ambushed by bandits, who set about 12 vehicles ablaze.
A resident, who also spoke on condition of anonymity, said the attack occurred a day after soldiers discovered improvised explosive devices (IEDs) along the road.
He said the discovery apparently led some travellers to believe that the route was safe, prompting them to resume their journey.
He said the convoy came under attack at a section of the road where construction work had yet to begin.
“The bandits attacked them, and people opened the cars and ran for safety. Others were killed, while some survived the attack,” he said.
The resident alleged that the assailants had laid an ambush and set about 12 vehicles on fire.
The incident came after hundreds of commuters were reportedly stranded at Magamin Maitarko for more than eight days, resulting in substantial losses of perishable goods and livestock.
A trader identified as Muhammad Salisu Dansadau lamented what he described as the lack of adequate security support for traders travelling to their communities.
He said prolonged delays had led to the loss of tomatoes, pepper and livestock, while some travellers became ill and others were reduced to begging.
He, however, commended residents of Magamin Maitarko for providing stranded travellers with food, water and shelter.
“We are grateful for the hospitality of the people of Magamin Maitarko. They gave our people food, water and shelter for days, but their supplies have now been exhausted,” he said.
 
Bandits kill vigilantes at Kaikaice
Also on Saturday, bandits reportedly killed three members of a local vigilante group known as Askarawa and one other person in Damba district on the outskirts of Gusau, while one other member sustained gunshot wounds.
A resident said the vigilantes were attacked at a village called Kaikaiche, near Karazau, after allegedly being tracked by the assailants.
He suspected that informants might have disclosed the vigilantes’ movements to the attackers.
According to him, the group had visited the area to harvest rice the previous day and returned safely before the assailants allegedly laid in ambush for them on their second trip.
The resident alleged that four people were killed, while one survived with gunshot wounds.
He added that residents spent a day and a night searching for one of the missing victims before his body was eventually found around the Yandoto axis.
 
Attack on mining site
These incidents happened the same week residents of Bindin village in Bungudu LGA claimed that nine soldiers and three mobile policemen were killed when bandits attacked a mining site and a military camp in the area.
A resident, who spoke to Daily Trust on condition of anonymity, said the attack occurred last Wednesday.
He blamed the attack on notorious bandit leader Gwaska Dankarami, who reportedly operates around Dangulbi in Maru LGA, Bindin in Bungudu and parts of Bagege in Anka LGA.
According to him, the attack was a reprisal after miners resisted an attempt by one of Dankarami’s men to impose the group’s rules at a gold mining site outside its area of control.
He said the miners killed the bandit, prompting Dankarami and his men to launch an attack on the site.
“Gwaska Dankarami went to the mining site and killed people,” the resident alleged.
He said the mining site was close to Bindin village, forcing people fleeing the attack to seek refuge in the community, where the assailants reportedly pursued them.
“When he attacked the mining site, the people ran to the village for safety, and the bandits followed them,” he said.
The resident said the actual number of casualties remained uncertain because bodies were still being recovered from mining pits and surrounding bushes.
“Nobody can tell the actual number of people killed because some were even killed in the pits. As I speak to you, many bodies are being discovered, and I believe others will still be found either at the mining site or in the bush,” he claimed.
He further alleged that nine soldiers and three mobile policemen were killed when the bandits attacked a security camp in the area.
The resident said it was not the first time Dankarami had attacked a military camp, recalling an alleged attack last year in which two or three soldiers were killed.
The incident, he said, had heightened fear among residents, particularly amid reports that the military was considering relocating its personnel from Bindin to Dangulbi.
“What we are hearing is that the military base is preparing to relocate to Dangulbi village. This has thrown the people into fear and uncertainty over their continued stay in Bindin,” he said.
Efforts by Daily Trust to get comments from the Zamfara State Police Command spokesperson, DSP Yazid Abubakar, were unsuccessful as of the time of filing this report.
Attempts to reach the Acting Army Information Officer at the Joint Task Force North-West Headquarters, 8 Division of the Nigerian Army, Gusau, Lt. Col. Aliyu Danja, were also unsuccessful, as his phone was unreachable.
 
Troops destroy 3 IEDs
Meanwhile, troops of Operation Fansan Yamma have recovered and neutralised two explosive devices allegedly planted by terrorists along the Magami-Hannutara-Dansadau road in Maru Local Government Area of Zamfara State.
The operation, according to a statement posted on the social media platforms of the joint task force, said the development followed credible intelligence about the explosive threats to commuters using the road.
It said troops secured the affected area and conducted a search, during which they discovered two locations where the devices had been planted.
“The team destroyed one device and safely recovered and rendered the other harmless, averting a potential tragedy for road users,” the statement said.
The military urged members of the public to remain vigilant and promptly report suspicious objects or activities to the nearest security agency.
The Zamfara State Government has also pledged to support security agencies until communities are safer and livelihoods restored.
Briefing journalists last week on the 30th anniversary of the creation of Zamfara State, the Secretary to the State Government (SSG), Malam Abubakar Nakwada, noted that Zamfara had endured years of banditry, kidnapping and disruption of rural livelihoods.
He said security remained the foundation of the state government’s transformation agenda.
He said the government had continued to provide operational vehicles, armoured platforms, surveillance drones, specialised motorcycles and other logistics to the Armed Forces, police, Department of State Services (DSS), NSCDC and other security agencies operating in the state.
The SSG also said the government established the Community Protection Guards (CPG) to complement conventional security agencies through grassroots intelligence, early warning, knowledge of local terrain and community-level support.
“We recognise that the security challenge is not yet over. Government therefore remains resolute in providing every legitimate support within its capacity until our communities are safer, livelihoods are restored and our people can pursue their daily activities without fear,” he said.

items.content:
Records have it that there are over 300 ethnic groups in Nigeria making the country the fourth most diverse in the world after Indonesia, India and Papua New Guinea.
But none of the countries mentioned have three large and most distinct ethnic groups as Nigeria.
In Indonesia by far the largest and most dominant ethnic group are the Javanese who constitute up to 45 per cent of the total population of the country. In India, the Hindustani make up about 40 per cent of the total population of India dwarfing the Punjabis, Bengalis and the Kolkatas. In these countries the dominant culture and ethos are influenced to a very large extent by the largest ethnic groups invariably.
In Nigeria however, the three largest ethnic groups do not have the sufficient numbers to claim full dominance over the country and between themselves. The Hausa/Fulani have about 25 per cent, Yorubas 21 per cent and Igbos 18 per cent of the population of Nigeria and this means that between them there is a fierce competition over who will exert the most influence in the Nigerian political, social and economic space. To a very large extent much of Nigeria’s history since colonial times to date has been shaped by this very factor.
For these three large ethnic groups can very much in their own rights, be countries by themselves. It is both a plus and a minus to have three huge, perpetually squabbling potential countries existing within the same space. If Nigeria is often likened to a pressure cooker, this is what makes it so in many respects.
So how do these ethnic groups see Nigeria and how do they try to exert their claims to a ‘’living space’’ within the geographical area called Nigeria?
Let us start with the Igbos. Of the three, it is the Igbos who cannot claim to have a history of pre-colonial spatial expansion through conquest and domination. There are no historical records of a dominant Igbo empire or Kingdom that conquered other Igbo or non-Igbo entities and brought them under its control before the advent of colonialism.
Igbo scholars attribute this to the fact that Igbo societies being ‘’Republican’’ in construct where clans were the structure, did not allow for a dominant state to rule over them.
So, when the British colonialists came to set up their structures, they did not have to ‘’negotiate’’ with any potentate over the establishment of colonial rule in Igboland. But in context it turned out to be an advantage in that the Igbos became the most mobile ethnic group in colonial Nigeria. When the colonial authorities needed to build the colonial infrastructure, it was to the Ibos they turned because they did not have to seek the ‘’cooperation’’ of a ruler for that.
So as the Igbos built the colonial railways, the telecommunications, the electricity grid, the ports etc they were also building the new Nigeria politically and economically. This took them to the nooks and crannies of Nigeria in great numbers and in due time Igbos became the single most influential ethnic group in the country controlling not just the political and economic structures in their region but competing favourably in the Western and Northern regions as well as the federal level.
Up until the civil war in 1967, the dominant position of the Igbo elite in Nigeria’s political, economic and social life was unassailable. Igbos not only saw themselves as of right and by their achievements, the unchallenged leaders of the Nigerian political firmament, but of Africa as a whole. This was the political philosophy espoused by Igbo political leaders like Nnamdi Azikiwe and cascaded down to Igbo ordinary folks in daily life even to this day notwithstanding the civil war and its aftermath.
What about the Yorubas?
The late Attorney-General of Nigeria Bola Ige was quoted to have said ‘’Yorubas are the most educated and sophisticated ethnic group in Nigeria’’. On the basis of historical records this claim may well be true in the context of modern Nigeria. Although the coastal states of the Niger-Delta could lay claim to the record of being the first to come into contact and influence of European states dating back to the fifteenth and sixteenth century, it was in the Yoruba areas that Europeans first set foot as Christian missionaries, traders and adventurers. This brought great social developments in the form of education and other forms of awareness that led to changes in Yoruba land which was lacking in other parts of Nigeria. Lagos and Abeokuta for instance, played host to these developments and as far back as the second half of the nineteenth century there were Yorubas who were in contact and hobnobbing with Europeans.
From these contacts Yorubaland, Lagos especially, became the hub of ‘’modern’’ ways and ‘’sophistication’’ in terms of education and social awareness. Many Yorubas some of whom had returned as liberated slaves and had been educated abroad added to this development. Thus, it came as no surprise that Yorubaland produced the first Nigerian Lawyer in the person of the Ijesha born Sapara Williams in addition to many firsts in other professions in Nigeria. And today Lagos and Yoruba land, to a large extent, lays strong claim to being the pacesetter in educational advancement and standards of social awareness, modernity and urbane sophistication.
The Hausa/Fulanis believe that the Igbo and Yoruba claims are largely superficial. They believe that claims of superiority and sophistication by Igbos and Yorubas in Nigeria are not based on originality. A top northern personality I spoke to on this subject said that Igbos and Yorubas are basing their claims on their historical connections and contact with Europeans. In this regard he asked a rhetorical question ‘’What were the Igbos and Yorubas before the advent of the British? Did they have any civilization based on established administrative structures? The Yoruba Oyo empire had disintegrated and the Igbos had no known state. But in the North, there was a functioning entity which predated the British and which covered what is northern Nigeria today. Indeed, the British learnt administration from us and without this they could not have ruled Nigeria effectively. The Igbos and Yorubas cannot claim what they did not build originally. If the British did not come, what would they show as their concrete claim to civilization and achievement?’’
The contesting claims to who is more influential and who by extension should be the bellwether in Nigerian affairs between the three has become a subject of serious national debate. Most often one hears statements like ‘’We are the ones that can make Nigeria great’’. Other times we hear statements like ‘’Without us Nigeria can never be great’’ or so and so are dragging Nigeria down.
Despite all this claims no part of Nigeria stands as model of development fit to speak of. Nigeria still remains at the bottom or near bottom of indices of underdevelopment despite all the resources available to it.
The truth is that until these three ethnic groups eschew bitter and meaningless competition for power and influence between them and find a common ground to face the necessary task of national development, Nigeria will continue to atrophy to the utter and everlasting disappointment of all Nigerians and people of African descent the world over.

items.content:
Nigeria is not facing a crisis of statistics; it is facing a crisis of lived reality. Behind every headline announcing economic growth are families struggling with food prices, businesses weighed down by rising costs and millions of young Nigerians searching for work in an economy that seems unable to absorb their ambition.
The country must confront a question that no impressive economic figure can answer: What is the value of growth if it does not improve the lives of ordinary Nigerians?
GDP is important. Economic growth matters. Government revenue, foreign reserves, investment and macroeconomic stability are all signs of a functioning economy. But none of them, by itself, puts food on a family’s table, pays school fees, creates a job or gives a farmer the security and resources to produce.
But Nigeria cannot live on GDP alone. The true measure of progress is whether Nigerians can live with greater dignity, security and opportunity. This is not an argument against economic growth; it is an argument for growth that reaches households, expands productive capacity and improves welfare.
Nigeria’s challenge, therefore, is not merely to enlarge the economy but to convert economic activity into better living conditions. When statistics and daily experience tell different stories, the task is to close that gap.
A durable solution requires producing more of what we consume and creating greater value from what we produce. That means raising agricultural productivity, developing livestock, expanding manufacturing, strengthening small and medium-sized enterprises and investing in services and technology.
Agriculture, in particular, must be treated as a serious economic sector rather than simply a social intervention. The farmer needs security, affordable inputs, irrigation, extension services, storage, rural roads, finance and reliable markets.
The livestock producer needs pasture, water, veterinary services, animal-health infrastructure, security, markets and processing investment.
The manufacturer needs electricity, affordable credit, infrastructure and a predictable business environment.
Young Nigerians need skills and an economy capable of absorbing their energy. These are not separate demands. Together, they form the productive foundation of a stronger economy.
The disconnect between economic statistics and daily experience is most visible in the food market. When food becomes unaffordable, everything else becomes secondary. A nation that cannot feed its population remains vulnerable, regardless of the size of its economy.
We must produce more grains, roots and tubers, vegetables, poultry, fish, beef, milk and other livestock products.
But production alone is insufficient. What we produce must be preserved, processed locally, transported efficiently and connected to consumers.
The greatest opportunity lies in building complete agricultural value chains from farm and ranch to processing plant, warehouse, transport system, market and export destination. That is how agriculture becomes an engine of national wealth while lowering food costs and strengthening household security.
Insecurity is not only a security problem; it is an economic one. A farmer who cannot safely reach the farm cannot produce. A pastoralist who cannot protect livestock cannot sustain an enterprise. A transporter operating under constant threat cannot move goods efficiently. An investor will hesitate to commit capital where people and assets cannot be protected. It reduces production, destroy livelihoods, discourage investment and deepen poverty.
Security policy and economic policy must work together. Every community made safe for productive activity becomes an economic asset.
Nigeria does not necessarily need government to spend more. It needs government to spend more effectively. Every major expenditure should answer one question: What productive capacity will this investment create?
Public expenditure must therefore be judged by outcomes, not merely by the size of its appropriation. Borrowing should be tied to investments capable of increasing productivity, reducing costs or generating future economic returns.
Citizens should not have to depend on political speeches to know whether public projects are succeeding.
Growth becomes meaningful to citizens only when their incomes retain or increase their value. A worker whose salary rises while food, transport, rent and basic services rise faster does not experience that as progress.
Nigeria must therefore reduce the cost of production. Energy, transportation, finance, logistics and multiple taxation all affect the prices consumers pay and the jobs businesses can create.
We must invest seriously in human capital. Education should place greater emphasis on literacy, numeracy, technical competence, digital skills and employability. Universities, technical institutions and businesses should work together to expand apprenticeships and industry-linked training.
Economic recovery does not rest entirely with government. Citizens also have responsibilities.
Nigerians must become more productive, support legitimate local enterprises, acquire useful skills, reject corruption and pay legitimate taxes. But citizens must also become more demanding of those who manage public resources.
Political promises should no longer be enough. At every level of government, Nigerians should ask four simple questions: What was promised? What was delivered? What did it cost? Who benefited?
Government, for its part, must set clear goals, publish results, protect productive activity and correct policies that fail.
The immediate national priorities should be clear: food production and productive infrastructure; reliable and affordable energy; lower costs of doing business; security for productive communities; disciplined public investment; human-capital development; and transparent accountability.
These priorities are interconnected. Secure farms increase food production. Better roads and electricity reduce production costs. Affordable finance helps businesses expand. Skilled young people become more productive. Transparent public investment ensures scarce resources are directed towards projects that generate economic value.
Nigeria has the resources to build such an economy: vast agricultural land, enormous livestock potential, mineral resources, entrepreneurial citizens, a large domestic market and a young population.
Our challenge is to convert these advantages into productive capacity and ensure that the benefits are widely shared.
The ultimate measure should therefore not be the size of GDP alone, but whether more Nigerians have productive jobs, whether farmers produce profitably, whether food becomes more affordable, whether businesses survive and expand, whether electricity becomes more reliable, whether communities are secure and whether young Nigerians can build meaningful futures at home.
The time for excuses and impressive statistics has passed. Nigeria must choose production over dependence, results over rhetoric and people over numbers.
Let us build an economy Nigerians can live on – not merely a GDP they can read about.
 
Ahmad resides at FMA2, off Yaya Abubakar Road, Fadamar Mada, Bauchi Email: masalihu@aol.com

items.content:
One hundred and fifty children at the Wassa IDP Camp Clinic in Abuja have benefited from a menstrual health outreach organised by the Light for Less Privileged Foundation (LLPF), in partnership with the Al-Mustapha Foundation for Youth Development (AFYD) and other organisations.
The outreach, held on Saturday, was organised ahead of the 2026 International Day of the Girl Child, observed on October 11.
The programme targeted 100 girls and 50 boys, with the girls receiving sanitary pads intended to last six months.
Speaking during the outreach, AFYD Founder and Executive Director, Al-Mustapha A. Mustapha, said the initiative was aimed at helping girls manage menstruation with dignity while addressing the stigma surrounding the natural process.
“No girl should have to feel ashamed of a natural process or miss out on learning because she lacks sanitary products or the right information,” he said.
Mustapha said boys were included because menstrual health education should not be left to girls alone.
“Boys need to understand these issues and learn to support girls without teasing, discrimination or stigma,” he said.
 
He added that the programme provided children with information on menstruation, personal hygiene, puberty and bodily changes.
 
Mustapha called on the government, corporate organisations, development partners and individuals to sustain interventions supporting vulnerable children beyond commemorative events.
 
“Beyond marking special days, we need sustained interventions that support their health, education, safety and development,” he said.
 
The outreach was organised by LLPF in partnership with AFYD, Mento Missy Initiative, Pent Foundation and Her Health Initiative.

items.author: Anjali Jain
items.content:
Bengaluru-based Mesa School of Business has raised ₹110 Cr ($11.4 Mn) in its Series A funding round in a mix of debt and equity. The round pegged the business school at a post-money valuation of ₹385 Cr ($40 Mn), cofounder Ankit Agarwal told Inc42.
While the ₹85 Cr equity round was co-led by Dharana Capital and existing backer Elevation Capital, the remaining ₹25 Cr was raised via venture debt from InnoVen Capital and Alteria Capital.
Mesa plans to utilise the fresh capital to strengthen its leadership team, integrate artificial intelligence (AI) into its programmes, deepen partnerships with startups and launch new courses.
Founded in 2023 by Agarwal and Varun Limaye, Mesa offers on-campus educational programmes for individuals. It currently offers three full-time programmes targeting early-career professionals, fresh graduates and undergraduate students.
While the startup charges ₹25.4 Lakh in tuition fees for its one-year post-graduate programme, its one-year Forge programme for fresh graduates has a starting fees of ₹15.4 Lakh. The undergraduate programme costs ₹48 Lakh over four years.
Training Talent For Startups
Despite being one of India’s fastest-growing employment segments, the local startup ecosystem continues to face a talent gap. Speaking with Inc42, Agarwal said that the talent paucity is especially acute in non-technical roles, which account for nearly 80% of jobs in the sector.
While graduates from premier institutions often have established recruitment pathways into startups, students without access to such networks, Agarwal said, lack a structured route to enter the startup ecosystem.
“If you want to go and work in a startup, there is no one place which sort of builds the right network,” he said.
Unlike conventional business schools, Mesa does not employ full-time faculty, relying instead on startup founders, executives and industry experts to design and deliver its curriculum. Around 2,000 industry professionals have interacted with our students in some capacity, Agarwal said.
“The institutions just don’t have the capability or the incentives to keep changing their curriculum and to keep it super agile over time, and that’s where we felt that we should come in and create talent for the startup ecosystem across levels and functions,” Agarwal said.
On the business front, Mesa’s revenue comes primarily from programme fees, which it collects annually and largely in advance. The experienced-professional postgraduate programme contributes around 40% of revenue, while the undergraduate programme accounts for 35-40%. The fresh-graduate programme contributes around 20%, according to Agarwal.
While the startup is yet to achieve profitability, founder Agarwal claims that most of Mesa’s programmes are approaching operational breakeven. Mesa claims to have grown its business around 2.5X annually over the past two years, Agarwal said, projecting that it will continue to grow at a similar pace in upcoming years.
Where Are Mesa Graduates Headed?
Mesa claims that its first three postgraduate cohorts have produced around 300 alumni, who have joined more than 120 startups. The startup claims that its graduates take up roles across founders’ offices, product management, partnerships, account management and venture capital.
Agarwal claims that the experienced-professional postgraduate programme reports average salaries of ₹26-28 LPA. He also claimed that Mesa has so far incubated more than 50 student startups, which have clocked ₹50 Cr in annual revenue. The school also claims to provide equity-free grants and incubation support to student ventures.
This comes three years after Mesa last raised ₹34 Cr in a round led by Elevation Capital in 2023 to launch its startup leadership programme. Angel investors such as CRED’s Kunal Shah, Meesho’s Vidit Aatrey, and Urban Company’s Abhiraj Bahl also participated in the round.
Mesa operates in an emerging segment of alternative business education, competing most directly with Gurugram-based Masters’ Union, which combines industry-led management programmes with entrepreneurship support. Masters’ Union recently received full university status from the Haryana government.
Other competitors in re-skilling and upskilling space include upGrad, Great Learning, Masai School, Eruditus and Springboard, among others.

items.content: Mumbai: India's top 10 listed blue-chips have steadily lost their share of the country's total market capitalisation, with their combined weight falling to a near-decade low led by sustained foreign portfolio investor (FPI) selling and the underperformance of large-cap stocks.The top 10 companies accounted for around 17.65% of the total market capitalisation of all listed firms as on October 9, a level last seen in January 2017. Their combined market cap stood at ₹84.84 lakh crore, the lowest since December 2023, while the market cap of all listed companies was around ₹480.82 lakh crore till last weekend.Heavy foreign selling has weighed on large-cap stocks.134905140"FPIs have withdrawn above ₹3 lakh crore from Indian secondary markets since the start of 2026, with the top 10 companies accounting for nearly 60-70% of the selling," said Rajesh Singla, CEO and fund manager, Alpha AMC. "A weaker rupee has added to the pressure."The concentration of market value among the country's largest companies has steadily declined over the past few years. The top 10 companies accounted for around 25% of total market capitalisation at the start of 2023, falling to nearly 22% in early 2024 and 21% in January 2025. The share slipped below 20% earlier this year before declining to current levels.Read more: Polycab India’s F&O exit: NSE sets December 30 deadline; NCLAT stays insolvency orderAt the same time, domestic flows have continued to support the broader market. As smaller companies outperformed large-cap stocks, their share as a proportion of the total market cap went up.The combined share of small- and mid-cap companies in the total market capitalisation of listed companies rose to 20.6% and 23.1%, respectively, in September 2026, from around 18% at the start of the year 2024, according to ET calculations."The shift reflects changing investor perceptions about which companies and sectors are best positioned to capture India's next phase of growth," said Swagatam Biswas, head of public equities at Avendus Wealth Management.Read more: Jubilant Pharmova block deal: Quant Mutual Fund offloads Rs 190 crore stake amid Rs 800 crore fundraising plan; Abakkus buys 11 lakh sharesInvestors are looking beyond traditional index heavyweights towards companies benefiting from emerging opportunities, including public infrastructure, he said. "The large-cap fatigue is largely happening due to this," Biswas said.The underperformance of several index heavyweights has contributed to the decline in the top 10 companies' share of total market capitalisation. Reliance Industries, India's largest company by market cap, has declined 26% this year. HDFC Bank and Bharti Airtel have fallen 27% and 15%, respectively, while TCS is down 32%. Larsen & Toubro has declined 11%, LIC 7% and Bajaj Finance 3%. ICICI Bank and State Bank of India have remained broadly flat, while Kotak Mahindra Bank has gained 1%.

items.title: As Jantar Mantar loses protest site tag, CJP plans get disrupted
items.summary: The Cockroach Janta Party recently approached the Delhi Police to organize a protest addressing issues with the electoral roll. In a surprising move, the police removed Jantar Mantar from the list of protest sites, leading to frustration within the party. This resulted in heightened security measures and barricades throughout Delhi, significantly impacting daily activities.

items.title: 6.1-magnitude earthquake strikes off Panama
items.summary: On Monday evening, Panama was shaken by a 6.1 magnitude earthquake, closely following a more powerful 7.7 quake that had already wreaked havoc. Homes, roads, and public infrastructure suffered severe damage, especially in Coclé province and Panama City. In response, the government declared a state of emergency to manage relief efforts, while the US Embassy alerted nations across Central and South America about possible aftershocks and tsunami risks.

items.author: Henry Oduah
items.content:
The Federal Road Safety Corps (FRSC), Oyo Sector Command, has confirmed the death of a female corps member in a road crash on Monday in Ibadan.
The Sector Commander in Oyo State, Corps Commander Kehinde Dahunsi, disclosed this in an interview with the News Agency of Nigeria (NAN).
Dahunsi said that the crash involved a motorcycle and an articulated truck.
According to him, the female corps member lost her life in the accident while the motorcycle rider sustained a fracture in his leg.
He said that while the body of the corps member had been deposited at the State Hospital morgue, the motorcyclist was rushed to the University College Hospital (UCH), Ibadan, for medical attention.
The sector commander noted that details of the late corps member could not be ascertained at the time of the rescue operation.
“We recorded a traffic crash today around Agodi Gardens within the Ibadan metropolis. It involved a truck and a motorcycle carrying a corps member.
“Unfortunately, we lost the corps member, and the rider also sustained a fracture in his leg.
“We carried out emergency rescue operations; we conveyed the body of the late corps member to the State Hospital morgue, while the injured rider was rushed to the University College Hospital (UCH), Ibadan,” he said.
Meanwhile, Mrs Abimbola Faniyi, the National Youth Service Corps (NYSC) Public Relations Officer in the state, said efforts were underway to obtain the deceased’s details, including her Place of Primary Assignment (PPA).
(NAN)
