items.author: Liam Anderson
items.content:
When speaking freely can have a cost, young people turn to music to challenge political silence
Originally published on Global Voices
A group of men during a peaceful protest; one of them holds a microphone and a banner. Photo taken by Stephanie Douglas. Nigeria. Via Pexels. Pexels License.
In Mozambique, freedom of expression is regulated by the Law on the Right to Information No. 34/2014, a constitutionally guaranteed right under Article 48 of the Constitution of the Republic of Mozambique. However, for many young people, speaking publicly about corruption, inequality, police violence, or accountability continues to carry risk, showing the gap between the promises of democracy and actual daily experience.
In music, for example, this contradiction is clear. Over the past two decades, hip-hop has become a key space for urban youth to voice social criticism, particularly in the capital city, Maputo. More than simply a musical genre, hip-hop became a way of documenting the concerns of a generation that grew up with, on one hand, political democratization and multipartyism from the early 1990s, but on the other, high youth unemployment, economic inequalities, and growing distrust in public institutions led by the ruling FRELIMO party.
Through musical narratives, groups like GPRO and artists like Azagaia created a language that reflected people’s daily experiences in public and institutional spaces. Perhaps the question Azagaia poses in the song “O ciclo da Censura” (Cycle of Censorship) remains relevant: “Who said that in this country there is freedom of expression?” This is not just a provocative artistic comment. It is a reflection on the material and political conditions that determine who can speak, about what, and with what consequences.
New forms of citizenship
Mozambican youth have been reinventing ways of participating politically. While for many years citizenship was strongly associated with political parties and state organizations, today it also flows through other organizations such as feminist collectives like the Woman’s Forum, digital platforms for monitoring local governance, cultural associations, and artistic initiatives. This change points to a generation that does not accept politics being limited to elections, and demands the right to continually participate in the shaping of public spaces.
However, these new forms of participation often conflict with authorities that continue to view protest as a threat to public order. One of the most striking events happened in 2016, when feminist organizations took to the streets to protest the banning of miniskirts in state schools. The measure was presented as a response to sexual harassment, but it implied that female students’ clothing choices were the cause of the harm they suffered.
By holding the girls accountable instead of the aggressors, the debate revealed something deeper: the dispute over control of the female body and the right of young women to define their own identity. During the demonstrations, the Spanish activist Eva Anadón Moreno was detained and subsequently expelled from Mozambique for participating in the protest.
Silence is also political
In recent years, censorship in Mozambique has rarely come in the form of explicit prohibitions. However, that does not mean that fear and self-censorship are entirely absent. In a 2010 interview, Azagaia observed that the biggest obstacle to freedom of expression in Mozambique was not necessarily direct police intimidation, but rather economic precarity. When many job opportunities depend, directly or indirectly, on relationships with established power structures, public criticism can put people at risk.
This results in what could be called the “economy of silence.” Journalists avoid certain topics, artists moderate what they say, public officials keep their opinions quiet, and young activists learn that words can carry a high cost. Freedom then ceases to be merely a legal issue and becomes a matter of survival. In this context, protest music takes on a particular political value. It breaks the collective silence and develops communities of recognition-building, where experiences of injustice find language, memory, and solidarity.
The mirage of freedom of expression
The Mozambican Constitution affirms the right of all citizens to freedom of expression and opinion. But a democracy is not measured only by rights on paper, but also by the real conditions in which they can be exercised. The mirage of freedom lies in this contradiction: Citizens are asked to believe they can speak freely, while informal mechanisms of surveillance, stigmatization, and exclusion limit who can participate in public space. It is not necessary to prohibit all voices; it is enough to make the costs of dissent intimidatingly high, such as, for example, the increase of telecommunications tariffs above the real cost.
In this context, the youth activism symbolizes this ambivalence. They amplify historically marginalized voices and make them more visible. The greater the capacity of an artist, activist, or youth collective to mobilize people, the greater the risk of intimidation, disinformation, or economic isolation.
Amplifying youth voices
Despite the challenges, youth continue to create new forms of political hope. Art, music, and digital activism show that citizenship is not just a legal status, but a daily practice of participation, imagination, and resistance. The real challenge of protecting Mozambicans is not just freedom of expression as written in the constitution, but creating conditions for everybody to exercise it without fear of economic, social, or political reprisals. The fundamental question for Mozambique is not just whether young people can speak, but whether they can speak without putting their safety, their job, or their ability to participate in public life at risk.
Written (Português) by Tirso Sitoe

items.author: Dr Imtiaz Ahmad
items.content:
Uraan Pakistan, the national economic plan launched at the end of 2024, aims to raise exports to $60 billion a year by 2029. It expects provinces to finance a major share of their development budget. For the last few years, the Ministry of Commerce has emphasised that exports cannot be raised by the federal government alone and provinces must play their part. This view now appears to have been adopted at the highest level.
In September, Deputy Prime Minister Ishaq Dar called again for "a coordinated, whole-of-government approach" to exports. Such an approach implies that the Ministry of Commerce, other federal ministries, the State Bank of Pakistan, the Federal Board of Revenue and the provincial governments all work towards a common export target. Of these, the role of provinces is perhaps the most important and the least defined. The convergence of views within the government on the role of provinces must be duly appreciated.
However, the fundamental question that arises is how provinces can be asked to share responsibility for a national target when nobody knows how much each of them already exports. The Pakistan Bureau of Statistics (PBS) publishes exports by product and by destination. The SBP does the same for export receipts. Neither publishes export figures by province.
Customs records identify the port which cleared a shipment and the firm whose name is on the invoice. As such, any attempt to construct provincial numbers ends up tracking the port of exit or, at best, the registered address of the exporter. On this basis, a mango grown in Multan but shipped through Karachi appears as an export of Sindh. Marble quarried in Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa but cut and invoiced in Karachi is treated likewise. This implies that basic questions have no answer. It is not clear how much Punjab exported last year, or what is in the export basket of Balochistan. Without a baseline, there can be no provincial target. Without a target, nobody can be held accountable for missing it.
The problem, however, goes beyond accountability. The absence of provincial figures gives rise to at least four issues. The first relates to the incidence of trade costs, which falls unevenly on particular places. Since the closure of the Pak-Afghan border in October 2025, the loss, by one estimate about $890,000 a day, has fallen on transporters and perishable exporters in K-P and, to some extent, in Punjab. Similarly, 30-40% of mangoes and other perishables are lost for want of cold storage. The lost sales, put at over $200 million a year, belong to farmers in southern Punjab and Sindh. Consequently, nobody can tell how much of a province's trade these losses eat up or where removing them would yield the highest return.
The second issue is that national figures leave export policy blind to regional differences, even though export structures differ widely across provinces. Punjab's strengths lie in textiles, surgical instruments and pink salt. Sindh has chemicals, garments, fish and the port of Karachi. K-P has marble, furniture and gypsum, plus border trade through Torkham and Ghulam Khan. This trade amounted to almost $1.4 billion in 2024-25, prior to the border closure. Balochistan has minerals, dates, livestock and fish. Federal policy, however, treats Faisalabad and Gwadar alike.
The third issue relates to competitiveness. A country that cannot see where its exports originate cannot tell which industrial clusters are gaining and which are losing ground. Nor can it see where logistics costs bite hardest. A furniture maker in Peshawar must transport goods over 1,000 km to reach Karachi; a garment maker in Korangi need not. Policy which ignores this difference will continue to favour exporters already located near the port.
The final issue relates to traceability. From the end of 2026, the deforestation regulation of the European Union will require leather and wood to be traced to the land where the cattle were raised or the trees grown. The EU forced-labour regulation, which applies from December 2027, permits the flagging of risky products and regions. Exporters to Pakistan's most important GSP+ market will, therefore, have to demonstrate exactly where their goods were made.
India, by contrast, publishes exports by the state of origin and NITI Aayog ranks states on export preparedness. In Pakistan, nobody keeps score. There are two reasonable grounds for caution. Trade policy is a federal subject and devolving it could fragment it. Also, provincial competition could degenerate into a subsidy race. However, publishing data is not the same as devolving trade policy. Following the 18th Amendment, the provinces control much of what determines export costs. Provincial accounts would simply enable them to see the results of their own choice. Competition over a public scorecard is, in fact, healthier than competition over handouts.
A whole-of-government approach needs a whole-of-government scoreboard. Until exports are counted where they are made, the target of $60 billion will remain a federal headline rather than a provincial commitment. Data alone will not, however, be sufficient. Provinces also need an incentive to act and the capacity to do so. Three steps are recommended.
First, provincial export figures must be published. Customs records of the FBR, SBP payments data and the exporters' registry should be linked to the origin of goods. Much of the required data already exists in customs declarations, sales tax registrations and factory addresses. What is missing is the effort to integrate it.
Second, each province should be given an export target for at least five priority sectors. These should combine established sectors with those that could diversify the export basket. Punjab, for example, might pair surgical goods, sports goods and rice with auto parts and pharmaceuticals. Each target must have a budget attached, financed mainly from provincial development budgets, with matching funds from the federal government. The funds should be used for testing laboratories, cold storage and certification rather than tax concessions.
Third, a trade desk should be set up in each provincial Board of Investment. It would gather market intelligence for the province's export basket and share it with Pakistan's trade missions abroad. A desk in Quetta tracking Chinese demand for dates is likely to pick up signals that a federal ministry can easily miss. The desk should also help small firms meet the standards of buyers. In addition, it must work with the Intellectual Property Organisation of Pakistan to register and defend the geographical indications of a province. Much of Khewra's pink salt, for instance, is sold abroad as generic "Himalayan" salt.
Pakistan's exporters already bear the cost of the country's blind spots, at the border, at the port and on the factory floor. A whole-of-government approach to exports must begin by counting what they make and where they make it.
The writer is Head of Policy (Trade, Investment and Industrial Cooperation) at the Centre of Excellence for CPEC, PIDE

items.author: Shakeel Ahmad Ramay
items.content:
Climate Just Transition (CJT) is a buzzword these days. It urges the world to move away from unsustainable, climate-intensive practices and towards sustainable, climate-neutral and climate-friendly practices. The need for transition has grown as climate change-related disasters and impacts become more frequent. The cost, both monetary and human, is rising sharply.
For example, the 2022 floods cost Pakistan around $30 billion, and the human tragedy cannot be calculated. Climate change has further worsened food insecurity over the years. Pakistan is not the only country facing climate disasters or impacts; the same story is unfolding everywhere. In this context, the transition is a necessity, neither a luxury nor a choice.
However, the transition must be human-centric, not business-centric. It must be designed around human needs and grounded in fairness. Fairness demands a transition that gives due focus and respect to the needs of marginalised communities and groups, as well as poor and developing countries. The transition must not compromise people's decent livelihoods and opportunities to grow. Moreover, countries should not be pushed or lured by funding into commitments or actions beyond their capacity or historical responsibility. Thus, it will be a complex and tedious task, but with wisdom and fairness, it is achievable.
For that purpose, the scope of transition must be designed according to the countries' capacity, not the wishes of developed countries or the greed of the private sector. In this context, the Just Transition must be anchored in the first principle of Article 4 of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC). The principle states, "The parties should protect the climate system for the benefit of present and future generations of humankind, on the basis of equity and in accordance with their common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities. Accordingly, the developed country parties should take the lead in combating climate change and the adverse effects thereof." Therefore, there is broader consensus that the UNFCCC's first principle inspires the Just Transition concept.
A deeper analysis of the principle indicates that it was devised to achieve two objectives. First, to care for the needs of present and future generations; as noted, humans exploited resources without regard for future generations' needs. Second, to act according to capabilities and to ensure the implementation of common and differentiated responsibilities, as well as historical responsibilities. Common and differentiated responsibilities indicate that climate change is a shared threat.
However, determining each nation's responsibility requires considering historical responsibility and capacity, including financial, technical, technological and human resources. Historical responsibility was considered essential to create justice among present, past and future generations.
Unfortunately, the principle was never implemented in its true spirit. Developed countries refused to fulfil their responsibilities under the historical responsibility clause or to act on their commitments at the UN. The story began with their refusal to implement the binding commitments under the Kyoto Protocol to reduce GHG emissions. They never took it seriously, repeatedly postponed action, or watered down their commitments to reduce GHG emissions.
The same policy or strategy has been applied to financial commitments or promises. Instead of fulfilling their financial obligations, developed countries are trying to exploit the situation in their own interest and create opportunities for their companies and states. For example, they promote loans or expensive debt through private institutions or multilateral bodies. Oxfam reports on climate financing and debt are eye-opening and provide us with a clear picture of what is happening in the name of climate financing.
At the same time, they have begun introducing new measures and deploying tools to pressure developing and poor countries to take actions beyond their capacity and responsibility. For instance, the European Union has introduced the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM). Through the CBAM, the EU imposes a levy on imported goods by comparing carbon emissions within the EU with those of the importing country for a given product.
For example, if producing one unit of a product emits 10 kg of carbon in the EU, but the same product is manufactured in another country at a lower price but with higher carbon emissions, it will be subject to a carbon levy. On the face of it, it is a policy to fight climate change and its related impacts. They also promote it as an innovative tool to fast-track the climate transition. In reality, it aims to maintain the competitiveness of EU companies and discourage them from investing outside the EU.
Developing countries too disagree with the EU. They see it as contrary to the principles of equity and historical responsibility. They argue that they have limited resources to adopt new technologies and energy sources necessary for the transition. On the other hand, developing countries view CBAM as discouraging FDI from EU companies and others. It has a detrimental impact on their dream of economic growth and development. In the long run, it also hampers the green transition agenda. If the EU wants developing nations to fast-track the transition, it must provide financial assistance without taxing them irrationally. This is a genuine concern and demand.
Despite the harsh environment and injustice, developing and poor countries remain committed to the Just Climate Transition because they are highly vulnerable to climate impacts and disasters. Against this background, developing countries have two choices. First, they can continue with their current practices and delay implementing the climate transition agenda. This will have severe implications for the global climate change agenda.
Second, build their own financial resources by introducing new import levies on goods from the EU and other countries, such as a historical responsibility tax on EU companies. A historical tax should also include private companies, which are major contributors to global GHG emissions and beneficiaries of the Industrial Revolution. Developing and poor countries should strongly pursue the concept of historical taxation at the upcoming COP in Turkey. This is rational, as developed countries promote the private sector as a leader in fighting climate change; they must also pay for their historical contribution to GHG emissions. As the host, Turkey can facilitate the process.
Before concluding the discussion, it is important to highlight one area of concern in the CJT debate. Unfortunately, planetary needs and boundaries are largely missing from the transition debate. The debate focuses more on reducing GHG emissions, promoting green and new energies, private-sector interests, and economic growth, with less attention to human needs. The planet seems to have been taken for granted, with a focus on business needs. This continued neglect of planetary needs and respect for boundaries is feared to have a detrimental impact on climate, sustainable development and the future of humanity and the planet. It also contradicts the rights of future generations. Thus, to make the transition just, we also need to balance human needs with planetary needs and boundaries.
In conclusion, we can draw four key inferences. First, securing support from all public groups, countries and society is essential. Without society's support, no transition can succeed, let alone the fundamental lifestyle changes it requires. Therefore, to ensure a just transition, we must balance the ambition to reduce GHG emissions with human needs.
Second, the West will not fulfil its commitments and will continue to divert attention and responsibility towards poor countries. The story is the same from the Kyoto Protocol to the Loss and Damage Fund. They will also continue to lure poor countries with financial incentives into commitments beyond their capacity. Third, developing and poor countries need to be innovative and develop ideas, such as historical taxation, to counter developed countries' strategies to shift responsibility or action. Fourth, this debate on a just climate transition must recognise and include planetary needs and boundaries and policies and actions must reflect those needs and boundaries.
THE WRITER IS A POLITICAL ECONOMIST AND A VISITING RESEARCH FELLOW AT HEBEI UNIVERSITY, CHINA

items.title: No straight path for markets
items.summary:
Pakistan stock market's extraordinary rally from around 40,000 to beyond 180,000 in 2.5 years from June 2023 to January 2026 reflected improving fundamentals (from low 3.5x price-to-earnings (P/E), liquidity (rate cut from 22% to 11.5%), sentiment and diplomatic goodwill. Much good news arrived – and was priced in remarkably quickly. After roughly eight frustrating months, investors are questioning equities and eyeing property or fixed income. With the index closing October 1 near 168,637, disappointment is understandable. But consolidation after an exceptional advance does not invalidate the investment case.
In my August 25, 2025 Tribune column, "KSE-100 races to 150,000 – too fast, too soon?", I highlighted the rapid re-rating from 6x to 8x earnings. On February 23, 2026, I wrote: "The KSE-100's long-term average P/E of 8x to 9x has been reached relatively quickly." The implication remains relevant: earnings must eventually catch up with expectations.
items.author: AAH Soomro
items.content:
Pakistan stock market's extraordinary rally from around 40,000 to beyond 180,000 in 2.5 years from June 2023 to January 2026 reflected improving fundamentals (from low 3.5x price-to-earnings (P/E), liquidity (rate cut from 22% to 11.5%), sentiment and diplomatic goodwill. Much good news arrived – and was priced in remarkably quickly. After roughly eight frustrating months, investors are questioning equities and eyeing property or fixed income. With the index closing October 1 near 168,637, disappointment is understandable. But consolidation after an exceptional advance does not invalidate the investment case.
In my August 25, 2025 Tribune column, "KSE-100 races to 150,000 – too fast, too soon?", I highlighted the rapid re-rating from 6x to 8x earnings. On February 23, 2026, I wrote: "The KSE-100's long-term average P/E of 8x to 9x has been reached relatively quickly." The implication remains relevant: earnings must eventually catch up with expectations.
The government deserves credit for navigating a prolonged regional war. September's $3 billion Eurobond, sovereign-rating upgrades and fiscal consolidation demonstrate resilience. SBP still projects the FY27 current-account deficit within 0-1% of GDP. UAE deposits were repaid, although Saudi support helped finance the outflow. These are meaningful achievements, although borrowed reserves must ultimately give way to export earnings and investment.
Successful IMF reviews would unlock $1.2 billion later this year, subject to board approval. I would support another two or three years of reform continuity under an IMF framework, if necessary. Pakistan needs durable institutions and export competitiveness; fresh dollars, bilateral deposits and prospective swap facilities cannot substitute for them.
The export package offers a tangible bridge towards growth. Budget measures reduced collection on export proceeds from 2% to 1.25%, with super-tax exemption for qualifying exporters. Working-capital financing at 8.5% and long-term financing at 2% for two years, followed by 5% for eight, can support investment. Rebates apply to incremental exports: 1% where annual growth is up to 10% and 2% where it exceeds 10%.
Redirecting fiscal space from remittance incentives towards productive capacity is sensible; the discontinued incentives reportedly cost around Rs76 billion last year. Policymakers should also review Naya Pakistan Certificate yields against global alternatives, balancing overseas investors' expectations with sovereign borrowing costs.
Domestic demand has support too. Around Rs60 billion has been disbursed under the prime minister's Apna Ghar programme, with a substantially larger approved pipeline. Progress towards privatising Fesco, Gepco and Iesco could become a stronger catalyst than another financing announcement, provided ownership changes deliver investment, lower losses and better service.
Energy remains the principal threat. Refined-product prices, freight and insurance can magnify the crude-oil shock. Disrupted LNG supplies through Hormuz and reliance on expensive replacement fuels threaten electricity costs, industrial margins and household purchasing power. Sustained oil prices below $100 would improve the outlook. A sudden 4-5% rupee depreciation or rate increase exceeding one percentage point could postpone recovery by several quarters; these are stress scenarios, not mechanical thresholds.
Companies are adapting. Nishat Mills and DG Khan Cement recently announced solar-and-battery projects, while Lucky Cement is expanding renewables. Textile firms such as Nishat Mills, Indus Dyeing, Kohinoor Textile, Gul Ahmed, Premium Textile, Saif Textile, etc are installing large-scale solar, wind and battery projects. Such investments can improve resilience and margins. But industrial migration away from the grid leaves remaining consumers carrying more fixed costs. Competitive incremental energy pricing and removal of industrial cross-subsidies must accompany DISCO reform.
Recovery also requires discrimination. SBP reports improving activity after a weak June quarter. September results, largely available by end-October, should help distinguish sustainable volume growth, operating-margin improvement and cash generation from tax relief or exceptional gains. Investors should identify businesses capable of compounding earnings over the next two to three years.
Market participation offers another encouraging signal. PSX had 656,218 investors in September, roughly 0.25% of Pakistan's population. India's NSE reported 127 million unique investors in January, approximately 9% of its population. Although reporting dates and coverage differ, Pakistan's participation gap is enormous. Digital onboarding and simpler KYC can broaden ownership; lasting stability requires regular saving, rather than leveraged retail speculation.
Recent IPOs and the listing pipeline broaden the opportunity set across electronics, dairy, poultry, tyre exports, property, oil marketing, pharmaceuticals and credit information. Successful offerings demonstrate demand, but subscriptions are no substitute for valuation discipline. New businesses must prove cash generation, governance and returns on reinvestment. For young savers, equities also overcome practical property barriers: large deposits, title verification, transaction costs, maintenance and slow exits. Diversified shares or equity funds permit smaller, regular investments and partial withdrawals. Accumulate quality on weakness with a five- or ten-year horizon, reinvest distributions and avoid leverage. Owning businesses means participating in production, employment and capital allocation – not merely betting on the next price tick.
Expectations must normalise. A 15-20% nominal annualised return is a reasonable long-term ambition under favourable conditions, not an annual entitlement. Entry valuations, inflation, taxes and costs matter. At 15%, capital roughly doubles in five years and quadruples in ten; eight disappointing months do not destroy that arithmetic.
If war risks recede and earnings strengthen, my conditional December 2027 scenario is 225,000-250,000. A valuation near 9x forward earnings would require commensurate earnings growth and dividend yields; the multiple alone cannot establish an index target. To highlight, KSE-100 companies earned Rs2,000 billion profits in fiscal year 2026 and that is real money not speculative crypto coins. A sustained 10-12x P/E rating would demand much stronger foundations: export- and investment-led growth above 5%, better ties with eastern and western neighbours, political accommodation, widening tax-to-GDP ratio, improved security in Balochistan and Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa and goodwill converted into FDI.
A high index level does not automatically mean expensive businesses. The opportunity is to buy improving businesses at sensible prices while uncertainty persists. Buybacks such as of Engro Holdings support that assessment, but cannot replace it. Pakistan's next durable rally must be earned through productivity, exports and reform. Young investors who save consistently stand to benefit more.
The writer is an independent economic analyst.

items.title: Need for National Tax Court
items.summary:
Law Reform Report No 142 of the Law and Justice Commission of Pakistan proposes an International Commercial Court of Pakistan as a specialised Federal Superior Court. Pakistan's tax jurisprudence is now too economically consequential, technically complex and internally contested to remain dispersed among departmental appellate authorities; two tax tribunals, five High Courts, the Federal Constitutional Court (FCC) and Supreme Court. The recent super-tax litigation illustrates the problem. In January 2026, the FCC upheld Sections 4B and 4C of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 ["the Ordinance"]. Its detailed judgment treated Section 4C as a standalone tax on a composite concept of "income", capable of reaching income otherwise falling under normal, final, minimum and separate-block regimes. The FCC expressly held that dividend, profit on debt and capital gains could enter the Section 4C base even where the ordinance otherwise treats them under special charging provisions. For exporters under the then final tax regime, it accepted the "imputable income" mechanism under Section 4C(2)(iii), grossing up final tax to derive an income figure for super-tax purposes.
The reasoning is consequential. Export proceeds for tax years 2022 and 2023 were taxed under Section 154 as final tax based on receipts. Dividend income is specifically charged under Section 5, while Section 8 declares the tax imposed under Section 5 to be final and keeps that amount outside the computation of taxable income under the ordinary heads.
The FCC nevertheless reasoned that Section 4C does not tax these streams twice; it counts them once for a distinct super-tax charge. In the case of exporters, it expressly held that the imputation mechanism brings a final-tax-regime exporter into comparability with a normal-regime taxpayer. That construction may be defended as giving effect to parliament's express inclusion of dividends and imputable income in Section 4C(2). It nevertheless raises a serious issue of statutory coherence: what does "final" mean if another income tax can subsequently be imposed upon the same separately treated stream without an express overriding clause? Will any foreign direct investment come after such erratic over-taxation!
The issue became sharper in July 2026 when the Supreme Court decided Commissioner Inland Revenue vs Saudi Pak Industrial & Agricultural Investment Company and connected matters. A bench comprising Chief Justice Yahya Afridi and Justice Aqeel Ahmed Abbasi rejected the tax department's attempt to tax corporate dividend income at the normal corporate rate under Section 39 of the Ordinance. Justice Abbasi, writing for the court, held that dividend constitutes a separate block of income governed by the specific charging provision in Section 5. Section 39 is residual; machinery provisions cannot dilute a substantive and specific charge.
The Saudi Pak judgment did not discuss Section 4C. However, the interpretive principle it reiterates is important: where parliament has created a specific charging regime, courts should not lightly permit other provisions to destroy its statutory character. Applying this principle, FCC may review its judgment to this extent while deciding thousands of pending review petitions. This is precisely why Pakistan needs specialised tax adjudication. Complex tax disputes are not merely arguments about rates. They require simultaneous command of charging provisions, computation rules, final-tax regimes, accounting concepts, constitutional legislative entries, retrospective taxation, international transactions and the relationship between general and special provisions.
A court deciding these matters must also understand that certainty itself is an economic asset. The proposed Article 212A provides a constitutional route. Instead of creating an International Commercial Court concerned primarily with cross-border contracts and arbitration, parliament should use Clause (3) to establish a specialised taxation division – or, preferably, a National Tax Court within the same constitutional architecture. The commission itself envisages expansion of the proposed court's jurisdiction to taxation and other economic matters. Such a court should absorb the appellate jurisdiction presently fragmented between the Appellate Tribunal Inland Revenue and Customs Appellate Tribunal, with judges selected for demonstrated expertise in taxation, commercial law and accounting. This is not an argument for another layer of litigation. The opposite is required. The appellate chain should be shortened. Fact-finding should terminate at the specialised forum; only substantial questions of law should travel further through a tightly defined route to the National Tax Court. Identical federal tax provisions should not acquire different meanings merely because proceedings originated in Karachi, Lahore, Peshawar, Quetta or Islamabad.
The super-tax controversy teaches another lesson. Tax law cannot become predictable merely by declaring parliament supreme in fiscal policy. Parliament unquestionably levies taxes. Courts still have to determine what parliament actually enacted, how one charging provision interacts with another, whether retrospective legislation disturbs vested or past-and-closed transactions, and whether constitutional limits on legislative competence have been crossed.
Indeed, the FCC itself subsequently struck down Section 7E after holding that, in substance, it was a tax on the capital value of immovable property falling outside federal legislative competence. That judgment demonstrates an elementary but vital principle: the label attached to a tax cannot determine its constitutional character; substance must. Pakistan does not need a National Tax Court to collect more for the state or to grant more relief to taxpayers. It needs one to produce coherent law. Proposed Article 212A offers an opportunity to create that institution before another generation of tax disputes travels from assessment to tribunal, High Court, constitutional court and/or Supreme Court. The test should be simple: one federal tax law should produce one authoritative interpretation across Pakistan. Tax certainty is not a concession to business. It is part of the rule of law.
The writer is the Advocate Supreme Court, Adjunct Faculty at Lahore University of Management Sciences, member Advisory Board and Visiting Senior Fellow of PIDE

items.author: Faraz Ahmed
items.content:
Pakistan may have stabilised its economy, but it has yet to make that stability work. Inflation is no longer at crisis levels, external pressures have eased and foreign exchange reserves have recovered. Yet these improvements have not translated into a corresponding sense of opportunity for businesses or households. For the young graduate, the small manufacturer or the entrepreneur trying to expand, macroeconomic stability remains a distant statistic unless it creates jobs, investment and rising incomes.
This is the central weakness of Pakistan's recovery. Stabilisation was necessary, but it was never meant to be the destination. It was supposed to create breathing space for the harder work of expanding production, attracting investment, increasing exports and creating employment. The question now is whether that breathing space is being converted into a stronger economic base. There is reason for some optimism. Foreign direct investment has improved in the opening months of FY27. Net FDI reached $494.5 million during July-August, up 24.1% from $398.6 million a year earlier, while August alone recorded $315.9 million. These are encouraging numbers. But they need to be viewed in the backdrop of the low base effect in FY26, when annual FDI remained modest. More importantly, the recent improvement remains selective, with financial and power businesses accounting for a significant share of inflows. There is still limited evidence of a broad investment wave flowing into manufacturing, exports and new productive capacity.
Foreign investors had faced delays in repatriating profits and dividends during the foreign-exchange shortages, creating an uncomfortable memory for international investors about the ease of taking legitimate returns out of Pakistan. Those restrictions have since eased as foreign-exchange availability improved, with the recent profit and dividend repatriation data showing repatriation of $557.6 million in the first two months of FY27. But while restoring repatriation is important for rebuilding confidence, the earlier experience is likely to remain part of investors' assessment of Pakistan. For new foreign investors, the question is therefore not only whether they can bring capital in, but whether they can confidently take legitimate returns out in the future.
And this is where the perception of the business environment becomes important. The recently released National Citizen Survey 2026, conducted by the Institute for Public Opinion Research (IPOR), offers a revealing domestic perspective. Based on 5,155 face-to-face interviews across all four provinces, the survey found that 91% of respondents considered it difficult to start or run a business in Pakistan. Taxes were identified as the biggest obstacle, while access to finance, corruption and bribery, high energy costs and government regulation also featured prominently. The significance of these findings goes beyond the difficulties faced by Pakistani businesses. A foreign investor considering a factory, technology operation or export platform in Pakistan is effectively asking the same questions as a local entrepreneur: how predictable is taxation, how costly is energy, how easily can capital be accessed, how much regulatory friction will be encountered and how reliably will contracts and rules be enforced? The difference is that a foreign investor can choose another country.
A factory is a long-term commitment. An investor therefore looks beyond the next year's inflation rate or the latest increase in foreign-exchange reserves. The questions are more fundamental: will the tax regime remain predictable? Can electricity be obtained at a competitive price? Can contracts be enforced? Can profits be repatriated when due? Will regulations remain broadly consistent? These are not peripheral considerations; they determine whether an investment is viable.
Pakistan therefore needs to move beyond improving financial indicators towards improving the conditions under which businesses actually operate. A tax refund delayed for months is not simply an administrative inconvenience. It is working capital trapped outside a business. Expensive energy is not merely a utility problem; it reduces international competitiveness. Regulatory uncertainty is not simply frustrating; it raises the cost of committing capital.
The investment problem is inseparable from the export problem. Pakistan cannot permanently resolve its external vulnerability by borrowing whenever foreign exchange becomes scarce. External financing can provide valuable time and borrowing is not inherently harmful when it finances productive investment. But repeated borrowing to fill a structural foreign-exchange gap merely postpones the underlying problem. The lasting solution is to increase the economy's capacity to earn. Exports are therefore not just another growth indicator. They are the foundation of external resilience. A country that earns more foreign exchange through competitive exports can import machinery and technology, service its external obligations and expand without repeatedly hitting the same balance-of-payments constraint.
This requires a change in the way investment is viewed. The objective should not simply be to attract more dollars, but to attract capital that expands productive capacity. Investment in export-oriented manufacturing, technology, logistics, agro-processing and other tradable sectors can generate a continuing stream of foreign exchange. It can also create domestic supply chains, transfer skills and raise productivity.
Pakistan's investment rate remains low for an economy seeking sustained growth, while its export base is still narrow. An economy with a modest investment base and limited export footprint will struggle to generate the productivity gains and employment required to transform living standards. This is why the debate over stabilisation should ultimately move beyond inflation, reserves and financing arrangements. Those indicators matter, but they are means rather than ends. The real test is whether businesses are investing, whether firms are becoming larger and more productive, whether exports are becoming broader and more competitive, and whether employment is expanding. The connection to ordinary households is direct. Investment expands productive capacity. Productive capacity creates jobs. Jobs generate incomes. Higher productivity raises wages and competitiveness. Greater exports generate foreign exchange.
THE WRITER IS A FINANCIAL MARKET ENTHUSIAST AND IS ASSOCIATED WITH PAKISTAN'S STOCKS, COMMODITIES AND EMERGING TECHNOLOGY

items.title: 12 Killed and 309 Injured in Houthis Attack on King Khalid International Airport Riyadh
items.summary:
At least 12 people were killed and 309 others injured in an attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh on Saturday, according to Saudi Arabia’s civil aviation authority.
The authority said the victims included four Saudi nationals and two Bangladeshi citizens.
One citizen each from the United States, Egypt, Jordan, Syria, Palestine and Sudan was also killed in the attack.
Meanwhile, officials said some of the injured remain in critical condition.
Authorities have shifted all injured people to different hospitals, where they are receiving necessary medical treatment.
The Saudi civil aviation authority also confirmed that the attack caused damage to property at the airport.
However, officials have not yet disclosed the full extent of the damage.
Authorities are currently assessing the affected property and determining the scale and nature of the losses.

items.author: Business Desk
items.content:
US President Donald Trump has told supporters in Tennessee that they would still applaud him if he said “the stupidest things” and defended his political campaign as a matter of common sense.
Trump made the remarks at a rally in Clarksville, Tennessee, on Saturday while reflecting on the enthusiastic reception he receives from crowds. The audience laughed and clapped when he suggested they would applaud even his most foolish remarks.
“There is such love in these rooms,” Trump said, describing the atmosphere at his rallies. He then added, “I could say the stupidest things and you’d clap.”
Trump quickly followed the remark with a defence of his message, saying his speeches were based on common sense rather than simply conservative politics.
“But we don’t say the stupidest things. We say things of common sense. We say things that make sense,” he said.
He argued that several of his political priorities were matters of common sense, including border security, lower taxes and a strong military.
“We want to have a border, we want to have low taxes, we want to have a great military,” Trump said, adding that these were the kinds of things he believed made sense to ordinary Americans.
Trump appeared in Tennessee to support Republican candidates Marsha Blackburn, who is running for governor, and Senator Bill Hagerty, who is seeking the governorship.
Trump also questioned why he needed to campaign in a state where he said the Republican candidates were already doing well. He said he had come just to thank supporters.

items.title: FPSC Stops Hiring in KP
items.summary:
The Federal Public Service Commission (FPSC) has postponed its General Recruitment Tests scheduled in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa from October 12 to October 19, 2026.
The commission announced the decision in a public notice issued on October 11, 2026.
According to the FPSC, the postponement applies to the Phase-III/2026 General Recruitment Tests in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, including examination centers in Peshawar and Dera Ismail Khan.
The commission said it delayed the tests due to the prevailing situation in the province. It also cited requests received from candidates and local invigilation staff.
However, FPSC recruitment tests scheduled in other provinces and areas will proceed according to the previously announced timetable.
Revised Schedule
The FPSC said it will issue a revised schedule for the postponed tests in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa at a later date.
Candidates have been advised to regularly check the official FPSC website for further updates regarding new test dates and related instructions.

items.author: AFP
items.content:
The campaign of Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva accused tech giant Meta of election interference on Saturday after his social media content was allegedly blocked on the company's platforms.
The leftist leader is seeking a fourth non-consecutive term in the October 25 runoff, where he will face Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of far-right former president Jair Bolsonaro.
In a statement, Lula's campaign reported instances where platforms owned by Meta -- the parent company of Facebook, WhatsApp, and Instagram -- allegedly restricted the distribution of his content.
The campaign claimed that in recent days, Meta "prevented President Lula's profile from promoting Instagram feed posts," while a post from his official account "experienced an interruption in view counts, which affected its reach."
It also said that prior to last Sunday's first round of voting -- in which Flavio Bolsonaro finished first -- the profiles of Lula and other leftist leaders "suddenly disappeared from Instagram's search function."
"The series of technical issues... raises strong suspicions that Meta's actions constitute an attempt to interfere in the Brazilian electoral process to the benefit of Flavio Bolsonaro's candidacy," the statement added.
Brazil's Superior Electoral Court (TSE) on Saturday gave the social media giant 48 hours to clarify whether it reduced the reach of posts by Lula's campaign and to explain the irregularities reported.
Read More: Bill Gates warns cyberattacks most imminent AI threat
Meta was ordered to "report, profile by profile, all the measures applied" to "Lula's official accounts" and to "explain the anomalies in the metrics" of the videos, the TSE said.
Meta's Brazil office denied the charges, calling them "simply false" and "not supported by the facts."
"Many of the technical issues mentioned did not affect only Brazil or specific accounts," Meta told AFP in an email.
"We comply with electoral regulations and are committed to a level playing field regarding the use of our platforms."
Lula's campaign has filed a complaint with the electoral court over the alleged social media blocks.
Following the first round of voting, Lula -- who does not use a mobile phone -- launched a social media push that includes videos of him addressing his online followers.

items.title: Bill Gates warns cyberattacks most imminent AI threat
items.summary:
Bill Gates on Sunday warned that unregulated artificial intelligence poses a growing threat and predicted an escalation in AI-powered cyberattacks in the coming year.
The Microsoft co-founder said the risk of AI "getting out of control" remained years away and emphasized that the immediate concern was "bad people" using existing systems without safeguards.
"The front that we'll probably see most dramatically in the next year is cyberattacks," Gates said in an interview with ABC News.
"The real danger right now is not the AI's getting out of control. We need to work on that, but that's years away in terms of the big impact that might have," he said.
"It's really bad people using AI, particularly in AI where you can take out all the safeguards," he said, adding that increased restrictions were needed to prevent bad actors using AI for bioterrorism and cyberattacks.
Read More: Anthropic discloses fake tip to police among new rogue AI
items.author: Reuters
items.content:
Bill Gates on Sunday warned that unregulated artificial intelligence poses a growing threat and predicted an escalation in AI-powered cyberattacks in the coming year.
The Microsoft co-founder said the risk of AI "getting out of control" remained years away and emphasized that the immediate concern was "bad people" using existing systems without safeguards.
"The front that we'll probably see most dramatically in the next year is cyberattacks," Gates said in an interview with ABC News.
"The real danger right now is not the AI's getting out of control. We need to work on that, but that's years away in terms of the big impact that might have," he said.
"It's really bad people using AI, particularly in AI where you can take out all the safeguards," he said, adding that increased restrictions were needed to prevent bad actors using AI for bioterrorism and cyberattacks.
Read More: Anthropic discloses fake tip to police among new rogue AI incidents
"But right now, you're allowed to take all those safeguards out. So when you have bad people, no safeguards, and then the latest models, that's where, over the next year, primarily in the cyber area, we are going to have a lot of negative surprises," he told ABC.
Gates -- who warned in a lengthy August post that the world was dangerously unprepared for the upheaval brought by AI, especially to employment -- is the latest tech magnate to sound the alarm on the threats posed by the new technology.
In his interview Sunday, he dismissed the idea -- advocated by US President Donald Trump -- that self-regulation by AI companies was sufficient to keep the world safe.
"The idea that for the most dangerous technology humans ever invented, that that's the final word, that just the companies themselves are the only check that society has...it's clear we're not doing enough," Gates said.

items.author: Web Desk
items.content:
Jamiat Ulema-e-Islam-Fazl (JUI-F) chief Maulana Fazlur Rehman on Sunday accused the government of backing out of negotiations with the Pakistan Tehreek-i-Insaf (PTI) and the opposition despite initially agreeing to their demands, and categorically rejected the imposition of governor’s rule or an emergency in Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa (K-P).
Speaking to the media, Fazl said his party rejected the government’s decision to impose an emergency or governor’s rule in the province, describing it as an attack on democracy and the rights of the people.
“This is an assault on democracy and the rights of the people,” he said, adding that the JUI-F would use all democratic avenues to oppose the move, including taking the matter to the public, parliament and the courts.
Read: Emergency, governor's rule imposed in K-P after president signs summary on PM Shehbaz's advice
Explaining the sequence of events, Fazl said he had returned to Pakistan on Oct 7 after performing Umrah and met a PTI delegation the same day. The party had expressed a desire for him to play a role in resolving the crisis, he added.
He said he had conveyed to the PTI delegation his view that the government had left no room for negotiations. Despite this, he met a government delegation the following day, which also asked him to play a mediatory role.
Following his involvement, Fazl said, the PTI confined its long march to K-P and suspended its plan to move towards Islamabad, while making no major announcement. The government, meanwhile, postponed its plan to impose governor’s rule, which, according to his information, had been scheduled to be announced on that day.
“Since steps towards the long march were postponed on one side and the decision to impose an emergency was deferred on the other, we thought both sides were serious about reaching an understanding,” he said.
Fazl said Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif subsequently invited him to dinner, an offer he accepted after consultations within his party. However, he added, the positions of the two sides became clear during the meeting.
“The government’s position was that the long march should first be called off, while the PTI demanded that it be allowed to meet Imran Khan and that Khan sahib be taken to a hospital for treatment in accordance with court orders,” he said.
Fazl said he asked both sides whether they agreed to these demands and suggested that they avoid arguing over which side should act first. If both agreed to the demands, he said, they could then decide whether he should assume the role of negotiator.
He said he first contacteDPM d the PTI leadership and held a conference call attended by K-P Chief Minister Sohail Afridi and party chairman Gohar Ali Khan along others. He asked the PTI whether it was willing to call off the long march, to which the party responded that it would be prepared to do so if its demands were accepted.
Fazl said he met the prime minister on Sunday, who agreed to accept the PTI’s demands. Both sides had agreed to reach a decision before a Cabinet meeting scheduled for the morning, with the possibility of postponing the meeting until the evening if necessary, he added.
According to Fazl, the prime minister called him at 9:30am and said he would present the proposals he had made before the Cabinet. Fazl said he initially took this as a positive indication that the prime minister wanted to take the Cabinet into confidence.
However, about an hour later, Deputy Prime Minister (DPM) and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar called him and informed him that the Cabinet had decided to impose governor’s rule.
“At 10:30am, DPM Dar called and said the Cabinet was leaning towards imposing governor’s rule and an emergency,” Fazl said. “I asked him on what grounds an emergency or governor’s rule could be imposed in K-P and told him to explain the reasons.”
He said DPM Dar cited the provincial government’s ineffectiveness in the fight against terrorism as the reason for the proposed action.
“I asked him whether the Balochistan government had not failed in dealing with terrorism, and why an emergency was not needed there but was needed here,” Fazl said.
The JUI-F chief accused the government of reneging on its commitments despite agreeing to the proposals.
“I am a witness to the fact that the government backed out after agreeing to the demands,” he said, asking why it had broken its commitment.
Fazl rejected the use of the fight against terrorism as a justification for imposing an emergency and criticised the role of the Pakistan Peoples Party (PPP), a coalition partner in the federal government.
He said it was the third or fourth time that the PPP, which presented itself as a champion of democracy, had been in government when an elected provincial administration faced what he described as an assault on democracy or an emergency.
“Whenever a provincial government has been subjected to an assault, or an emergency has been imposed, it has happened when the PPP is in government and Asif Ali Zardari is president,” he said.
Discussing military operations, Fazl blamed what he called flawed policies pursued from the era of former military ruler Gen (r) Pervez Musharraf to the present for the country’s deteriorating security situation. Repeated military operations had failed to produce results, he said, describing this as a failure of policy.
He said he had been asked to support a military operation in the region and had no objection to doing so, but demanded an account of the outcomes of operations conducted between 2010 and the present.
Pointing to the deteriorating security situation in K-P, Fazl said people could no longer move freely in Dera Ismail Khan and police were unable to remain safely inside their stations.
“Police stations are emptied, and police personnel spend the night in houses in neighbourhoods rather than staying at their stations,” he said.
He questioned why the government wanted to focus only on terrorists while refusing to discuss its own failures and flawed policies.
“Will we discuss only the terrorists and not your failures? Will we not discuss your flawed strategy?” he asked.
Fazl said that if an emergency had to be imposed, it should be imposed on the federal government, which he described as illegitimate.
Reiterating his opposition to the decision, the JUI-F chief said his party would challenge the move through parliamentary and judicial forums.
“We categorically reject the decision to impose an emergency and will use parliament and the courts to oppose it,” he said.

items.author: Onsa Mustafa
items.content:
Copyright protected content copied from PhoneWorld website.
WhatsApp is introducing a new security alert that requires users to update their device’s operating system before they can log in to the messaging app. The change applies to both Android and iOS devices and aims to improve account security by encouraging users to install the latest available software updates.
According to WABetaInfo, WhatsApp displays an alert when users try to access the app from a device running an outdated operating system. The alert instructs them to open their device settings and install the latest available update before continuing.
Users cannot skip this requirement, meaning they must update their device software to regain access to WhatsApp if the app blocks their login.
WhatsApp Introduces New Security Alert for Android and iPhone Users
The new requirement works through a server-side update. This means users do not need to install a new version of WhatsApp to receive the alert. Instead, the change comes from WhatsApp’s servers and applies to supported Android and iOS devices.
WhatsApp has not yet specified which operating system versions will trigger the login restriction. The rollout may also take time to reach all users.
The new measure highlights the importance of keeping smartphones updated. Operating system updates often include security patches that fix vulnerabilities and protect devices against potential attacks.
Why WhatsApp Wants Users to Update Their Devices
Outdated operating systems can expose devices to known security vulnerabilities. Cybercriminals may exploit these weaknesses to install malicious software, access sensitive information, or intercept data stored on affected devices.
Although WhatsApp offers security features to protect conversations and accounts, the overall security of the app also depends on the device it runs on.
By requiring users to install available operating system updates, WhatsApp aims to reduce risks associated with outdated software. The alert also helps users understand why keeping their devices updated is important for digital security.
WhatsApp Is Also Working on Other New Features
Alongside the security change, WhatsApp is developing and rolling out several other features for Android, iOS, iPad, and Mac.
On iOS, WhatsApp is introducing a refreshed video player with Apple’s Liquid Glass design. The updated interface features a translucent progress bar with rounded corners and a redesigned control bar. The new design is also reaching the iPad and Mac versions of the app.
WhatsApp is also testing a dedicated Contacts tab for Android. It will provide a central place to view contacts, identify people who are online, check birthday reminders, and invite new users. The feature will also let users sort contacts by activity or alphabetically, while respecting their existing privacy settings.
Another improvement allows Android users to play WhatsApp Status updates at double speed. Users can activate 2x playback by pressing and holding the right side of the screen. The faster playback remains active only while they hold the screen.
Meanwhile, WhatsApp is testing a redesigned navigation experience for iOS chats. The new interface adds a shortcut to access useful conversation options without opening the chat information screen.
The company is also testing a redesigned Settings interface on iOS. The proposed layout separates frequently used options from other settings, making it easier for users to find features related to privacy, notifications, storage, linked devices, and parental controls.
What Users Should Do
WhatsApp users should regularly check their smartphone settings for available operating system updates. Installing these updates can help protect their devices from known security threats and maintain compatibility with apps.
For now, WhatsApp has not confirmed the exact operating system versions that will trigger the new login restriction. Users who receive the alert should follow its instructions and install the latest update available for their device.

items.author: Ahtesham Bashir
items.content:
Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf’s (PTI) long march effectively fizzled out in Swabi on Sunday amid heightened security arrangements following the imposition of an emergency and Governor’s rule in K-P.
Police were deployed at key locations across the district to prevent possible protests and restrict the movement of the long march caravan led by former chief minister Sohail Afridi. Mobile phone networks and PTCL internet services remained suspended across Swabi, causing inconvenience to residents and disrupting routine communications.
Read More: PTI rejects emergency, governor's rule in K-P as unconstitutional, vows to continue struggle
According to sources, the PTI caravan was expected to reach Swabi on the night of October 11. However, the party’s local leadership remained largely absent, and no significant protest activity was reported anywhere in the district on Monday.
Heavy police contingents were stationed at important locations, including Aman Chowk in Swabi, Topi, Swabi Interchange and Shiwa Adda in Razaar tehsil. In view of security concerns, containers were also brought to Swabi Interchange, Jahangira Bridge and the Indus River bridge on the M-1 Motorway.
Despite these arrangements, the Peshawar-Islamabad Motorway and the Grand Trunk Road remained open to traffic.
Police sources said raids were conducted at several locations in Shiwa Adda and adjoining areas following reports of the expected arrival of the long march. The action was aimed at arresting PTI workers, but no arrests were reported.
Sources said PTI leaders had directed party workers to assemble at the Razaar Sports Complex to make arrangements for the march, prompting police to step up security and surveillance.
Some PTI workers and youth wing members gathered at Shiwa Adda ground and Ismaila Interchange in preparation for the march. However, police dispersed some of the workers, and the anticipated mobilisation failed to materialise.
Following the imposition of the emergency, the situation at Aman Chowk remained completely normal, with traffic moving smoothly and businesses operating as usual.
Police said security measures had been put in place to deal with any eventuality. With no major demonstration reported and the party’s local leadership largely absent, the long march showed little sign of proceeding through Swabi as anticipated.
Police vow action against rioters, violence
Meanwhile, K-P Police resolved to deal firmly with protest demonstrations, warning that those involved in rioting, vandalism or disrupting law and order would face the full force of the law.
Authorities made clear that no damage to government installations, buildings or public property would be tolerated during any protest or disturbance. The public had been advised to stay away from illegal gatherings, violent activities or any form of provocation. Failure to do so would result in the strictest legal action.
Police said they would take action against anyone who threatened peace, attacked security forces or buildings, or endangered citizens’ lives and property. Citizens had been urged to remain peaceful, respect the law and avoid being misled by troublemakers.
Special security arrangements were being put in place to protect police stations, government buildings, banks, petrol pumps, commercial centres and major highways. All protest activities and police responses would be video-recorded to support any subsequent legal proceedings.
To ensure an effective response, the police would maintain close coordination with the district administration and other relevant agencies. Officials emphasised that while peaceful expression of views was a right, violence and lawlessness would not be allowed under any circumstances.
Peshawar cantonment sealed
Even before the formal imposition of emergency and governor’s rule in K-P, authorities sealed the Cantonment area of Peshawar, bringing commercial activity and traffic to a standstill.
Saddar Bazaar and other commercial centres inside the Cantonment remained closed. Containers were placed at key points to seal all access routes into the area. Roads leading to the Provincial Assembly, Mall Road, Khyber Road and the High Court were also blocked. Containers had been brought into the city overnight and positioned at Firdous Chowk, Assembly Chowk, University Road, Pajagi Road, Kohat Road and other approaches to Saddar.
The sealing of Cantonment roads also forced the closure of markets in Saddar Bazaar. Traffic movement was suspended, leaving residents facing significant difficulties in daily movement.

items.content:
Copyright protected content copied from PhoneWorld website.
The Islamabad Chamber of Commerce and Industry (ICCI) and the National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency (NCCIA) have agreed to strengthen cooperation to address the issues related to cybercrime faced by the business community and improve digital security awareness among traders and entrepreneurs.
Both institutions also decided to establish a joint coordination committee, set up a dedicated cybercrime committee at the ICCI, and organize special awareness sessions to help businesses understand cyber threats and adopt preventive measures.
The decisions came during a meeting at the ICCI House between NCCIA Additional Director Muhammad Shoaib Khan and ICCI President Muhammad Zakria Akbar Zia. Senior Vice President Muhammad Ashfaq Hussain Chattha and Vice President Muhammad Waqas Khan also attended the meeting.
ICCI and NCCIA Agree to Strengthen Cooperation Against Cybercrime
During the meeting, the NCCIA representative reviewed the concerns of the business community regarding cybercrime and assured participants of the agency’s full cooperation in addressing their issues.
The two sides agreed to form a joint coordination committee comprising representatives from both institutions. The committee will improve communication, develop a coordinated strategy to address business-related concerns, and help ensure the timely resolution of complaints.
The institutions also agreed to arrange special awareness sessions for traders and business owners. These sessions will focus on emerging cyber threats, digital security, and practical steps businesses can take to protect their data, financial transactions, and online activities.
ICCI President Muhammad Zakria Akbar Zia said protecting the business community from growing cyber threats remains a top priority. He stressed that stronger cooperation between the chamber and the NCCIA has become essential as businesses increasingly rely on digital platforms for communication, financial transactions, and commercial activities.
Moreover, he said preventing cybercrime and improving digital protection are necessary to build confidence in the digital economy. He also announced that the ICCI would establish a dedicated cybercrime committee, similar to its other specialized committees.
The proposed committee will identify cybercrime-related problems faced by businesses, coordinate with the NCCIA, and help affected chamber members find practical solutions.
ICCI Senior Vice President Muhammad Ashfaq Hussain Chattha and Vice President Muhammad Waqas Khan also highlighted the challenges businesses face because of cybercrime. They assured the NCCIA of the chamber’s full support and emphasized the importance of regular communication between the two institutions.
They said stronger institutional coordination and greater digital security awareness among traders would help prevent cybercrime and improve the business community’s ability to respond to emerging online threats.
See Also: NCCIA Recovers Rs300,000 in Online Fraud Case in Peshawar and Returns Money to Citizen
ICCI Executive Member Abrar ul Haq also briefed the NCCIA Additional Director on specific concerns affecting the Islamabad Computer Association, Islamabad Mobile Association, and Islamabad Realtors Association. He emphasized the need for a coordinated mechanism to address the distinct challenges faced by businesses in different sectors.
Other ICCI executive members and representatives attended the meeting, including Israr Mashwani, Syed Imran Bukhari, Chaudhry Mazhar, Malik Rashid Tufail, Shoaib Arshad Malik, and Shahid Abbasi, along with other chamber members.
Participants expressed confidence that the joint coordination committee, the proposed cybercrime committee, and the planned awareness sessions would strengthen cooperation between the two institutions. They said these initiatives would help Islamabad’s business community address cybercrime-related concerns and conduct commercial activities with greater digital security and confidence.

items.author: Reuters
items.content:
US President Donald Trump said on Sunday that Ukraine and Russia had agreed to what he described as an "energy ceasefire", hours after Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelenskiy had pushed back against US pressure for a unilateral end to strikes on Russian refineries.
In a social media post, Trump said the energy ceasefire would take effect immediately, but did not elaborate further.
In an interview with Axios, Zelenskiy said Trump's post was the first he had heard of the deal, though a senior Ukrainian official told Reuters that Ukraine was ready to agree to such a ceasefire if Russia was.
Trump, whose war in Iran has been blamed for high diesel prices that are weighing on Republicans' prospects at next month's midterm elections, had previously announced an energy ceasefire in Ukraine in mid-September, though neither side ever confirmed such an agreement was reached.
"Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!" Trump wrote on Truth Social.
Earlier on Sunday, Zelenskiy had repeated Ukraine's long-standing position that it was willing to halt attacks on Russian refineries but only if Moscow ceased its own strikes on Ukrainian power infrastructure.
Any such deal would need to come with "real guarantees", Zelenskiy said.
"The real cause of the war in Europe is Russia and Russia alone," Zelenskiy said. "It's possible to stop strikes on energy infrastructure as early as today, but Putin does not want to do so."
Promise of elections
In a dramatic deterioration in their relations, Trump on Saturday had warned Zelenskiy that he had "better damn well stop" attacking Russian refineries, and had urged Ukrainians to replace him as their leader via new elections because he had missed several opportunities to strike a deal with Moscow.
Read More: Trump says ‘it’s time for Ukraine to get a new president’ who can ‘make a deal’ with Russia
Appearing on ABC's "This Week" on Sunday, Zelenskiy responded that he would organise elections in Ukraine if Russian President Vladimir Putin agreed to a 60-day ceasefire.
Zelenskiy said it was "up to Ukrainians" to choose their leader, but noted that there needed to be an end to the fighting first. Ukrainian law prohibits elections under martial law for security reasons.
"Please tell Putin, give us two months, 60 days of total ceasefire, 60 days, and we will organise elections," Zelenskiy said.
The Ukrainian leader rejected being blamed for energy price rises, adding that "everybody in the world" knew that the war in the Middle East was a bigger factor.
The steep rise in global diesel prices, which followed the outbreak of the Iran war in February, has become a political liability for Trump's Republican Party ahead of the midterms, when opposition Democrats could gain control of one or both houses of Congress.
On Saturday, Zelenskiy had responded angrily to Trump's announcement of a diesel supply deal with Russia, saying it would embolden Moscow's attacks on Ukraine and lead to a greater loss of civilian lives.
I just spoke with @MarkJCarney, @alexstubb, and @SecGenNATO Mark Rutte. We discussed the energy ceasefire announced by President Trump. Ukraine supports the ceasefire, and it is important that Russia support it as well. We are awaiting details from the American side. For our…
— Volodymyr Zelenskyy / Володимир Зеленський (@ZelenskyyUa) October 11, 2026
Analysts said Trump's diesel supply agreement with Moscow was unlikely to lead to sustained lower fuel prices as the volumes involved were too small.
The diesel deal was also criticised by US lawmakers, including one of Trump's fellow Republicans, Representative Don Bacon, who said it was time to apply more sanctions, not lift them.
Kyiv residents angry
On the streets of Kyiv, several residents expressed anger at Trump's suggestion that Ukraine should find a new leader willing to make a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
"No one has the right to tell us what to do, especially since elections cannot be held during wartime," said Sabina, a 40-year-old primary school teacher. "In my view, it is a betrayal by our partners," she said, describing Trump's remarks.
Zelenskiy said he would continue discussions with European leaders on Sunday, and there were daily conversations around additional air defence packages, including ammunition for combat aircraft that are used to down Russia's jet-powered drones.
On Monday, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha is due to participate in a European Union Foreign Affairs Council meeting that is expected to discuss increasing sanctions pressure on Russia and advancing negotiations on Ukraine’s EU accession.

items.author: SHAHID HAMEED
items.content:
Governor’s rule has been imposed in Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa (K-P) for the fourth time, transferring powers once again from the provincial government to the Governor.
The first imposition came in 1975 under the central government of Zulfikar Ali Bhutto. An emergency was declared after Hayat Muhammad Khan Sherpao was assassinated in a bomb blast while addressing a gathering at the Department of History of Peshawar University. The National Awami Party (NAP) was banned and arrests were made as the province came under Governor’s rule.
The second instance occurred in 1994 when Benazir Bhutto’s federal government moved against the Muslim League administration of Pir Sabir Shah. Assembly members were made to disappear, a no-confidence motion was brought against Chief Minister Pir Sabir Shah, and Aftab Ahmad Khan Sherpao subsequently formed the government.
The third imposition followed the 1999 counter-coup by then-army chief Pervez Musharraf against the Nawaz Sharif government. Muslim League Governor Mian Gul Aurangzeb was removed and replaced by Lieutenant General (retd) Muhammad Shafiq.
He was later succeeded by Lieutenant General (retd) Syed Iftikhar Hussain, who administered the province with his own cabinet until the formation of the Muttahida Majlis-e-Amal (MMA) government in November-December 2002.
Read More: Emergency, governor's rule imposed in K-P after president signs summary on PM Shehbaz's advice
Now, for the fourth time, the Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf government of Sohail Afridi has been suspended and Governor’s rule imposed. Governor Faisal Karim Kundi will run the province with an interim cabinet.
This latest imposition is unique in that emergency has simultaneously been declared in 12 districts of the province under Article 232 of the Constitution of Pakistan. The districts include the eight merged tribal districts (former tribal agencies), Khyber, Mohmand, Kurram, Orakzai, Bajaur, North Waziristan, South Waziristan Upper and South Waziristan Lower, along with the southern districts of Dera Ismail Khan, Tank, Bannu and Lakki Marwat.
The emergency applies fully in the Bannu and Dera Ismail Khan divisions and partially in the Peshawar, Kohat and Malakand divisions. The Hazara and Mardan divisions remain exempt.
The disruption of internet services caused widespread confusion across the province.

One of the main highlights of the XPeng L03 REEV is its claimed electric-only range of 250 kilometers. This means drivers can cover that distance using electric power alone under the stated conditions.

This setup could appeal to buyers who want the benefits of electric driving without relying entirely on charging stations for longer journeys. However, actual driving range may vary depending on road conditions, driving style, and other factors.

The XPeng L03 REEV also supports 123 kW DC fast charging. According to the announced figures, the vehicle can charge from 10% to 90% in around 20 minutes under suitable charging conditions.
Fast charging can make electric vehicles more convenient for drivers who need to recharge during longer trips. However, the actual charging time may depend on the charging station, battery temperature, and other conditions.
The vehicle’s full charging specifications and compatibility with charging infrastructure in Pakistan will be important details for potential buyers.

XPeng will launch the L03 REEV in Pakistan on October 12, 2026. The event is expected to provide more information about the locally offered model, including its price, features, and availability.
These details will help buyers compare the vehicle with other electric and range-extended models available in Pakistan.
