items.title: Ola Electric’s ₹1,000 Cr Rights Issue To Open On October 22, Issue Price Set At ₹27
items.summary:
Ola Electric’s ₹1,000 Cr rights issue is set to open for subscription onOctober 22 and close on October 30, its board of directors finalised today. The last date for on-market renunciation of rights entitlements has been set at October 26.
At an issue price of ₹27 per share, the company expects to raise ₹999.74 Cr, assuming full subscription and payment of call monies. To note, the issue price is set at a discount of over 5% to Ola Electric’s closing price today (₹36.30).
The rights issue will comprise 37.03 Cr partly paid-up equity shares with a face value of ₹10 each. Shareholders will be entitled to two rights shares for every 25 fully paid-up equity shares held as of the record date of October 13.
The ₹27 issue price includes a ₹17 premium. Shareholders will have to pay ₹16.20 per share, or 60% of the issue price, on application. The remaining ₹10.80 per share will be payable through a first and final call.
The company’s board approved the rights issue on September 28.
items.author: Anne Florentyna
items.content:
Ola Electric’s ₹1,000 Cr rights issue is set to open for subscription onOctober 22 and close on October 30, its board of directors finalised today. The last date for on-market renunciation of rights entitlements has been set at October 26.
At an issue price of ₹27 per share, the company expects to raise ₹999.74 Cr, assuming full subscription and payment of call monies. To note, the issue price is set at a discount of over 5% to Ola Electric’s closing price today (₹36.30).
The rights issue will comprise 37.03 Cr partly paid-up equity shares with a face value of ₹10 each. Shareholders will be entitled to two rights shares for every 25 fully paid-up equity shares held as of the record date of October 13.
The ₹27 issue price includes a ₹17 premium. Shareholders will have to pay ₹16.20 per share, or 60% of the issue price, on application. The remaining ₹10.80 per share will be payable through a first and final call.
The company’s board approved the rights issue on September 28. Following that, founder and CMD Bhavish Aggarwal pledged a 4.32% stake in the electric two-wheeler maker to fund his participation in the rights issue.
Ola Electric plans to split the proceeds between debt reduction, business expansion and general corporate requirements.
The company has earmarked ₹350 Cr for repaying or prepaying borrowings at Ola Electric and its material subsidiaries. The allocation will also cover accrued interest and any applicable prepayment penalties.
A larger ₹400 Cr will be directed towards organic growth, with the company planning to invest across its electric mobility and energy storage businesses. The spending will include manufacturing, R&D, stores and dealerships, service infrastructure, as well as sales and marketing.
The balance of the proceeds will be available for general corporate purposes. Ola Electric expects to utilise the funds during FY27 and FY28.
This would be the second fundraise for Ola Electric within 2026. The company raised ₹780.24 Cr via a qualified institutional placement (QIP) earlier in June.
Meanwhile, on the financial front, Ola Electric managed to trim its net loss for the June quarter (Q1 FY27) by 22% to ₹336 Cr from ₹428 Cr in the year-ago quarter. Operating revenue declined 45% to ₹455 Cr from ₹828 Cr in Q1 FY26.

items.author: Reuters
items.content:
Most US voters think President Donald Trump's administration and Congress are not taking AI risks seriously enough and want the government to ​write new regulations for the technology, according to a new Reuters/Ipsos poll.
The six-day survey, which ended on Monday, showed that large swaths of the electorate see AI as a major threat to American jobs, underscoring growing scepticism of the technology across the political spectrum.
The fast-advancing technology has become a matter of keen national interest amid reports of AI agents running amok and hacking into corporate computer networks, and warnings from prominent researchers that it could one day pose an existential threat to humanity. Noisy, power-hungry data centres that power AI also increasingly pose a nuisance when they pop up near neighbourhoods while jacking up ​utility bills.
Read: OpenAI safety employee quits, says ‘time for trial and error is over’
Some 57% of registered voters in the poll — including a third of self-identified Republicans — said the Trump administration has not taken AI risks seriously enough or at all. ​Some 54% said the same about Congress.
AI has become a significant campaign issue ahead of the November 3 midterm elections when control of Congress ⁠is up for grabs. Some 62% of voters in the poll said the technology could get out of control and risk the future of humankind, roughly the same share of voters with ​that view in a Reuters/Ipsos poll from August of last year.
SITUATION EXPLAINED: 69% of Americans want stricter AI regulation, including 61% of Republicans.
• 84% of voters see AI as a threat to American workers, more than see illegal immigration as one
• 56% back limits on building data centers, including 43% of Republicans, despite… pic.twitter.com/RcIRV50biO
— MTS (@MTSlive) October 7, 2026
Trump has repeatedly voiced unhesitating support for AI and the construction of data centres, arguing they are vital to US competitiveness even as bipartisan ​criticism of the technology grows. He often says the US tech industry will fall behind its Chinese counterparts when asked why his government has not set limits on the technology's use and development, a point that AI safety advocates say is misguided.
"That's an important concern, but it's not top of mind for most Americans, nor should it be," said Daniel Kokotajlo, a former OpenAI staffer who quit in 2024 because he believed the company was not behaving responsibly.
The ​more pressing concern is that AI could cost people their jobs or threaten human health and safety, he said.
In a statement to Reuters about the president's handling of AI, a White House ​official pointed to Trump's new task force, which he said is in charge of ensuring that "America continues to lead the world" on the technology.
"The Trump administration’s priority is to ensure there is a booming economy so that ‌workers have ⁠many opportunities and experience limited volatility from any short-term disruptions," the official said when asked about voters' AI-related employment fears.
Little federal action
While high-profile leaders ranging from US Senator Bernie Sanders — a democratic socialist who caucuses with Democrats — to Steve Bannon — a hard right ally of President Donald Trump — have called for federal action, little has come so far.
Trump last week said executives from the six leading AI developers agreed to a set of voluntary safety principles, including working with "independent auditors" to assess whether AI systems are working as their designers intended.
Read More: Trump, AI CEOs sign voluntary safety pact, back data centre expansion
The safety agreement with the companies — Nvidia, SpaceX, OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta and ​Alphabet’s Google — includes no stated consequences if a ​company chooses not to comply. Congress has ⁠so far failed to agree on legislation that would set guardrails on the technology, and lawmakers are expected to be away from Washington until after the midterms.
The new Reuters/Ipsos poll found 84% of voters saw AI as a threat to American workers. By comparison, only 60% saw illegal immigration as ​a threat to American workers, while 74% viewed competition from foreign workers that way and 73% said the same of large corporations.
A bipartisan ​majority of voters - including 80% ⁠of Democrats and 61% of Republicans - said they supported stricter government regulation on AI.
Many voters also oppose building the data centres that power AI, which has become a pressing issue in congressional and statewide races across the country as candidates from both parties urge a pause in the current construction boom.
Fifty-six per cent of voters in the Reuters/Ipsos poll back limits on building data centres, including 69% of Democrats, 55% ⁠of independents and ​43% of Republicans.
The poll also found growing unease with the ways that AI could be used in warfare. Some ​57% of voters think the US government should not use AI to determine the target of a military strike, up from 49% in a Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted in August 2025.
The Reuters/Ipsos poll, which was conducted online and nationwide, gathered responses from ​4,506 US adults, including 3,526 registered voters. The survey has a margin of error of 2 percentage points.

For many results, the company also released proofs written in Lean, a programming language that enables computers to check whether mathematical arguments follow logically. It plans to add more as they become available.
OpenAI published 10 summaries of the model’s reasoning and estimates of the computing power used. It said the average result required computing power equivalent to roughly three hours of ChatGPT Pro “thinking.”
Completely unrelated to the rest of the ships today, but our models did solve some important math problems and the team documented it in the following blogpost. Remarkable new era of scientific progress.https://t.co/AYSuteVNiA

The company said it consulted the independent Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence at the Institute for Advanced Study on how to present and share the research.
"This is an important event for mathematics, with consequences both for mathematics and for the mathematical community that extend far beyond the individual results," the group said, stressing its advisory role did not amount to an endorsement of the results.
“Making this work public is a first step. This release is the beginning, not the completion, of the process of human understanding and the incorporation of the work into mathematical knowledge,” it added. “The future of mathematical research cannot consist only of understanding results produced by AI labs.”

items.author: Anjali Jain
items.content:
Former senior Flipkart executives, including Flipkart’s former CEO Mukesh Bansal, former CFO Sanjay Baweja and former chief business officer Ankit Nagori, have reportedly urged Walmart to buyback their vested employee stock options (ESOPs) amid uncertainty over the ecommerce major’s public listing plans.
The group is said to have written to Walmart’s board, which includes Flipkart group CEO Kalyan Krishnamurthy, urging for a complete exit opportunity.
“This is not merely a request for goodwill. We contributed our time, effort, expertise and commitment to building the business and creating the value that exists today,” the letter read, as per a report by ET.
Demanding a “fair treatment” towards the vested stock options granted to them 10-15 years ago, the ex-Flipkart heads argued that former employees should not be disadvantaged simply because they are no longer on Flipkart’s payroll.
The push comes months after Walmart conducted the second tranche of Flipkart’s employee stock buyback programme. The July transaction reportedly valued Flipkart at around $38.2 Bn, but eligible employees could liquidate only up to 5% of their vested options.
A Walmart spokesperson said that the company would examine the issues raised by the former executives. “We appreciate the perspective of all employees—current and former—and value their feedback. As with anything raised, we take it seriously and look into the matter.”
“As we’ve said, an IPO remains an active part of our strategic roadmap, and we will move forward when the timing is right. Transitioning to public markets brings great opportunities, but also real operational responsibility. A thoughtful and disciplined approach will help support a successful transition to public markets,” the statement added.
Inc42 has reached out to Flipkart, Walmart, Mukesh Bansal, and Sanjay Baweja for comments on the matter. The emails had not received a response at the time of publishing. The story will be updated upon receiving a response.
Flipkart Defers IPO Amid Profitability Push
At the heart of the matter is Flipkart’s deferred plans as parent Walmart seeks a valuation of $50 Bn for the ecommerce giant.
While the company has reverse flipped to India in a bid to list on the domestic bourses, it doesn’t have a concrete timeline for its public market debut.
As of now, the company is said to have deferred the IPO till 2028 as it focuses on enhancing its bottom line. Flipkart is targeting breakeven at an EBITDA level by FY27.
Flipkart is currently doubling down on its quick commerce vertical, Flipkart Minutes, with projections of it doubling its dark store count to 2,000 by mid-2027.
It is also looking to enter new businesses like food delivery and event ticketing in the near future.
The company is yet to disclose its financial performance for the fiscal year FY26. For the fiscal year FY25, Flipkart Internet, the group’s marketplace arm, reported a 36.7% decline in consolidated net loss to ₹1,494.2 Cr in FY25, while total income increased 14% YoY to ₹20,807.4 Cr.

items.content:
Existential and financial risks posed by the artificial intelligence (AI) boom were top ​of mind for investors and policymakers at two conferences in Singapore on Wednesday, highlighting a cautious shift in ‌mood around the AI trade.
Concerns that once centred on frothy valuations have broadened into a wide swathe of fears, including autonomous systems slipping out of human control, AI-designed bioweapons and the possibility that massive spending on the technology may never pay off.
"Anyone who tells you I've ​got absolute control over my autonomous agent... obviously doesn't know what he's talking about. So loss of control ​is a real threat," Singaporean Foreign Minister Vivian Balakrishnan said at the Milken Institute Asia ⁠Summit.
"There is a revolution going on in AI, in biotech, and in energy."
At #MIGlobal Asia Summit 2026 today, Vivian Balakrishnan, Minister for Foreign Affairs, Singapore spoke about how capital, tech innovation, and trade are reshaping Asia's economic future.
Watch all session… pic.twitter.com/ek8rdBcuRb
— Milken Institute (@MilkenInstitute) October 7, 2026
Last month, the heads of leading US AI labs came together in a rare show of unity to call for slowing the ​technology's development, warning it could soon improve on its own and slip beyond human control.
Read: Bill Gates warns AI is powerful enough to 'cause a billion deaths'
Claude maker Anthropic plans to caution potential ​investors in its IPO that advanced AI could pose "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity," Reuters reported last week.
Balakrishnan said on Wednesday the risk of state and non-state actors using the technology to build new weapons, "whether it's in chemistry or biology or in weapons of mass destruction, ​is very real."
Kiran Mazumdar-Shaw, founder and chairperson of Indian biopharmaceutical firm Biocon, said that while AI was a force ​for good, bad actors could use it to design new viruses or pathogens.
"The real existential threat is bioterrorism," she said at the Forbes ‌Global ⁠CEO Conference, calling for guardrails and governance. "I don't think self-governance is going to work."
Bubble worries linger
Investors' faith in the AI trade has propped up the stock market even as higher energy prices and episodic routs in the bond market have pushed borrowing costs in major economies to multi-decade highs.
But worries over how long the AI rally could last and what it ​means for global markets have persisted.
Read More: AI risk warnings rattle global markets
"If ​the AI narrative is ⁠unwound because of safety issues, regulation or because, as we go through 2027, end users don't see sufficient ROI (return on investment), there could be issues," said Rohit Sipahimalani, chief investment ​officer at Singapore state investor Temasek.
"The biggest risk to the market is the AI ​narrative. Right now, it ⁠seems very strong," Sipahimalani said at the Milken Institute event.
Bridgewater Associates founder Ray Dalio was less sanguine, saying AI was in a "classic bubble" and there was a difference between "how terrific a technology is and how terrific an investment is."
He told the Forbes ⁠event that ​rising rates and changing circumstances had not "yet harmed ​other things," but that there was pressure for interest rates to rise further.
Once higher rates began to bite, the bubble would start to burst, Dalio ​said. "I think we're close to that."

items.author: Web Desk
items.content:
The federal government on Wednesday increased the price of petrol by Rs1.82 per litre, while decreasing the price of high-speed diesel (HSD) by 91 paisas per litre for October 8.
According to a notification issued by the Petroleum Division, the price of petrol was fixed at Rs396.65 per litre, while HSD would cost Rs394.94 per litre for Thursday.
The latest revision comes a day after the government increased the price of petrol by Rs1.19 per litre, while decreasing the price of HSD by Rs1.91 per litre for October 7.
Read: Govt increases petrol by Rs1.19, cuts diesel by Rs1.91 for Oct 7
On July 17, the government announced a new pricing mechanism under which petroleum product prices would be reviewed and notified daily, replacing the weekly pricing mechanism, as renewed tensions between the United States and Iran continued to drive volatility in global oil markets and raise concerns over fuel supplies.
On September 13, PM Shehbaz announced a special relief scheme offering Rs100 per litre off petrol for motorcycles, three-wheeler rickshaws and cars with engines up to 800cc, in an attempt to shield lower-income consumers from the impact of rising petroleum prices.
Under the proposal, an estimated 11.8 million beneficiaries would be covered. Around 10 million two-wheeler users and 800,000 three-wheeler users would be entitled to relief on 20 litres of fuel per month, translating into a maximum monthly benefit of Rs2,000 per beneficiary.
Another one million users of cars up to 800cc would receive relief on 30 litres per month, providing them with a maximum benefit of Rs3,000 each.
On Sept 17, the government reintroduced austerity and fuel conservation measures amid rising fuel prices, tightening business operating hours and restricting public events.
Under the measures, notified with immediate effect, shops, markets, shopping malls, bazaars, departmental stores, grocery stores, general stores and kiryana shops would close by 9pm throughout the week, according to a notification issued by the Cabinet Division.
Marriage halls, marquees and other commercial venues hosting festive events would close by 10pm, while restaurants, cafes, eateries, food outlets and standalone fruit and vegetable shops would be allowed to operate until 11pm. Takeaway and home delivery services would remain exempt from the timing restrictions.
Global geopolitical developments continue to pose significant risks. International oil prices are influenced by decisions taken by OPEC+, conflicts in the Middle East, sanctions on oil-producing nations, and disruptions in critical shipping routes such as the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea. Any interruption in these supply chains can immediately increase crude oil prices and freight costs. Since Pakistan imports the majority of its petroleum requirements, these developments quickly translate into higher domestic fuel prices.
Oil prices rose on Wednesday, with Brent ‌futures holding above $100 a barrel on supply concerns as investors weighed a surprise drop in US crude stocks, global war-driven bottlenecks, and a storm heading for US oil-producing regions.
Brent crude futures were up $1.29, or 1.28%, to $101.87 a barrel at 10:52 am ET (1452 GMT). US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude was up 22 ​cents, or 0.25%, to $89.66.
"The release of strategic oil reserves should help contain near-term price spikes by offsetting declines in commercial inventories. However, such releases provide only temporary relief, as they do not eliminate the underlying tightness in ​the global oil market," UBS analysts wrote.

items.title: Mir Raza commission closes but mystery remains
items.summary:
Fifteen sittings, 49 witnesses and weeks of questioning later, the judicial commission probing Mir Raza’s death concluded its proceedings on Wednesday, but several key questions surrounding the case remained unanswered.
Raza, the 25-year-old entrepreneur, went missing from Karachi’s PECHS area on July 28. His body was found the following day in bushes near a wedding hall in Gulistan-e-Johar.
The final hearing turned into a searching examination of the police investigation, with the commission questioning the handling of the crime scene, missing CCTV footage, leaked private chats, cryptocurrency transactions and conflicting medical opinions.
Investigating officer (IO) Deputy Superintendent of Police (DSP) Siraj Lashari told the commission that the probe was continuing to determine whether Raza had committed suicide or had been murdered. “Police could have easily picked up someone and beaten a confession out of them, but we want justice in this case,” he said.
Rea
items.author: Our Correspondent
items.content:
Fifteen sittings, 49 witnesses and weeks of questioning later, the judicial commission probing Mir Raza’s death concluded its proceedings on Wednesday, but several key questions surrounding the case remained unanswered.
Raza, the 25-year-old entrepreneur, went missing from Karachi’s PECHS area on July 28. His body was found the following day in bushes near a wedding hall in Gulistan-e-Johar.
The final hearing turned into a searching examination of the police investigation, with the commission questioning the handling of the crime scene, missing CCTV footage, leaked private chats, cryptocurrency transactions and conflicting medical opinions.
Investigating officer (IO) Deputy Superintendent of Police (DSP) Siraj Lashari told the commission that the probe was continuing to determine whether Raza had committed suicide or had been murdered. “Police could have easily picked up someone and beaten a confession out of them, but we want justice in this case,” he said.
Read: Judicial commission visits Mir Raza murder site, summons key witness
Lashari said a super medical board was proposed because of discrepancies between the reports of Dr Usama and Dr Summaiya Syed, adding that the circumstances and evidence contradicted both reports.
Commission head Justice Umar Sial, however, questioned why the opinion of a single doctor appeared to be carrying so much weight when an eight-member medical board had already conducted the post-mortem. “The Sindh government is facing embarrassment because of Dr Usama. One Usama appears to outweigh everyone else,” he remarked.
Citizens Police Liaison Committee (CPLC) representative Kashif told the commission that its analysis of call detail records, geofencing and CCTV footage had not produced any concrete conclusion. He said geofencing began on July 28 and 29 and no suspicious activity or unusually frequent contact with a particular number was found.
Raza’s internet remained active until 4:25am, while Apple Maps was accessed between 4:10am and 4:20am. Police approached the National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency (NCCIA) and Apple for IP-related information.
The CPLC had 46 cameras in Gulistan-e-Jauhar Blocks 1 to 4, but the incident location fell outside their coverage. Raza appeared on only three cameras. The commission also questioned five missing hours of CCTV footage from Masjid Khizra. Kashif attributed the problem to the mosque’s outdated surveillance system.
Justice Sial sharply questioned the police over the preservation of the crime scene, noting that dozens of officers had entered the area.
He also questioned the evidentiary value of footage recorded on a mobile phone by Station House Officer (SHO) Adeel Afzal and noted that a guesthouse DVR had been found in the officer’s vehicle. “The crime scene was made a mess,” the judge remarked, questioning why no action had been taken against those responsible.
درجنوں پولیس افسران شامل ہوئے جس سے کرائم سین کا کباڑا کر دیا گیا، جوڈیشل کمیشن کے سخت ریمارکس
مزید پڑھیں : https://t.co/zWtDwjnO3c#MirRazaCase #Karachi #Latestnews #Expressnews pic.twitter.com/SXkK9Q8ij7
— Express News (@ExpressNewsPK) October 7, 2026
He also asked whether the police’s claim that the crime scene unit reached the spot within 15 minutes was accurate, asking: “Is the IG Sindh lying?”
Read More: ‘You botched the case, you’re also suspicious’: Judge grills SSP over Mir Raza probe
The commission grilled Lashari over Ali Shaz, whose name had surfaced in connection with a voice note.
Justice Sial questioned whether police had adequately investigated Shaz’s movements, his departure abroad, his brother’s arrival in Karachi and his apparent concern for Raza. The judge noted that two suspicious vehicles had emerged during the investigation and that Shaz owned similar vehicles.
Lashari said investigators had found no link between Shaz and the incident and that there was no record placing him near the crime scene.
The alleged leak of private conversations between Raza and his fiancée Salwa also came under scrutiny.
Lashari confirmed that police had taken Salwa’s phone and extracted private chats. Justice Sial questioned how the chats later appeared on social media. “If a private chat has been leaked, it is a crime,” the judge said, directing police to identify those responsible and register a case if necessary.
Police also told the commission that transactions worth around Rs90 million had taken place through three cryptocurrency accounts.
Lashari said the NCCIA had been approached for details. Jibran Nasir, counsel for the family, said an examination of bank accounts had identified three individuals and cryptocurrency-related payments had reached Raza’s account.
Lashari said a review of the crypto account showed a shortfall of around Rs30 million, apparently treated by the platform as a loss.
Justice Sial directed police to obtain the platform’s profit-and-loss ledger to establish the actual position.
At the close of proceedings, Justice Sial told Raza’s family that their concerns had proved justified. “No government representative contacted or met us,” he said, adding that the family had not been provided sufficient information. “Had you been kept informed, the situation would have been different,” he said.
Also Read: Mir Raza commission seeks answers from senior police officers
He rejected criticism that the commission had given the case an ethnic colour and defended questioning people associated with a mosque. “We questioned those whom we found suspicious. Saying that someone should not be questioned merely because of a mosque is not right,” he said.
Lashari said the police wanted justice rather than simply arresting someone and forcing a confession. “Whether it is suicide or murder, the investigation is continuing. Whatever the truth is, it will come out,” he said.
According to commission Registrar Abdul Majid, 15 sittings were held, and statements of 49 witnesses were recorded. The commission had concluded its proceedings and would now prepare its report and recommendations. Justice Sial said the report would be placed at the disposal of the chief minister.
The judicial commission was constituted on August 24, while the Sindh cabinet approved an extension of its tenure on October 1.
The case findings
Police initially treated Raza's death as a possible suicide, but the court ordered a second post-mortem exam to conclusively determine the cause of death after the first post-mortem report failed to give detailed insight into the victim’s demise. The second autopsy conducted after Raza’s exhumation found a firearm entry wound, multiple ante-mortem injuries and signs of internal bleeding, leading investigators to treat the case as murder.
The initial post-mortem had faced several objections, with the Karachi police surgeon identifying 14 deficiencies, including the absence of an X-ray, failure to collect hand swabs for gunshot-residue analysis and the lack of chemical examination of gunpowder marks around the bullet wound.
Also Read: Mir Raza judicial commission’s term extended until October 15
The investigation subsequently came under scrutiny from Raza’s family, who alleged serious lapses in the handling of evidence and CCTV footage and sought the formation of a joint investigation team. The Sindh High Court later rejected the family’s plea for a JIT but directed the relevant authorities to conduct the investigation impartially, fairly and expeditiously.
Police told a Senate committee in September that they had recorded statements from 78 people but had not found evidence linking anyone to Raza’s alleged murder. Investigators nevertheless continued to treat the case as murder, while reviewing medical, chemical, forensic and digital evidence.
The Sindh government had meanwhile established a judicial commission headed by Sindh High Court Justice Umar Sial to examine the circumstances surrounding Raza’s death, the conduct of the investigation and any possible negligence or concealment of evidence by police or other officials.
The judicial commission had so far examined police records, witness statements and the circumstances surrounding Mir Raza Ali’s death, with its proceedings raising discrepancies in witness accounts, the handling of evidence and the initial post-mortem. The commission also questioned senior police and health officials over the investigation, including the handling of CCTV footage, Raza’s phone and smartwatch, and the initial focus on a possible suicide.

items.content:
The African Democratic Congress (ADC) governorship candidate in Gombe State, Bala Bello Tinka, has pledged to review the restrictions placed on commercial motorcycle operators, popularly known as Achaba, by the state government if elected.
Daily Trust reports that Governor Muhammadu Inuwa Yahaya had in June 2025 imposed a night time restriction on commercial motorcycle operations, in Gombe metropolis and environs from 7:00 PM to 6:00 AM to reduce crime.
Speaking while addressing residents and supporters across Gombe metropolis, Tinka said if elected, he would lift the restrictions on Achaba operations, subject to appropriate safety and regulatory measures, and allow operators to resume full-time services across the state.
He specifically promised to restore 24-hour Achaba operations, arguing that thousands of young people depend on the business for their livelihoods, while many residents rely on commercial motorcycles for transportation, particularly during late hours.
Tinka also outlined key priorities that would guide the early months of his administration, saying he would take decisive action against phone and handbag snatching if elected governor.
The ADC candidate said that within the first two months of assuming office, his administration would take firm measures to tackle street crime, particularly the activities of criminals who snatch mobile phones and handbags from residents, motorists and pedestrians.
He said residents should be able to move freely within their communities without fear of criminal attacks, adding that his administration would strengthen security efforts and work closely with relevant security agencies and community stakeholders to address street-level crime.
Tinka also reiterated his commitment to free education from primary school through university, saying the policy would ensure that children from poor and less privileged families are not denied educational opportunities because of financial constraints.
He said investing in education would give young people more opportunities to acquire the knowledge and skills needed to contribute meaningfully to Gombe State’s development.
On healthcare, Tinka pledged to provide free antenatal care for all pregnant women and free medical treatment for children from birth to five years of age. He said the measures would reduce the financial burden on families and improve access to essential maternal and child healthcare services across the state.
Tinka said his administration would prioritise security, free and accessible education, maternal and child healthcare, youth employment and economic empowerment, describing them as key areas for improving the welfare and living standards of ordinary residents across Gombe State.

items.author: Gaurav Bagur
items.content:
Consumer electronics manufacturer Lumio raised $12 Mn (around ₹102.5 Cr) in a Series A funding round led by Blume Ventures, with participation from existing backers Stellaris Venture Partners and 3one4 Capital.
“This funding gives us the opportunity to invest further in our products and software, explore new categories, and strengthen quality and after-sales support as we grow,” said cofounder Raghu Reddy in a social media post.
The startup also plans to expand its retail presence, enabling customers to see and try its products offline before making a purchase.
“India’s 3-3.5 Cr affluent households are reimagining their living rooms, and no longer default to legacy brands. Raghu and Kailash have leveraged their deep experience in home entertainment and customer insights to create a compelling home entertainment brand in Lumio,” said Sajith Pai, partner, Blume Ventures.
Established in 2024 by ex-Xiaomi India CBO Reddy and ex-Flipkart exec Kailash Sankaranarayanan, Lumio launched its first smart TV lineup in early 2025 and has since expanded its hardware portfolio to include projectors and speakers.
Aside from its catalogue, it has also created an AI-powered personalised content discovery engine called TLDR backed by multiple patent filings and available in nine Indian languages.
The brand aims to leverage software as its differentiator from legacy electronics makers.
To enhance speed and performance of their smart TVs, Lumio also compliments its products with high-performance SoC for rapid app launches, ample RAM to prevent slowdowns during multitasking, and a fine-tuned network chipset for stable connectivity in variable Indian internet conditions.
Lumio currently claims to serve over 35,000 households across 5,000+ pin codes. It claims to have crossed ₹100 Cr in GMV within 13 months of commercial sales, more than tripling its GMV YoY for the April-August period in 2026..
Prior to this, it had raised a $4.3 Mn seed funding round in July 2024 from Stellaris Venture Partners, 3one4 Capital, Mamaearth’s Varun Alagh, and Tracxn’s Abhishek Goyal, as well as other angel investors.
The startup competes with established players like Samsung, LG, Sony, and Xiaomi in India’s consumer electronics market, which is estimated to grow at 6.6% CAGR over the next eight years to reach $158.4 Bn by 2034.

Dan selang satu tahun sejak generasi sebelumnya, akhirnya HUAWEI Indonesia mengumumkan secara resmi harga HUAWEI WATCH GT 7 Series, yang kembali tersedia dalam setidaknya tiga opsi berbeda. Namun tidak hanya fokus tingkatkan fitur kesehatan, HUAWEI WATCH GT 7 Pro kini bisa melacak lebih banyak data saat digunakan untuk jenis olahraga tertentu, termasuk bersepeda hingga bermain ski. Sehingga wajar bila harga HUAWEI WATCH GT 7 Series tahun ini mengalami kenaikan pada semua opsi yang ditawarkan.
Baca juga: Berkunjung ke HUAWEI Ox Horn Campus, Pusat Pengembangan dengan Nuansa Kastil Ala Hogwarts
Harga HUAWEI WATCH GT 7 Pro Mulai Rp5 Jutaan
Langsung saja, untuk opsi yang paling terjangkau, harga HUAWEI WATCH GT 7 41mm dibanderol Rp3,999 juta, alias naik sekitar Rp500 ribu dibandingkan generasi sebelumnya. Sementara untuk opsi 46mm, dijual Rp4,399 juta. Keduanya memiliki kelengkapan fitur setara, hanya saja berbeda dimensi (yang tentunya juga sedikit berdampak pada daya tahan baterainya).
Sementara untuk harga HUAWEI WATCH GT 7 Pro, kini dibanderol Rp5,499 juta untuk ketiga opsi warna yang ditawarkan—semuanya mengusung bahan strap yang sama. Kabar baiknya, selama periode penjualan perdana hingga 6 November 2026 mendatang, konsumen diberikan bonus senilai Rp1,3 juta untuk pembelian WATCH GT 7 Pro. Yakni berupa TWS HUAWEI FreeBuds SE 2, gratis membership HUAWEI Health+ selama tiga bulan, serta strap tambahan berbahan kulit vegan.
Konsumen yang membeli WATCH GT 7 standar juga tetap mendapatkan bonus senilai hingga Rp865 ribu, terdiri dari TWS HUAWEI FreeBuds SE 2 dan gratis membership HUAWEI Health+ selama tiga bulan. Harga HUAWEI WATCH GT 7 Series juga bisa didapatkan lebih murah lagi, bila Gizmo friends berhasil mendapatkan cashback tambahan Rp500 ribu, yang diberikan sembari merayakan 12 tahun eksistensi perangkat wearables HUAWEI, hingga 15 November 2026.
HUAWEI WATCH GT 7 Pro tersedia dalam tiga pilihan warna, yakni Green, Yellow, dan Black. Sementara untuk WATCH GT 7, tersedia opsi warna Grey, Black, Yellow, dan Blue untuk ukuran 46mm, dan Grey, Blue, serta White dalam ukuran 41mm.
Punya Fitur Pelacakan Kesehatan dan Olahraga Lebih Komplit
HUAWEI WATCH GT 7 varian 41mm & 46mm
Salah satu aspek yang ditingkatkan dalam segi desain pada HUAWEI WATCH GT 7 Series, adalah EasyCross strap yang memungkinkan penggunaan lebih praktis, karena ujung strap akan tersembunyi dibuat tersembunyi, demi tampilan lebih rapi atau seamless. Semua varian juga dilengkapi dengan layar AMOLED yang bisa menyala cerah hingga 3000 nits.
Sementara pada HUAWEI WATCH GT 7 Pro, digunakan sejumlah material premium seperti bezel berbahan keramik nanocrystal, yang dirancang tahan gores serta korosi. Bodinya sendiri mengusung bahan titanium alloy, dan bagian layar tetap terproteksi kaca safir demi perlindungan maksimal.
Dalam melakukan proses pemantauan kesehatan, WATCH GT 7 Series bisa menghasilkan insight komprehensif yang dapat membantu pengguna memahami kondisi tubuhnya—termasuk melalui fitur baru, yakni skor physical readiness berbasis AI untuk membantu melihat kesiapan tubuh sebelum beraktivitas.
Semua varian HUAWEI WATCH GT 7 Mendukung fitur pemantauan risiko diabetes dini, dan khusus varian Pro, menghadirkan Advanced Heart Health Management yang mencakup Coronary Heart Disease Risk Study pertama di industri, pelacakan EKG, pelacakan aritmia jantung tersertifikasi, hingga Arterial Stiffness Assessment. Ditambah fitur pelacakan aktivitas olahraga yang juga komplit, daya tahan baterai WATCH GT 7 Series diklaim bisa sampai 21 hari (atau 14 hari khusus varian 41mm).

items.title: Selling Intelligence Was the Warm-Up For AI. Owning Vertical Markets May Be The Play
items.summary:

In a previous piece for Inc42, I argued that the black box was losing the boardroom, and that enterprise AI built on the customer’s own terms was the opening worth chasing. The months since have made the argument more literal than expected. The frontier labs are now moving into their customers’ markets, and they are doing it in plain sight.

items.author: Pranav Pai
items.content:
The most profitable move in artificial intelligence may no longer be selling intelligence. It is selling a model to a company, wiring it into that company’s most valuable work, learning the business from the inside, and then shipping the product that competes with it.
In a previous piece for Inc42, I argued that the black box was losing the boardroom, and that enterprise AI built on the customer’s own terms was the opening worth chasing. The months since have made the argument more literal than expected. The frontier labs are now moving into their customers’ markets, and they are doing it in plain sight.
The Pattern Has Hardened Into A Playbook
Read the moves of the past year together and a sequence emerges. Sell the model to the world’s most valuable businesses. Help wire it into their most sensitive and highest-margin work. Map how the business runs from the inside. Then turn those learnings into a product and stand up as the customer’s competitor.
Each step, taken alone, reads as partnership. Assembled, they read as strategy.
Of course, a lot still depends on execution. Just because a model company knows how a customer runs its business does not mean it can run that business better than the customer. However, the labs would say this is simply where the technology leads, and that is part of the truth.
It is also the most dependable way to convert a supplier relationship into a market entrant position.
Figma is the clearest illustration. It partnered with Anthropic on AI design tooling, the kind of collaboration that looks like validation for a newly public company. Then Mike Krieger, Anthropic’s chief product officer, resigned from Figma’s board, and three days later Anthropic launched Claude Design, a standalone tool aimed squarely at Figma.
The stock fell around 7% on the day, and the activist fund Findell Capital has since pushed the board to review the entire Anthropic relationship.
Asked about it at a closed event, Figma’s Dylan Field reached for the exact phrase OpenAI’s board once used to remove Sam Altman, saying the lab had not been “consistently candid.” The partner had become the competitor inside a single news cycle.
Harvey is a more practical example, because the evidence sits on Anthropic’s own website, which still features the legal startup as a customer success story for contract analysis, due diligence and litigation. In May, Anthropic launched Claude for Legal and began selling those same workflows directly to law firms.
Harvey carries an $11 Bn valuation, and the model that powered the challenger now stands beside it as a rival.
The pattern repeats wherever a workflow is worth owning. Intercom built its support agents on OpenAI’s models, and OpenAI now sells Presence, its own voice and chat support agent. Abridge and Ambience built clinical documentation on OpenAI’s API, and OpenAI now sells ChatGPT for Healthcare to hospitals, with a free tier for individual clinicians and documentation built in.
Benchling embedded Claude into biotech R&D across more than 1,300 companies, and Anthropic now sells its own research workbench, Claude Science.
The same logic is reaching financial services, where Claude connects to market-data providers and runs credit memos and know-your-customer checks inside banks. In each case the supplier watched the customer prove the market, then walked into it.
The strength of this incentive also shows up clearly in the earliest partnerships within the industry. Microsoft owns roughly 27% of OpenAI. It had bought GitHub in 2018 for $7.5 Bn. OpenAI is now building a jobs platform for professional hiring and, as per reporting in The Information, a code repository, moves that would sit against LinkedIn and GitHub, both Microsoft properties.
This is not a claim that anyone has been denied. It is a measure of how far the pull toward the customer’s market reaches, when it can tug even against an early strategic investor’s own businesses.
Pharma Is Where the Trap Is Sharpest
Drug discovery is the case that should give every board pause. Novo Nordisk and Bristol Myers Squibb route revenue and workflow data into Claude, treating Anthropic as a supplier. In May, BMS placed Claude before more than 30,000 employees as what it called a shared intelligence platform across research, clinical development and manufacturing.
On 30 June, Anthropic launched Claude Science and, in the same breath, announced it would run its own preclinical drug discovery programmes.
The customers, through their unchecked reliance on the model, are funding what they treat as a vendor but is in fact a competitor lurking in the shadows, and are helping to sharpen the very capability that may one day contest their pipelines.
The market read it at once. On the day, Schrödinger fell as much as 8.3%, Recursion 3.3% and IQVIA more than 2.3%. Anthropic frames the work around neglected diseases that large pharma overlooks, and that framing is fair as far as it goes. It does not change the structural fact that the vendor has walked onto the customer’s field.
The Economics Make Restraint Implausible
Follow the money and the behaviour explains itself. Anthropic’s revenue run rate reached about $65 Bn by the end of July, up from roughly $1 Bn in December 2024, at a $965 Bn valuation, with a filing already lodged for a listing that could come this autumn. OpenAI has roughly doubled to about $40 Bn in revenue.
Eight of the Fortune 10 are already Claude customers, a sign of how much of the real economy now runs through a single supplier. Selling tokens is a commodity business with thin and contested margins. Selling the finished application into a market with real returns on capital is where the value pools.
A company carrying a near-trillion-dollar valuation into public markets cannot credibly promise to leave the richest layer of the stack to its customers forever. None of this requires bad faith. The incentive is obvious, which is exactly what makes the move more likely.
The AI Narrative Is Getting Harder To Reconcile
This is where the public story and the operating record pull apart, and founders are reading one against the other.
The labs speak the language of safety, abundance and responsible stewardship, and in the same year they have entered design, law, support, healthcare and drug discovery. The mood at the frontier can run further still.
On the All-In podcast in August, investor Gavin Baker said he had been told by people he trusts that Dario Amodei has floated the idea that Anthropic “might be the only private company in the world” at some point, with only governments beside it.
Anthropic rejected the account outright, with one of its researchers calling it false and Amodei rebutting it directly. Mark Zuckerberg has since published an essay making the opposite case, for open models and a distribution of power rather than its concentration.
This episode matters not because it is settled, but because it is not. The claims are second-hand, disputed and changing week to week, and that instability is itself the point.
Nobody, inside these companies or outside them, can tell you today how this resolves. Of course, this narrative is great support and justification for the enterprise value of an IPO this large. What is not in doubt is the direction of the incentive and the exposure it creates for everyone who builds on top.
Alex Karp of Palantir has named the mechanism most plainly, arguing that enterprises are “paying for tokens that create no value” while surrendering their alpha, the proprietary edge that makes a business defensible.
Michael Burry put it more bluntly, remarking that Anthropic was eating Palantir’s lunch. The narratives will keep shifting. The opportunity arithmetic underneath them will not.
Own Your Alpha
For India the exposure is doubled. The country’s software firms and its 1,900-plus global capability centres are among the heaviest consumers of frontier APIs, and its services industry wires client workflows through those same models, sending client alpha upstream with every integration. The lesson from the cases above is that being a large and loyal customer is no shield. It may simply be the reconnaissance.
The opening is the same size as the risk, and it is the one I argued for last time, only more urgent now. Vertical AI built on domain depth the labs cannot see from the outside. Private and on-premise deployment of open models. Harnesses that keep proprietary data inside the building.
Open-weight models isolated from the internet and run for a single enterprise. Intercom has already moved its agent partly onto its own in-house open-weights model rather than depend on a supplier that competes with it, and that is the direction of travel.
India’s sovereign-model efforts and its vertical software builders should read this moment as the start of a new market preference forming.
Every Indian founder and CTO now faces the same reckoning before the next integration. It is to know precisely what alpha they are sending upstream, and whether they can protect it before it returns as somebody else’s product. The labs may or may not become the last companies standing. The firms that decide early to own their alpha will not have to find out.
The post Selling Intelligence Was the Warm-Up For AI. Owning Vertical Markets May Be The Play appeared first on Inc42 Media.

items.author: Onsa Mustafa
items.content:
Copyright protected content copied from PhoneWorld website.
Fixed-line broadband services in Pakistan remain expensive for consumers looking for high-speed internet, with monthly prices reaching up to Rs61,600 for a 1,000 Mbps connection. Some packages also come with monthly data limits and fair-usage policies.
According to the latest tariff comparison released by the Pakistan Telecommunication Authority (PTA), broadband prices vary significantly among operators and increase considerably as users move toward higher speeds.
Transworld Charges Rs61,600 for 1,000 Mbps
Transworld has the highest listed price among the packages included in the comparison. Its 1,000 Mbps FTTH package costs Rs61,600 per month, excluding taxes.
The company’s 500 Mbps package is priced at Rs36,550, while the 300 Mbps and 200 Mbps packages cost Rs19,675 and Rs10,099, respectively.
These prices show how quickly monthly broadband costs can increase for consumers seeking gigabit-level connectivity.
PTCL Packages Include Data Limits
PTCL offers a range of FTTH packages with different speeds and monthly usage limits. Its 40 Mbps package costs Rs3,350 and comes with a 2.5-terabyte volume limit.
The 100 Mbps package costs Rs6,900 with a 4 TB limit, while the 200 Mbps package is priced at Rs13,500 with a 6 TB limit. Its 350 Mbps package costs Rs23,000 and includes an 8 TB monthly limit.
The tariff data shows that faster advertised speeds do not always mean unlimited usage. PTCL’s FTTH packages have specified monthly volumes, while its DSL packages are listed as unlimited.
PTCL’s DSL services start at Rs2,999 for 10 Mbps and go up to Rs10,999 for 100 Mbps. The PTA lists an overage download charge of Rs100 per GB, although the service becomes unlimited after an additional 15 GB beyond the quota.
StormFiber, Optix and Other Providers
StormFiber’s packages range from Rs1,699 for 2 Mbps to Rs14,399 for 250 Mbps. Its 100 Mbps package costs Rs7,399, while the 180 Mbps option is priced at Rs12,299.
Optix offers 30 Mbps at around Rs2,328, 50 Mbps at Rs2,910, 75 Mbps at Rs3,783, 100 Mbps at Rs4,656 and 200 Mbps at approximately Rs8,004. However, these packages are subject to the company’s fair-usage policy.
Wateen’s FTTH packages start at Rs3,318 for 10 Mbps and reach Rs20,594 for 100 Mbps. Its 50 Mbps package costs Rs9,584.
WorldCall’s cable broadband remains one of the lower-cost options in the comparison. Its packages start at Rs699 for 1 Mbps unlimited service and go up to Rs3,500 for 10 Mbps.
For FTTH connections, WorldCall offers packages starting at Rs2,350 for 10 Mbps and going up to Rs11,400 for 100 Mbps.
Brainnet offers 8 Mbps at Rs1,799 and 15 Mbps at Rs1,999, while its 500 Mbps package is priced at Rs16,728.
Taxes Will Increase Final Cost
The PTA has clarified that the listed figures represent monthly charges and do not include applicable taxes. This means the final amount paid by consumers will be higher than the prices shown in the comparison.
The tariff data also highlights that internet users need to look beyond advertised speeds when choosing a broadband package. Monthly data limits, overage charges and fair-usage policies can significantly affect the overall cost.
The PTA has also noted that its comparison does not cover every location-specific or region-based package available in the market. Consumers are advised to check the latest tariffs and package conditions directly with their respective broadband providers before subscribing.
The comparison covers major fixed-line broadband operators, including PTCL, WorldCall Telecom, Wateen Telecom, Optix Pakistan, StormFiber, Transworld and Brainnet.
Overall, the PTA data shows a wide gap in broadband pricing across Pakistan, particularly at higher speeds, where monthly charges can reach tens of thousands of rupees.

items.author: Onsa Mustafa
items.content:
Copyright protected content copied from PhoneWorld website.
The Federal Board of Revenue (FBR) has proposed new rules for automated scrutiny of taxpayers. The rules also expand the use of artificial intelligence and automated systems for checking individual income tax returns.
Under the proposed mechanism, the system will automatically examine tax returns to identify factual errors, legal mistakes, and possible discrepancies. Taxpayers will be informed about these issues and given an opportunity to explain or correct them before the FBR takes any legal or penal action.
The proposed rules, titled “Procedure for electronic scrutiny and intimation of issues detected by the automated system,” have been introduced through amendments to the Income Tax Rules, 2002. The draft will be finalised after receiving feedback from relevant stakeholders.
FBR Unveils New Rules for Automated Scrutiny of Taxpayers
The new system will use information already available with tax authorities to analyse tax returns. It will cross-check the information declared by taxpayers against other available data to identify possible inconsistencies.
When the system detects an issue, it will generate an advance notification for the taxpayer through the FBR’s IRIS portal. The notification will explain the factual or legal issue and allow the taxpayer to provide clarification or correct the return.
Importantly, simply detecting a discrepancy through the automated system will not automatically lead to enforcement action.
Taxpayers to Get Time to Respond
Under the proposed rules, taxpayers will receive at least seven days to respond to a discrepancy identified in their tax return.
They will be able to explain the issue or make the required correction through the prescribed process. If a taxpayer does not respond within the given period, the system or relevant tax officer will issue another reminder, providing an additional period of at least seven days.
The relevant Inland Revenue officer will then review the taxpayer’s response. If there is no response, the officer will also consider that before deciding what action should be taken under the Income Tax Ordinance and applicable rules.
Human Oversight Will Remain
Although the new system will automate the initial scrutiny process, the final decision will remain with the relevant tax officer.
The officer will assess the discrepancy and the taxpayer’s response before deciding whether further action is necessary. This means the automated system will mainly serve as an early screening and notification mechanism rather than directly imposing penalties or starting legal proceedings.
The proposed framework could make the tax scrutiny process more systematic by allowing the FBR to identify potential errors at an early stage. At the same time, giving taxpayers an opportunity to clarify or correct discrepancies before enforcement action could help reduce unnecessary disputes.
The initiative represents another step toward greater automation in Pakistan’s tax administration and could increase the use of data-driven systems in the assessment and monitoring of taxpayers.

items.author: Usama Anjum
items.content:
Copyright protected content copied from PhoneWorld website.
The Ministry of Information Technology and Telecommunication (MoITT) has proposed a tougher competition regime for Pakistan’s telecom sector, including powers for the regulator to impose national roaming obligations on operators with Significant Market Power (SMP).
The proposals are contained in the draft Telecommunication Competition Rules, 2026, which seek to establish a sector-specific framework for regulating competition in telecom markets while placing greater emphasis on consumer welfare, market efficiency, and competitive impact.
Under the proposed rules, the Pakistan Telecommunication Authority (PTA) may require a licensee with SMP to provide national roaming access where it considers the measure necessary to promote effective competition, expand network coverage, protect consumers, or ensure efficient use of telecom infrastructure.
National roaming arrangements would have to be offered on fair, reasonable, transparent, and non-discriminatory terms. The Authority would also determine their technical feasibility, operational scope, and duration.
The proposed provisions could increase regulatory scrutiny of dominant operators at a time when Pakistan’s telecom industry is undergoing consolidation and preparing for wider 5G deployment.
PTA proposed broader enforcement powers
The draft rules would give the Authority additional powers to act against licensees found to have violated the proposed competition framework.
The PTA could issue directions, require corrective measures, impose proportionate regulatory obligations, and initiate proceedings under the relevant law.
The Authority would also be empowered to adjudicate disputes arising under the framework. In doing so, it may consider factors including market efficiency, consumer welfare, proportionality, technical feasibility, and the impact of a particular decision on competition.
The draft rules also clarify that the proposed telecom-specific framework would operate without prejudice to the jurisdiction of the Competition Commission of Pakistan (CCP) under the Competition Act, 2010.
The provision comes against the backdrop of a long-running jurisdictional dispute involving the MoITT, PTA, and CCP over the regulation of competition in the telecom sector. The Islamabad High Court has previously held that the CCP has overarching jurisdiction over competition matters.
The draft also proposes greater regulatory discipline for applications submitted to the Authority. Applicants would be required to pay fees prescribed under Schedule I, replacing the previous reference to “reasonable fees.”
In addition, the PTA would be authorized to issue guidelines, determinations, frameworks, and directions needed to implement the proposed rules.
The proposed national roaming regime builds on Pakistan’s earlier telecom policy. The 2015 Telecom Policy had envisaged national roaming for SMP operators on fair and non-discriminatory terms, with the objective of supporting wider network coverage.
The framework comes as issues surrounding market concentration, spectrum holdings, infrastructure access, and barriers to entry gain greater importance in Pakistan’s telecom market.
Recent PTA proposals have also suggested a 25 percent market-share threshold as an initial trigger for assessing SMP, alongside other factors such as market concentration, spectrum ownership, essential infrastructure, financial strength, network effects, and barriers to entry.
If implemented, the proposed rules would give the telecom regulator a broader set of tools to address competitive concerns while making consumer welfare and the impact on competition central considerations in regulatory decisions.

A modern Information Technology (IT) hub has been established in Zhob, Balochistan, to provide local youth with access to digital skills, technology training, and new employment opportunities.

The establishment of the IT hub is part of broader efforts to expand development and digital inclusion in remote areas of Balochistan. By bringing modern technology facilities closer to young people, the initiative aims to help them prepare for changing employment trends and the demands of the future economy.
The project is particularly significant for Zhob, where access to modern digital facilities and technology-related training can provide young people with opportunities that were previously difficult to access locally.
As digital services and remote work continue to expand, initiatives such as the Zhob IT hub could play an important role in connecting youth from less-developed areas with Pakistan’s growing digital economy.

items.author: Anjali Jain
items.content:
While the funding trends in the Indian startup ecosystem have been showing signs of stability over the past few months, investor appetite for startups operating across different sectors and stages is varying significantly.
Although Indian startup funding in the July-September quarter increased 5% YoY to $2.2 Bn across 210 deals, the startup investment story is increasingly turning into one of growth stage capital rather than late stage backing.
As per Inc42’s Indian Tech Startup Funding Report Q3 2026, capital deployed at the growth stage jumped 46% YoY to $1.1 Bn during the quarter. Meanwhile, funding lapped by late stage startups remained flat at $994 Mn.
Beyond the headline funding numbers, investors seemed to be more active in evaluating startups at the Series B and C stages as compared to late stage ones. During the quarter, growth stage deal count rose 38% to YoY 90, whereas late stage deals declined 10% to 27.
The divergence is also visible in cheque sizes. The median growth stage ticket size rose 4% to $8.3 Mn, while the median late stage check dropped 18% to $18 Mn.
The data points to a funding market where capital is flowing more readily into startups that still have substantial growth ahead, while investors are becoming more cautious about committing large sums to mature startups.
Investors highlighted a combination of factors behind this shift, including a growing pool of early stage capital, more inflated valuations at the late stage, greater scrutiny of business fundamentals and exit visibility, and a changing sector thesis.
Why More Capital Is Flowing Into Growth Stage Startups
One explanation lies in the expansion of India’s startup ecosystem, which now comprises about 2.5 Lakh businesses. A growing pool of investors backing startups at their earliest stages is creating a larger pipeline of businesses seeking subsequent rounds.
Vikram Gupta, founder and managing partner at IvyCap Ventures, said the number of early stage and micro VC funds in India has increased substantially, helping create this pipeline of capital as startups progress towards Series A and Series B rounds.
“If the number of early stage funds has increased, very naturally you will see a growth in the early to growth stage investments,” Gupta said.
The changing sector mix is also reinforcing this trend, with investor interest broadening beyond ecommerce, fintech and consumer internet startups towards frontier technologies such as AI, deeptech and cleantech.
AI emerged as the top funded sector in Q3 with $438 Mn, up 265% YoY, followed by cleantech at $433 Mn, up 267%, and deeptech at $290 Mn, up 176%. In contrast, fintech funding declined 11% and ecommerce funding fell 31%.
The quarter also saw some of the largest funding rounds concentrated in these newer categories. AI startup Emergent raised $130 Mn, EV startup River raised $120 Mn and spacetech startup Pixxel raised $100 Mn.
Gupta said the newer sectors — AI, spacetech, EVs — have longer gestation periods, meaning investors often wait for technology validation, customer adoption and other milestones before committing larger sums.
However, the growth of these newer segments doesn’t necessarily translate into investors shying away from more established segments like fintech, ecommerce or consumer companies, said Apoorva Ranjan Sharma, cofounder of Venture Catalysts. “Those are now more mature sectors and investors expect stronger numbers from them.”
Why Late Stage Capital Pool Remains Thin
Even as more startups reach the growth stage, the pool of investors capable of funding them at scale remains relatively small.
IvyCap’s Gupta believes that India has a limited number of investors capable of writing large late stage cheques.
Prior to the funding winter, India’s late stage ecosystem relied heavily on global investors such as SoftBank, Tiger Global, Insight Partners and Sequoia Capital, which were among the most active sources of large growth stage cheques.
“The larger dollar capital comes from the US and other geographies,” Gupta said, adding that changes in US policies and market conditions have made overseas deployment more difficult.
He said US government securities have also become more attractive as a lower-risk investment, making it harder for funds to raise and deploy capital in markets such as India.
While family offices, high-net-worth individuals and government-backed funds have stepped in to bridge some of the gap, Gupta said India would need at least $100 Bn of capital to become globally competitive.
This has created a funding asymmetry. India now has a growing base of early stage investors backing startups through initial rounds, but a much smaller pool of capital available when those companies need substantially larger cheques to scale further.
Why Late Stage Investors Are Holding Back
The availability of capital is only part of the problem. Investors active at the late stage are also becoming more selective.
According to Venture Catalysts’ Sharma, Series A and B investors can assess a startup’s product, revenues, customers and execution while the business still has significant room to grow. By Series C and beyond, valuations are substantially higher, leaving investors with less room for error and making the potential return harder to justify.
Several startups that raised capital at high valuations in earlier rounds are still working to deliver the business performance needed to justify the premiums, Gupta said. This is particularly relevant for deeptech companies, where technology development and commercialisation may take longer.
“If an investor is putting in $30-50 Mn, there has to be a clear plan for how that money will be used and what the company will achieve,” Sharma said. “Growth continues to be important, but growth alone is no longer enough.”
The shift is also changing how late stage rounds are structured. Gupta said investors may commit less capital upfront and release additional funds only when startups meet specific milestones. An investor capable of writing a $25 Mn cheque, for instance, could invest $15 Mn initially and reserve the remaining $10 Mn for a later tranche.
Similar structures of investment deals are also seen at early and growth stages as well. For instance, Fireside Ventures committed ₹100 Cr capital to Arovia Consumer, a new ecommerce rollup venture by ex-Soulfull MD Prashant Parameswaran, with investments flowing as and when the startup closes acquisitions.
Founders, meanwhile, are becoming more cautious about dilution and raising only what they need, Sharma said.
What Could Unlock The Next Funding Wave?
The current funding mix could eventually help narrow the late stage gap. The startups attracting Series A and B capital today — particularly in AI, deeptech, climate and manufacturing — could become a larger pipeline of companies seeking Series C, D and pre-IPO funding as they prove their technology, build markets and demonstrate commercial traction.
Gupta said AI-funded companies are now entering a phase where investors will be able to assess how much of the sector’s promise translates into actual business performance. Some could emerge as major winners, while others may struggle to justify their valuations.
Deeptech companies are also moving towards commercialisation, with recent public-market milestones providing investors with evidence that some of these businesses can scale beyond the venture stage. The bumper IPOs of SEDEMAC and ESDS Software Solution, along with Skyroot’s progress towards its next funding round, point to a broader pipeline of deeptech companies moving towards larger capital requirements.
The number of companies requiring late stage capital is also on the upward trajectory. Inc42’s investor survey found that 72% of investors have late stage startups in their portfolios that are at some level of IPO readiness.
But IPO readiness does not necessarily mean these companies will need another large private round. Sharma said mature startups can instead raise smaller amounts, facilitate secondary transactions or move towards public markets.
Gupta said greater visibility on a public market exit can itself unlock late stage investor interest, as investors become more comfortable when a company has a clearer path to an IPO.
Successful listings could therefore become an important catalyst for the next phase of late stage funding. Gupta expects more capital to return as investors see successful outcomes, while Sharma said stronger profitability, more realistic valuations and successful IPOs will be important for rebuilding confidence.
The bigger question is whether the companies now raising Series A and B capital can build the scale, profitability and exit visibility needed to attract the much larger pools of capital required at Series C, pre-IPO and beyond.
Edited by Akshit Pushkarna
Creatives by Abhyam Gusai

items.content:
Defence Minister Khawaja Asif on Wednesday said the government was trying to avoid imposing governor’s rule in Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa, but warned that it could resort to the option if no other way was left.
Speaking to reporters in Islamabad, the minister said that there was nothing impeding the imposition og governor’s rule in the province, but the government was trying not to use what he described as the “last option”.
“If there is no other way left, then we can use that option,” he said.
Read: Afridi calls Kundi's security meeting ‘attack on Constitution’, warns against 'another East Pakistan' situation
Asif also criticised the Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI), urging it to “play the role of a political party rather than a terrorist organisation”.
“We cannot leave the capital at their mercy so that every two or three months they join hands with the Taliban and march on the capital,” he said.
The minister described the Taliban as an “anti-Pakistan power” and said that if the PTI allied with it and attacked the capital, the government had the right and responsibility to protect Islamabad.
He referred to the PTI leadership’s alleged failure to attend the funerals of people killed in Taliban attacks and its failure to condemn explosions, claiming that these factors indicated, in his view, that the Taliban had a militant component within the K-P government.
Asif also described the PTI’s planned long march as an “attack on Islamabad”, saying previous attacks on the capital had also been motivated by political parties’ efforts to establish their credibility within their own ranks.
He attributed the failure of talks between the government and opposition to internal differences within the PTI.
“Differences within the PTI have intensified,” he said, adding that members of the PTI sitting in the National Assembly, its negotiating team and even its allies wanted a solution to the issue that was acceptable to the entire country.
Asked about the PTI’s demand for a meeting with Imran Khan before deciding whether to postpone its long march, Asif said he did not know about it.
Also Read: Govt will not accept demands by 'holding state hostage', Sanaullah warns PTI
He instead urged the PTI to look at its record.
“Look at your past. When we were imprisoned, what facilities did you provide us? Did you keep us at the Marriott?” he said.
Asif reiterated that the PTI should act as a political party rather than a terrorist organisation.
Later, in a post on X, Asif accused the K-P government of having “complete collusion” with terrorists and said there were ample examples and evidence of what he called a “facilitator ecosystem”, which, he said, could not be tolerated.
He criticised the provincial government for what he described as “complete detachment” from terrorism in the province and “criminal indifference”.
The minister said the PTI provincial government was focused on its “so-called failed political long march” while its alleged facilitators had unleashed a fresh wave of terrorism against the people of K-P.
پی ٹی آئی کی صوبائی حکومت کی صوبے میں دہشت گردی سے مکمل لاتعلقی اور مجرمانہ بے حسی جاری ...بس بہت ہوگیا!!!
پی ٹی آئی کی صوبائی حکومت نام نہاد ناکام سیاسی لانگ مارچ کے لیے سڑکوں پر گھوم رہی ہے جب کہ ان کے سہولت کاروں نے اِسی دوران KPK کے لوگوں کے خلاف ایک تازہ دہشت گردی کی لہر…
— Khawaja M. Asif (@KhawajaMAsif) October 7, 2026
He referred to the Oct 6 attack in Dera Ismail Khan, saying five people had been killed, including two customs officials.
“Completely numb to this serious matter, the entire provincial cabinet, including the chief minister, is fully engrossed in their political failed long march,” he said.
Asif accused the provincial government of neither condemning the deaths nor offering condolences to the families of the victims, attending their funerals or visiting their homes.
“This is inexcusable by any standard,” he said.
He further criticised the chief minister for allegedly scheduling a late-night meeting to reprimand the inspector general of police and chief secretary for attending the governor’s security meeting.
According to Asif, the chief minister and his cabinet had “completely abandoned” the people of the province to the mercy of terrorists.
He claimed that people in various parts of K-P were protesting against the provincial government.
“This can no longer be tolerated. Enough blood of K-P’s people has been spilt,” he said, alleging that there was “complete collusion” between the provincial government and terrorists.
Read More: PTI long march enters fourth day, heads to Khyber as party rallies behind K-P CM
The minister also contrasted the PTI government’s treatment of the Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz leadership with what he described as the PML-N’s conduct while in opposition.
He said Nawaz Sharif, his family and the PML-N leadership had been imprisoned during the PTI’s tenure, but the PML-N had continued to perform its parliamentary role under the Constitution.
“It did not hold the country and institutions hostage. It fought a legal and constitutional battle in the courts and parliament. It did not ally with the Taliban,” he said.
Asif said the time had come to make “crucial decisions”, adding that K-P could no longer be left “at the mercy of incompetent, insensitive rulers and Taliban allies”.
He also warned against putting the unity of the country at risk, saying an entire province could not be “held hostage”.
The issue of Governor’s Rule has become a major point of contention between the federal and K-P government. On September 21, Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi said the government was consulting the law ministry on legal options for the province, including Governor’s Rule, if the PTI proceeded with its long march. Two days later, however, Information Minister Atta Tarar ruled out any plan to impose Governor’s Rule, saying the federal government had no intention of removing the PTI administration.
Some federal ministers publicly raised the possibility of federal intervention in K-P. Federal Minister for Kashmir Affairs Amir Muqam said consultations were under way on the "constitutional and legal option" of imposing Governors' Rule.
Afridi, however, rejected the warnings and said he would not retreat from his position because of threats of Governors' Rule or an emergency. He also said PTI supporters could take to the streets at short notice if an attempt was made to remove him.
However, amid the speculation, just days before the PTI’s planned long march, the prime minister and the president formed a committee last week to negotiate with the PTI and other opposition parties over the march, while expressing concern over the province’s deteriorating law and order situation.
The government and opposition parties held negotiations over two days, and the talks initially appeared to be bearing fruit. However, just as the two sides were nearing agreement on most of the contentious issues, a deadlock emerged, bringing the negotiation process to a halt.
The government blamed the K-P government, particularly Afridi, for the deadlock and failure of the negotiations. The PTI, however, claimed that the talks broke down over its demand for a meeting with the party’s founder, which the government refused to accept.
As the negotiation process collapsed, CM Afridi began his long march towards Islamabad, further escalating tensions between the two sides, with both sides continuing to trade allegations.
As tensions peaked, PM Shehbaz once again entered the fray and extended an olive branch to the PTI, saying the government was prepared to engage with the opposition if the party ended its long march and sit-ins.
The PTI, however, rejected the offer as its march continued towards Islamabad, entering its fourth day on Wednesday. The convoy moved from Mattani towards Khyber, with Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa Chief Minister Sohail Afridi leading the procession.

items.title: Jaipur couple started with rented cows; now runs Rs 2.4 crore sustainable farm
items.summary: Founded in 2018 by Vibhor Jain and Ishita Jain, Kinaya Organic Farms began with a handful of Gir cows. Fast forward to today, they operate a flourishing farm with 100 cows, branching into a variety of dairy products and agroforestry practices. Their sustainable approach incorporates cow dung biogas, rainwater management, and solar energy, ensuring a self-sufficient model that yields impressive annual profits while promoting environmental stewardship.
